Using a simple Hebb-type learning rule in conjunc(cid:173) tion with the cortical dynamics which emerge from the anatomical and physiological organiza(cid:173) tion of the model, the simulations are capable of establishing cortical representations for differ(cid:173) ent input patterns. The basis of these representations lies in the interaction of sparsely distribut(cid:173) ed, highly divergent/convergent interconnections between modeled neurons. We have shown that different representations can be stored with minimal interference. and that following learning these representations are resistant to input degradation, allowing reconstruction of a representa(cid:173) tion following only a partial presentation of an original training stimulus. paragraphs: The paper builds a computer model of olfactory cortex using anatomical and physiological evidence. Its purpose is to connect the organization of this brain region with its ability to store and retrieve odor information. The simulation reproduces patterns of activity across both space and time under several conditions.

Learning combines a simple Hebbian rule with the activity dynamics produced by the modeled circuitry. Representations emerge through sparse connections that spread signals to many neurons and gather signals from many others. The simulations show that different input patterns can acquire distinct cortical representations while causing little interference with previously stored representations.

After learning, an incomplete version of an input can recover its fuller cortical representation. The model also allows the overlap between representations to change: similar inputs can become more distinguishable, while dissimilar inputs can acquire overlapping representations. These results connect reliable retrieval with flexible classification. The proposed circuitry can support both remembering an odor from partial evidence and adjusting which odors are treated as related.
summary.tldr: A biologically grounded olfactory-cortex simulation learns odor representations that support partial-input recall and flexible discrimination.

title: A Computer Simulation of Olfactory Cortex with Functional Implications for Storage and Retrieval of Olfactory Information

paragraphs: The paper proposes unsupervised learning that reduces redundancy among output neurons while preserving information from sensory inputs. Its goal goes beyond removing ordinary pairwise correlations. By accounting for higher-order statistical structure, the model seeks output components that are probabilistically independent without requiring Gaussian distributions at either the input or the output.

The architecture uses a volume-preserving transformation, which also preserves entropy in the formulation presented. Learning minimizes mutual information among the output neurons, reducing how much one output reveals about another. These two elements serve complementary purposes: the transformation preserves the input information, while the objective reorganizes that information into less redundant components.

The authors connect this framework to generalized principal component analysis and to the idea that cognition reduces redundancy. With nonlinear units, they describe nonlinear principal component analysis and reduction of nonlinear manifolds to their minimum dimension. The central contribution is an information-theoretic account of feature extraction that considers dependencies beyond covariance while explicitly making information preservation part of the architecture.
summary.tldr: An information-preserving network reduces higher-order statistical dependencies to extract independent features without assuming Gaussian data.

title: Higher Order Statistical Decorrelation without Information Loss

abstract: We propose a new learning method, "Generalized Learning Vec(cid:173) tor Quantization (GLVQ)," in which reference vectors are updated based on the steepest descent method in order to minimize the cost function . The cost function is determined so that the obtained learning rule satisfies the convergence condition. We prove that Kohonen's rule as used in LVQ does not satisfy the convergence condition and thus degrades recognition ability. Experimental re(cid:173) sults for printed Chinese character recognition reveal that GLVQ is superior to LVQ in recognition ability.

The cost function is determined so that the obtained learning rule satisfies the convergence condition. We prove that Kohonen's rule as used in LVQ does not satisfy the convergence condition and thus degrades recognition ability. paragraphs: The paper introduces Generalized Learning Vector Quantization, or GLVQ, as a way to train reference vectors for recognition. Reference vectors serve as representative points used by the classifier. Moving them during learning changes how the classifier organizes its input space, so the update rule directly affects recognition performance.

GLVQ derives those movements from a cost function and uses steepest descent to reduce it. The cost is selected so that the resulting learning rule satisfies a convergence condition. This gives the updates an explicit optimization basis. The authors also prove that Kohonen's rule, as used in LVQ, fails to satisfy that condition and associate this failure with degraded recognition.

Experiments on printed Chinese character recognition show better recognition with GLVQ than with LVQ. The result connects the mathematical design of the update rule with a practical classification benefit. The paper's main contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of the existing rule and a replacement whose cost function is constructed to support convergence.
summary.tldr: GLVQ derives reference-vector updates from a convergence-compatible objective and improves printed Chinese character recognition over LVQ.

title: Generalized Learning Vector Quantization

However, direct experimental evidence for the existence of such gradients has only emerged since 1995. The new data has provoked the discussion of a new set of models in the ex(cid:173) perimentalliterature. Here, the capabilities of these models are an(cid:173) alyzed, and the gradient shapes they predict in vivo are derived.

paragraphs: The paper examines how an ordered map can initially form between the retina and the tectum without depending on neural activity. The explanation under study relies on matching molecular cues whose expression changes across these structures. Such gradients could supply positional information, allowing the arrangement of connections to reflect spatial organization.

Experimental evidence for the existence of these gradients had motivated a new set of models in the experimental literature. The authors analyze what those models can accomplish and derive the gradient shapes they predict in living tissue. This turns the general idea of molecular matching into more specific consequences that distinguish the proposed accounts.

The contribution is therefore an analysis of candidate mechanisms and their predicted biological patterns. Establishing that gradients exist leaves a further question: which gradient arrangements can support the proposed mapping mechanisms? By deriving those arrangements, the paper connects models of initial map formation to the molecular distributions they would require or predict. Its scope is specifically the early, activity-independent formation of the map.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes molecular-gradient models of initial retinotectal mapping and derives their predicted gradient shapes.

title: Gradients for Retinotectal Mapping

abstract: We propose a new in-sample cross validation based method (randomized GACV) for choosing smoothing or bandwidth parameters that govern the bias-variance or fit-complexity tradeoff in 'soft' classification. Soft clas(cid:173) sification refers to a learning procedure which estimates the probability that an example with a given attribute vector is in class 1 vs class O. The target for optimizing the the tradeoff is the Kullback-Liebler distance between the estimated probability distribution and the 'true' probabil(cid:173) ity distribution, representing knowledge of an infinite population. The method uses a randomized estimate of the trace of a Hessian and mimics cross validation at the cost of a single relearning with perturbed outcome data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes randomized GACV, a method for choosing smoothing or bandwidth parameters in probabilistic binary classification. Here the learner estimates the probability of class membership for a given input. The tuning problem is to balance close agreement with the observed data against the complexity of the fitted probability function.

The target is Kullback-Leibler distance between the estimated probability distribution and the true population distribution. This makes the quality of the probability estimates central to parameter selection. The method uses an in-sample approximation to cross-validation to guide that choice, connecting the fit-complexity tradeoff to the population-level probability target.

Its computational device is a randomized estimate of the trace of a Hessian, a quantity describing aspects of the fitted objective's curvature. The procedure mimics cross-validation using a single additional learning run with perturbed outcomes. The contribution is therefore a way to approximate a validation-based tuning calculation at the cost of that one relearning step, while directing the choice toward the stated distributional objective.
summary.tldr: Randomized GACV tunes probabilistic classifiers by approximating cross-validation with one relearning step on perturbed outcomes.

title: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff and the Randomized GACV

abstract: This paper describes a simple and efficient method to make template-based object classification invariant to in-plane rotations. The task is divided into two parts: orientation discrimination and classification. The key idea is to perform the orientation discrimination before the classification. This can be accom(cid:173) plished by hypothesizing, in turn, that the input image belongs to each class of interest. The image can then be rotated to maximize its similarity to the train(cid:173) ing images in each class (these contain the prototype object in an upright orien(cid:173) tation). This process yields a set of images, at least one of which will have the object in an upright position. The resulting images can then be classified by models which have been trained with only upright examples. This approach has been successfully applied to two real-world vision-based tasks: rotated handwritten digit recognition and rotated face detection in cluttered scenes.

paragraphs: This paper makes template-based classification insensitive to rotations within the image plane by handling orientation before classification. The training images contain upright examples. The method uses those examples to generate candidate orientations of an input, allowing the later classifier to work with the upright views it was trained to recognize.

Orientation is estimated separately under each possible class hypothesis. For a given class, the input image is rotated to maximize similarity to that class's training images. Repeating this process produces several candidate images. The paper states that at least one of these views places the object upright, after which models trained only on upright examples can classify the candidates.

The authors report successful applications to rotated handwritten digit recognition and rotated face detection in cluttered scenes. The approach matters because it gives orientation discrimination an explicit role before the final recognition decision. Its class-dependent alignment procedure provides a simple, efficient route for using upright templates when the objects presented at recognition time may have arbitrary in-plane rotations.
summary.tldr: Class-specific rotation alignment lets classifiers trained on upright examples recognize rotated digits and detect rotated faces.

title: Making Templates Rotationally Invariant. An Application to Rotated Digit Recognition

abstract: Missing data is common in real-world datasets and is a problem for many estimation techniques. We have developed a variational Bayesian method to perform Independent Component Analysis (ICA) on high-dimensional data containing missing entries. Missing data are handled naturally in the Bayesian framework by integrating the generative density model. Mod- eling the distributions of the independent sources with mixture of Gaus- sians allows sources to be estimated with different kurtosis and skewness. The variational Bayesian method automatically determines the dimen- sionality of the data and yields an accurate density model for the ob- served data without overﬁtting problems. This allows direct probability estimation of missing values in the high dimensional space and avoids dimension reduction preprocessing which is not feasible with missing data.

The variational Bayesian method automatically determines the dimen- sionality of the data and yields an accurate density model for the ob- served data without overﬁtting problems. paragraphs: The paper develops independent component analysis for high-dimensional datasets containing missing entries. Rather than requiring a complete dataset before estimating independent sources, the method handles unobserved entries within a Bayesian generative model. Integrating that model allows learning to proceed using the information that is actually observed.

Each independent source has a distribution modeled by a mixture of Gaussians. This flexibility allows the sources to differ in skewness and kurtosis, capturing different distribution shapes. Variational Bayesian learning also automatically determines the data's dimensionality. The authors describe the resulting density model as accurate for the observed data and free of overfitting problems.

The learned density supports direct probability estimation for missing values in the original high-dimensional space. That is useful because the output can describe uncertainty about an absent entry rather than only supplying a replacement value. The approach also avoids a separate dimensionality-reduction preprocessing step, which the abstract identifies as infeasible with missing data. Missing-value inference and representation learning are thus handled within the same framework.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian ICA learns flexible source distributions from incomplete high-dimensional data and estimates probabilities for missing values.

title: Handling Missing Data with Variational Bayesian Learning of ICA

abstract: The decision functions constructed by support vector machines (SVM’s) usually depend only on a subset of the training set—the so-called support vectors. We derive asymptotically sharp lower and upper bounds on the number of support vectors for several standard types of SVM’s. In par- ticular, we show for the Gaussian RBF kernel that the fraction of support vectors tends to twice the Bayes risk for the L1-SVM, to the probability of noise for the L2-SVM, and to 1 for the LS-SVM.
originalAbstract: The decision functions constructed by support vector machines (SVM’s) usually depend only on a subset of the training set—the so-called support vectors. We derive asymptotically sharp lower and upper bounds on the number of support vectors for several standard types of SVM’s. In par- ticular, we show for the Gaussian RBF kernel that the fraction of support vectors tends to twice the Bayes risk for the L1-SVM, to the probability of noise for the L2-SVM, and to 1 for the LS-SVM.

paragraphs: An SVM’s decision function usually depends on only some training examples, called support vectors. This paper investigates how large that subset is for several standard SVM formulations. Rather than treating sparsity as a general property shared equally by all SVMs, it derives lower and upper bounds on the number of support vectors.

The bounds are asymptotically sharp, addressing behavior as the amount of training data grows. For Gaussian radial basis function kernels, the paper gives distinct limiting fractions: twice the Bayes risk for the L1-SVM, the probability of noise for the L2-SVM, and one for the least-squares SVM.

These results connect the retained fraction of training examples to both the SVM formulation and properties of the classification problem. In particular, a limiting fraction of one means that the least-squares formulation approaches using all training examples as support vectors in the stated setting. The conclusions describe asymptotic behavior for the specified kernel, rather than exact support-vector counts for an arbitrary finite dataset.
summary.tldr: Sharp asymptotic bounds show that Gaussian-kernel SVM variants retain different support-vector fractions tied to Bayes risk, noise probability, or the full dataset.

title: Sparseness of Support Vector Machines---Some Asymptotically Sharp Bounds

abstract: Experimental studies have observed synaptic potentiation when a presynaptic neuron fires shortly before a postsynaptic neuron, and synaptic depression when the presynaptic neuron fires shortly after. The dependence of synaptic modulation on the precise timing of the two action potentials is known as spike-timing dependent plasticity or STDP. We derive STDP from a simple computational principle: synapses adapt so as to minimize the postsynaptic neuron’s variability to a given presynaptic input, causing the neuron’s output to become more reliable in the face of noise. Using an entropy-minimization objective function and the biophysically realistic spike-response model of Gerstner (2001), we simulate neurophysiological experiments and obtain the characteristic STDP curve along with other phenomena including the reduction in synaptic plasticity as synaptic efficacy increases. We compare our account to other efforts to derive STDP from computational principles, and argue that our account provides the most comprehensive coverage of the phenomena. Thus, reliability of neural response in the face of noise may be a key goal of cortical adaptation.

paragraphs: The paper explains spike-timing-dependent plasticity through a proposed computational goal: making a neuron's response to a given input more reliable despite noise. In the experimental pattern it addresses, a synapse strengthens when the presynaptic neuron fires shortly before the postsynaptic neuron and weakens when that order is reversed.

The authors formulate learning as entropy minimization and use a biophysically realistic spike-response model. Their simulations of neurophysiological experiments recover the characteristic relationship between spike timing and synaptic change. They also reproduce other phenomena, including a reduction in plasticity as synaptic efficacy increases. These results connect a reliability objective to several observed features of synaptic adaptation.

The paper compares this explanation with other attempts to derive the timing rule from computational principles, and the authors argue that their account covers the phenomena most comprehensively. Their broader interpretation is that reliable responses in noisy conditions may be an important goal of cortical adaptation. That biological conclusion remains a proposed explanation supported by the model and its simulated behavior.
summary.tldr: Minimizing response variability produces STDP-like learning in simulations, suggesting neural reliability as a possible goal of cortical adaptation.

title: Reducing Spike Train Variability: A Computational Theory Of Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity

abstract: We propose a new Bayesian method for spatial cluster detection, the “Bayesian spatial scan statistic,” and compare this method to the standard (frequentist) scan statistic approach. We demonstrate that the Bayesian statistic has several advantages over the frequentist approach, including increased power to detect clusters and (since randomization testing is unnecessary) much faster runtime. We evaluate the Bayesian and fre- quentist methods on the task of prospective disease surveillance: detect- ing spatial clusters of disease cases resulting from emerging disease out- breaks. We demonstrate that our Bayesian methods are successful in rapidly detecting outbreaks while keeping number of false positives low.

We demonstrate that the Bayesian statistic has several advantages over the frequentist approach, including increased power to detect clusters and (since randomization testing is unnecessary) much faster runtime. We evaluate the Bayesian and fre- quentist methods on the task of prospective disease surveillance: detect- ing spatial clusters of disease cases resulting from emerging disease out- breaks. We demonstrate that our Bayesian methods are successful in rapidly detecting outbreaks while keeping number of false positives low.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the problem of detecting geographic concentrations of events, with emerging disease outbreaks as its application. A useful detector must recognize an unusual concentration quickly while avoiding too many false alarms. The authors introduce a Bayesian spatial scan statistic and compare it with the standard frequentist scan statistic for this task.

The proposed method changes the statistical approach used to assess spatial clusters. One practical advantage is that it does not require randomization testing. Eliminating that step makes the method much faster in the reported comparison. The authors also demonstrate increased power to detect clusters, meaning that the gain in runtime accompanies an improvement in detection capability.

The evaluation concerns prospective disease surveillance: identifying outbreaks as cases emerge. The Bayesian methods rapidly detect outbreaks while maintaining a low number of false positives in that evaluation. These findings matter because surveillance depends on both timely warnings and manageable false alarms; the reported results support the method on both dimensions.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian spatial scan method improves cluster detection power and runtime while rapidly detecting disease outbreaks with few false positives in the reported evaluation.

title: A Bayesian Spatial Scan Statistic

abstract: This paper presents representation and logic for labeling contrast edges and ridges in visual scenes in terms of both surface occlusion (border ownership) and thinline objects. In natural scenes, thinline objects in- clude sticks and wires, while in human graphical communication thin- lines include connectors, dividers, and other abstract devices. Our analy- sis is directed at both natural and graphical domains. The basic problem is to formulate the logic of the interactions among local image events, speciﬁcally contrast edges, ridges, junctions, and alignment relations, such as to encode the natural constraints among these events in visual scenes. In a sparse heterogeneous Markov Random Field framework, we deﬁne a set of interpretation nodes and energy/potential functions among them. The minimum energy conﬁguration found by Loopy Belief Prop- agation is shown to correspond to preferred human interpretation across a wide range of prototypical examples including important illusory con- tour ﬁgures such as the Kanizsa Triangle, as well as more difﬁcult ex- amples. In practical terms, the approach delivers correct interpretations of inherently ambiguous hand-drawn box-and-connector diagrams at low computational cost.

paragraphs: An image contour may mark the boundary of an occluding surface or represent a thin object such as a wire. Similar ambiguities arise in diagrams, where lines can be connectors or dividers. This paper develops representations and logic for assigning these interpretations to contrast edges and ridges in both natural and graphical scenes.

The approach encodes constraints among local image events, including edges, ridges, junctions, and alignments. It uses a sparse, heterogeneous Markov random field containing interpretation nodes and energy functions that express relationships between them. Loopy belief propagation is used to find a minimum-energy configuration representing a coordinated interpretation of the scene.

Across a range of prototypical examples, the resulting configurations agree with preferred human interpretations. These examples include illusory contours such as the Kanizsa Triangle and more difficult cases. The method also correctly interprets ambiguous hand-drawn box-and-connector diagrams at low computational cost. The results show how local visual constraints can support coherent contour labeling in the examples studied.
summary.tldr: A Markov random field encodes contour relationships to interpret occlusion and thin lines, matching human preferences in studied examples and resolving ambiguous diagrams.

title: Logic and MRF Circuitry for Labeling Occluding and Thinline Visual Contours

abstract: We consider apprenticeship learning—learning from expert demonstrations—in the setting of large, complex domains. Past work in apprenticeship learning requires that the expert demonstrate complete trajectories through the domain. However, in many problems even an expert has difﬁculty controlling the system, which makes this approach infeasible. For example, consider the task of teach- ing a quadruped robot to navigate over extreme terrain; demonstrating an optimal policy (i.e., an optimal set of foot locations over the entire terrain) is a highly non-trivial task, even for an expert. In this paper we propose a method for hier- archical apprenticeship learning, which allows the algorithm to accept isolated advice at different hierarchical levels of the control task. This type of advice is often feasible for experts to give, even if the expert is unable to demonstrate com- plete trajectories. This allows us to extend the apprenticeship learning paradigm to much larger, more challenging domains. In particular, in this paper we apply the hierarchical apprenticeship learning algorithm to the task of quadruped loco- motion over extreme terrain, and achieve, to the best of our knowledge, results superior to any previously published work.

paragraphs: Learning from expert demonstrations becomes difficult when even the expert cannot reliably demonstrate an entire task. The paper highlights quadruped locomotion over extreme terrain: specifying a complete sequence of optimal foot placements is itself demanding. Requiring complete trajectories can therefore prevent apprenticeship learning from being used in precisely the complex domains where expert knowledge would help.

The proposed method accepts isolated advice at different levels of a control hierarchy. This lets an expert contribute useful guidance without providing a complete execution from beginning to end. The hierarchy organizes how advice enters the control task, expanding the form of supervision that an apprenticeship-learning algorithm can use.

The authors apply the method to quadruped locomotion over extreme terrain and report results superior to previously published work, to the best of their knowledge. The broader contribution is an approach to using partial expert guidance in large, challenging domains. Its practical significance comes from making learning possible when complete demonstrations are difficult for the expert to supply.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical apprenticeship learning uses isolated expert advice at multiple control levels to teach quadruped locomotion over extreme terrain.

title: Hierarchical Apprenticeship Learning with Application to Quadruped Locomotion

abstract: We present a new reinforcement-learning model for the role of the hippocampus in classical conditioning, focusing on the differences between trace and delay conditioning. In the model, all stimuli are represented both as unindividuated wholes and as a series of temporal elements with varying delays. These two stimulus representations interact, producing different patterns of learning in trace and delay conditioning. The model proposes that hippocampal lesions eliminate long-latency temporal elements, but preserve short-latency temporal elements. For trace conditioning, with no contiguity between stimulus and reward, these long-latency temporal elements are vital to learning adaptively timed responses. For delay conditioning, in contrast, the continued presence of the stimulus supports conditioned responding, and the short-latency elements suppress responding early in the stimulus. In accord with the empirical data, simulated hippocampal damage impairs trace conditioning, but not delay conditioning, at medium-length intervals. With longer intervals, learning is impaired in both procedures, and, with shorter intervals, in neither. In addition, the model makes novel predictions about the response topography with extended stimuli or post-training lesions. These results demonstrate how temporal contiguity, as in delay conditioning, changes the timing problem faced by animals, rendering it both easier and less susceptible to disruption by hippocampal lesions.
originalAbstract: We present a new reinforcement-learning model for the role of the hippocampus in classical conditioning, focusing on the differences between trace and delay conditioning. In the model, all stimuli are represented both as unindividuated wholes and as a series of temporal elements with varying delays. These two stimulus representations interact, producing different patterns of learning in trace and delay conditioning. The model proposes that hippocampal lesions eliminate long-latency temporal elements, but preserve short-latency temporal elements. For trace conditioning, with no contiguity between stimulus and reward, these long-latency temporal elements are vital to learning adaptively timed responses. For delay conditioning, in contrast, the continued presence of the stimulus supports conditioned responding, and the short-latency elements suppress responding early in the stimulus. In accord with the empirical data, simulated hippocampal damage impairs trace conditioning, but not delay conditioning, at medium-length intervals. With longer intervals, learning is impaired in both procedures, and, with shorter intervals, in neither. In addition, the model makes novel predictions about the response topography with extended stimuli or post-training lesions. These results demonstrate how temporal contiguity, as in delay conditioning, changes the timing problem faced by animals, rendering it both easier and less susceptible to disruption by hippocampal lesions.

paragraphs: This paper models how the hippocampus helps animals learn when to respond to a stimulus that predicts reward. Its central comparison is between trace conditioning, where a gap separates stimulus and reward, and delay conditioning, where the stimulus remains present. The model uses reinforcement learning to explain why these situations respond differently to hippocampal damage.

Each stimulus has two interacting representations: an overall representation and a collection of temporal elements active at different delays. The proposed effect of hippocampal lesions is to remove long-delay elements while leaving short-delay elements intact. Bridging a trace interval requires the longer-delay elements. During delay conditioning, the ongoing stimulus supports responding, while shorter-delay elements help suppress responses that would occur too early.

Simulated damage disrupts trace but not delay conditioning at intermediate intervals, matching the empirical pattern described in the abstract. Longer intervals produce impairment in both procedures; shorter intervals produce neither. The model also predicts changes in response patterns with extended stimuli or lesions after training. Its explanation ties susceptibility to damage to the particular timing demands imposed by stimulus continuity.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learning model explains interval-dependent effects of hippocampal damage through interacting stimulus representations with different temporal delays.

title: A computational model of hippocampal function in trace conditioning

abstract: We consider the problem of using nearest neighbor methods to provide a conditional probability estimate, P(y|a), when the number of labels y is large and the labels share some underlying structure. We propose a method for learning error-correcting output codes (ECOCs) to model the similarity between labels within a nearest neighbor framework. The learned ECOCs and nearest neighbor information are used to provide conditional probability estimates. We apply these estimates to the problem of acoustic modeling for speech recognition. We demonstrate an absolute reduction in word error rate (WER) of 0.9% (a 2.5% relative reduction in WER) on a lecture recognition task over a state-of-the-art baseline GMM model.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor methods use nearby examples to help predict an input's label. This paper considers a setting with many possible labels that share underlying structure. Its objective is to estimate the probability of each label given an input, so the prediction expresses uncertainty as well as identifying plausible categories.

The proposed method learns error-correcting output codes that represent similarities among labels. These learned representations are combined with nearest-neighbor information to produce conditional probability estimates. The key idea is to incorporate relationships between output categories into a method that also uses proximity among examples. This gives label structure a direct role in the probability estimation process.

The authors apply the estimates to acoustic modeling for speech recognition. On a lecture recognition task, they report a word error rate reduction of 0.9 percentage points, equivalent to a 2.5% relative reduction, against a state-of-the-art Gaussian mixture model baseline. The result demonstrates a benefit for the reported speech task from combining learned label relationships with neighborhood information.
summary.tldr: Learned label codes improve nearest-neighbor probability estimates and reduce word error rate in a lecture recognition task.

title: Learning Label Embeddings for Nearest-Neighbor Multi-class Classification with an Application to Speech Recognition

abstract: We present a novel feature selection algorithm for the $k$-means clustering problem. Our algorithm is randomized and, assuming an accuracy parameter $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, selects and appropriately rescales in an unsupervised manner $\Theta(k \log(k / \epsilon) / \epsilon^2)$ features from a dataset of arbitrary dimensions. We prove that, if we run any $\gamma$-approximate $k$-means algorithm ($\gamma \geq 1$) on the features selected using our method, we can find a $(1+(1+\epsilon)\gamma)$-approximate partition with high probability.

Our algorithm is randomized and, assuming an accuracy parameter $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, selects and appropriately rescales in an unsupervised manner $\Theta(k \log(k / \epsilon) / \epsilon^2)$ features from a dataset of arbitrary dimensions. We prove that, if we run any $\gamma$-approximate $k$-means algorithm ($\gamma \geq 1$) on the features selected using our method, we can find a $(1+(1+\epsilon)\gamma)$-approximate partition with high probability.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select a smaller set of features while preserving a useful guarantee for k-means clustering. The selection is unsupervised, so it does not require class labels. The proposed randomized algorithm chooses existing features and rescales them, producing a reduced representation on which a clustering algorithm can operate.

For an accuracy parameter epsilon between zero and one, the number of selected features is on the order of k log(k/epsilon) divided by epsilon squared. This bound depends on the requested number of clusters and the accuracy parameter, rather than the dataset's original feature dimension. It makes explicit how demanding a tighter accuracy setting affects the representation size.

The guarantee also accounts for the clustering algorithm used afterward. If that algorithm is a gamma-approximation, the selected features allow a partition with approximation factor 1 + (1 + epsilon) gamma, with high probability. The result therefore quantifies how randomized feature reduction and approximate clustering compose. It supports a reduced-feature workflow while explicitly tracking the resulting quality bound.
summary.tldr: Randomized feature selection and rescaling reduce dimensionality while preserving a high-probability approximation guarantee for subsequent k-means clustering.

title: Unsupervised Feature Selection for the $k$-means Clustering Problem

abstract: Many problems in machine learning and statistics can be formulated as (generalized) eigenproblems. In terms of the associated optimization problem, computing linear eigenvectors amounts to finding critical points of a quadratic function subject to quadratic constraints. In this paper we show that a certain class of constrained optimization problems with nonquadratic objective and constraints can be understood as nonlinear eigenproblems. We derive a generalization of the inverse power method which is guaranteed to converge to a nonlinear eigenvector. We apply the inverse power method to 1-spectral clustering and sparse PCA which can naturally be formulated as nonlinear eigenproblems. In both applications we achieve state-of-the-art results in terms of solution quality and runtime. Moving beyond the standard eigenproblem should be useful also in many other applications and our inverse power method can be easily adapted to new problems.

Moving beyond the standard eigenproblem should be useful also in many other applications and our inverse power method can be easily adapted to new problems.

paragraphs: Many learning problems can be expressed as eigenproblems, connecting them to established numerical methods. Ordinary linear eigenvectors also have an optimization interpretation: they correspond to critical points of quadratic objectives under quadratic constraints. This paper extends that perspective to a particular class of problems whose objectives and constraints are nonquadratic.

The authors show how these problems can be understood as nonlinear eigenproblems and develop a corresponding generalization of the inverse power method. Their algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a nonlinear eigenvector. This guarantee concerns reaching an eigenvector within the proposed framework; it does not assert that every resulting solution is a global optimum of the associated optimization problem.

They apply the method to 1-spectral clustering and sparse principal component analysis, both of which fit naturally into the nonlinear formulation. For these applications, they report state-of-the-art solution quality and runtime. The broader contribution is a reusable connection between nonquadratic optimization and eigenvector computation, with the authors proposing that the method can be adapted to additional problems.
summary.tldr: A generalized inverse power method converges to nonlinear eigenvectors and achieves strong reported results in 1-spectral clustering and sparse PCA.

title: An Inverse Power Method for Nonlinear Eigenproblems with Applications in 1-Spectral Clustering and Sparse PCA

abstract: We derive algorithms for generalised tensor factorisation (GTF) by building upon the well-established theory of Generalised Linear Models. Our algorithms are general in the sense that we can compute arbitrary factorisations in a message passing framework, derived for a broad class of exponential family distributions including special cases such as Tweedie's distributions corresponding to $\beta$-divergences. By bounding the step size of the Fisher Scoring iteration of the GLM, we obtain general updates for real data and multiplicative updates for non-negative data. The GTF framework is, then extended easily to address the problems when multiple observed tensors are factorised simultaneously. We illustrate our coupled factorisation approach on synthetic data as well as on a musical audio restoration problem.

paragraphs: The paper develops a general framework for tensor factorization using the theory of generalized linear models. Tensor factorization represents multidimensional observations through constituent factors. The authors seek algorithms that accommodate different factorization structures and observation distributions within a common computational framework, rather than treating each combination as a separate problem.

Their algorithms use message passing and cover a broad class of exponential-family distributions. This includes Tweedie distributions associated with beta divergences. By bounding the step size in the GLM Fisher Scoring iteration, the authors derive updates for real-valued data and multiplicative updates for nonnegative data. The statistical model and update rules are therefore developed together.

The framework extends to coupled factorization, in which multiple observed tensors are factorized simultaneously. This makes the same approach applicable when the task involves several related arrays rather than a single tensor. The paper illustrates coupled factorization on synthetic data and a musical audio restoration problem, demonstrating uses of the framework across controlled examples and an audio application.
summary.tldr: A GLM-based message-passing framework derives updates for general tensor factorizations and extends to jointly factorizing multiple tensors.

title: Generalised Coupled Tensor Factorisation

abstract: Probabilistic logics are receiving a lot of attention today because of their expressive power for knowledge representation and learning. However, this expressivity is detrimental to the tractability of inference, when done at the propositional level. To solve this problem, various lifted inference algorithms have been proposed that reason at the first-order level, about groups of objects as a whole. Despite the existence of various lifted inference approaches, there are currently no completeness results about these algorithms. The key contribution of this paper is that we introduce a formal definition of lifted inference that allows us to reason about the completeness of lifted inference algorithms relative to a particular class of probabilistic models. We then show how to obtain a completeness result using a first-order knowledge compilation approach for theories of formulae containing up to two logical variables.

paragraphs: Probabilistic logics offer expressive ways to represent knowledge, but inference can become difficult when reasoning is carried out at the propositional level. Lifted inference addresses this difficulty by reasoning about groups of objects together at the first-order level. The paper investigates how to establish the scope within which such an inference method is complete.

The first contribution is a formal definition of lifted inference that makes completeness assessable relative to a specified class of probabilistic models. This provides a basis for asking whether an algorithm covers an entire class, rather than simply demonstrating successful reasoning on individual examples. The definition turns a broad methodological idea into a property that can support a theorem.

Using first-order knowledge compilation, the authors establish a completeness result for theories whose formulas contain up to two logical variables. The two-variable scope is central to what is proved. The result supplies a formal guarantee for that class and demonstrates how knowledge compilation can be used to analyze the coverage of lifted probabilistic inference.
summary.tldr: A formal definition of lifted inference enables a knowledge-compilation completeness result for theories with up to two logical variables per formula.

title: On the Completeness of First-Order Knowledge Compilation for Lifted Probabilistic Inference

abstract: Graph cut optimization is one of the standard workhorses of image segmentation since for binary random field representations of the image, it gives globally optimal results and there are efficient polynomial time implementations. Often, the random field is applied over a flat partitioning of the image into non-intersecting elements, such as pixels or super-pixels. In the paper we show that if, instead of a flat partitioning, the image is represented by a hierarchical segmentation tree, then the resulting energy combining unary and boundary terms can still be optimized using graph cut (with all the corresponding benefits of global optimality and efficiency). As a result of such inference, the image gets partitioned into a set of segments that may come from different layers of the tree. We apply this formulation, which we call the pylon model, to the task of semantic segmentation where the goal is to separate an image into areas belonging to different semantic classes. The experiments highlight the advantage of inference on a segmentation tree (over a flat partitioning) and demonstrate that the optimization in the pylon model is able to flexibly choose the level of segmentation across the image. Overall, the proposed system has superior segmentation accuracy on several datasets (Graz-02, Stanford background) compared to previously suggested approaches.

paragraphs: Image segmentation often starts from a flat collection of pixels or superpixels and assigns labels to those elements. The pylon model instead represents an image as a hierarchy of candidate segments. This makes it possible for the final partition to use regions from different levels of detail in different parts of the image.

The authors show that an energy combining unary and boundary terms on this hierarchical representation can still be optimized by graph cuts, retaining the associated efficiency and global optimality benefits for that formulation. The hierarchy therefore expands the available segmentation choices while preserving a useful optimization structure. Inference selects which segments from the tree form the resulting partition.

The model is applied to semantic segmentation, where regions correspond to semantic classes. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of reasoning over a segmentation tree and show that the method can flexibly choose segmentation levels across an image. The reported system achieves higher segmentation accuracy than previous approaches on Graz-02 and Stanford background, supporting the usefulness of this adaptive regional representation.
summary.tldr: The pylon model uses graph cuts on a segmentation hierarchy to select region detail flexibly and improve reported semantic segmentation accuracy.

title: Pylon Model for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Multi-metric learning techniques learn local metric tensors in different parts of a feature space. With such an approach, even simple classifiers can be competitive with the state-of-the-art because the distance measure locally adapts to the structure of the data. The learned distance measure is, however, non-metric, which has prevented multi-metric learning from generalizing to tasks such as dimensionality reduction and regression in a principled way. We prove that, with appropriate changes, multi-metric learning corresponds to learning the structure of a Riemannian manifold. We then show that this structure gives us a principled way to perform dimensionality reduction and regression according to the learned metrics. Algorithmically, we provide the first practical algorithm for computing geodesics according to the learned metrics, as well as algorithms for computing exponential and logarithmic maps on the Riemannian manifold. Together, these tools let many Euclidean algorithms take advantage of multi-metric learning. We illustrate the approach on regression and dimensionality reduction tasks that involve predicting measurements of the human body from shape data.

paragraphs: Multi-metric learning adapts the meaning of distance to different parts of a feature space. This can make even simple classifiers competitive because nearby relationships reflect local data structure. The difficulty is that the resulting distance measure is non-metric, which has obstructed principled extensions to regression and dimensionality reduction.

The paper proves that, after appropriate changes, learning these local metrics can be understood as learning a Riemannian manifold. This supplies a coherent geometric interpretation of the learned structure. It also provides a basis for defining operations needed to move beyond classification while respecting how distances vary across the space.

The authors give a practical algorithm for computing geodesics, together with algorithms for exponential and logarithmic maps. These tools let many algorithms originally formulated in Euclidean space use the learned geometry. The approach is illustrated through regression and dimensionality reduction involving predictions of human body measurements from shape data. The contribution combines a geometric foundation with computational tools that make that foundation usable.
summary.tldr: A geometric interpretation of local metric learning provides practical tools for extending it to regression and dimensionality reduction.

title: A Geometric take on Metric Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of sampling from a probability distribution defined over a high-dimensional discrete set, specified for instance by a graphical model. We propose a sampling algorithm, called PAWS, based on embedding the set into a higher-dimensional space which is then randomly projected using universal hash functions to a lower-dimensional subspace and explored using combinatorial search methods. Our scheme can leverage fast combinatorial optimization tools as a blackbox and, unlike MCMC methods, samples produced are guaranteed to be within an (arbitrarily small) constant factor of the true probability distribution. We demonstrate that by using state-of-the-art combinatorial search tools, PAWS can efficiently sample from Ising grids with strong interactions and from software verification instances, while MCMC and variational methods fail in both cases.

We propose a sampling algorithm, called PAWS, based on embedding the set into a higher-dimensional space which is then randomly projected using universal hash functions to a lower-dimensional subspace and explored using combinatorial search methods. Our scheme can leverage fast combinatorial optimization tools as a blackbox and, unlike MCMC methods, samples produced are guaranteed to be within an (arbitrarily small) constant factor of the true probability distribution. paragraphs: Sampling from a probability distribution over many discrete variables can be difficult, including when a graphical model specifies the distribution. The paper introduces PAWS, an algorithm that approaches sampling through transformations of the discrete search space and combinatorial search. Its design allows existing fast combinatorial optimization tools to serve as black-box components.

PAWS first embeds the original set in a higher-dimensional space. It then uses universal hash functions to project randomly into a lower-dimensional subspace, which combinatorial search methods explore. This embed-and-project construction provides a sampling guarantee: the resulting distribution is within an arbitrarily small constant factor of the target probabilities.

The authors demonstrate efficient sampling on strongly interacting Ising grids and software verification instances using state-of-the-art search tools. In those reported cases, MCMC and variational methods fail. The results connect a formal approximation guarantee with practical use of combinatorial solvers, showing that tools developed for discrete search can also support difficult probabilistic sampling tasks.
summary.tldr: PAWS combines universal hashing with combinatorial search to sample discrete distributions with a multiplicative approximation guarantee.

title: Embed and Project: Discrete Sampling with Universal Hashing

abstract: Nonparametric estimation of the conditional distribution of a response given high-dimensional features is a challenging problem. It is important to allow not only the mean but also the variance and shape of the response density to change flexibly with features, which are massive-dimensional. We propose a multiscale dictionary learning model, which expresses the conditional response density as a convex combination of dictionary densities, with the densities used and their weights dependent on the path through a tree decomposition of the feature space. A fast graph partitioning algorithm is applied to obtain the tree decomposition, with Bayesian methods then used to adaptively prune and average over different sub-trees in a soft probabilistic manner. The algorithm scales efficiently to approximately one million features. State of the art predictive performance is demonstrated for toy examples and two neuroscience applications including up to a million features.

We propose a multiscale dictionary learning model, which expresses the conditional response density as a convex combination of dictionary densities, with the densities used and their weights dependent on the path through a tree decomposition of the feature space. A fast graph partitioning algorithm is applied to obtain the tree decomposition, with Bayesian methods then used to adaptively prune and average over different sub-trees in a soft probabilistic manner. paragraphs: Predicting a response can require more than estimating its average. Its variability and the shape of its distribution may also change with the input features. This paper develops a model for estimating that entire conditional distribution when the feature space is extremely large, allowing these different aspects of the response to vary flexibly.

The model represents each conditional density as a weighted combination of dictionary densities, with nonnegative weights that sum to one. Which densities are used, and how much each contributes, depend on a path through a tree decomposition of the feature space. A fast graph partitioning algorithm builds this tree, providing the multiscale organization.

Bayesian methods then prune the tree adaptively and average probabilistically over different subtrees. This allows the model to combine alternatives instead of relying on one fixed tree resolution. The algorithm scales to approximately one million features, and the authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance on toy examples and two neuroscience applications, including settings at that feature scale.
summary.tldr: A tree-organized dictionary of densities estimates flexible conditional distributions and scales to approximately one million features.

title: Multiscale Dictionary Learning for Estimating Conditional Distributions

abstract: Thompson Sampling has been demonstrated in many complex bandit models, however the theoretical guarantees available for the parametric multi-armed bandit are still limited to the Bernoulli case. Here we extend them by proving asymptotic optimality of the algorithm using the Jeffreys prior for $1$-dimensional exponential family bandits. Our proof builds on previous work, but also makes extensive use of closed forms for Kullback-Leibler divergence and Fisher information (and thus Jeffreys prior) available in an exponential family. This allow us to give a finite time exponential concentration inequality for posterior distributions on exponential families that may be of interest in its own right. Moreover our analysis covers some distributions for which no optimistic algorithm has yet been proposed, including heavy-tailed exponential families.

Our proof builds on previous work, but also makes extensive use of closed forms for Kullback-Leibler divergence and Fisher information (and thus Jeffreys prior) available in an exponential family. This allow us to give a finite time exponential concentration inequality for posterior distributions on exponential families that may be of interest in its own right. paragraphs: Thompson Sampling had been demonstrated in complex bandit settings, but the available parametric guarantees discussed in this paper were limited to Bernoulli rewards. The authors extend the theory to one-dimensional exponential-family bandits. Their central result proves asymptotic optimality when the algorithm uses the Jeffreys prior.

The proof uses the structure of exponential families, particularly closed-form expressions for Kullback-Leibler divergence and Fisher information. These quantities also support the construction of the Jeffreys prior. This links the distribution family and prior choice directly to the argument establishing the algorithm's long-run performance.

That result describes posterior concentration and may be useful beyond the bandit proof itself. The covered distributions include some heavy-tailed exponential families for which the authors report that no optimistic algorithm had yet been proposed. The contribution broadens the theoretical foundation of Thompson Sampling while keeping its optimality claim tied to the stated family, prior, and asymptotic setting.
summary.tldr: Thompson Sampling with the Jeffreys prior is asymptotically optimal for one-dimensional exponential-family bandits.

title: Thompson Sampling for 1-Dimensional Exponential Family Bandits

abstract: The ever-increasing size of modern data sets combined with the difficulty of obtaining label information has made semi-supervised learning one of the problems of significant practical importance in modern data analysis. We revisit the approach to semi-supervised learning with generative models and develop new models that allow for effective generalisation from small labelled data sets to large unlabelled ones. Generative approaches have thus far been either inflexible, inefficient or non-scalable. We show that deep generative models and approximate Bayesian inference exploiting recent advances in variational methods can be used to provide significant improvements, making generative approaches highly competitive for semi-supervised learning.
originalAbstract: The ever-increasing size of modern data sets combined with the difficulty of obtaining label information has made semi-supervised learning one of the problems of significant practical importance in modern data analysis. We revisit the approach to semi-supervised learning with generative models and develop new models that allow for effective generalisation from small labelled data sets to large unlabelled ones. Generative approaches have thus far been either inflexible, inefficient or non-scalable. We show that deep generative models and approximate Bayesian inference exploiting recent advances in variational methods can be used to provide significant improvements, making generative approaches highly competitive for semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Large datasets often contain far more examples than reliable labels, making it important to learn from labeled and unlabeled observations together. This paper revisits generative modeling for semi-supervised learning. It develops models intended to generalize effectively from a small labeled collection to a much larger unlabeled one.

The approach combines deep generative models with approximate Bayesian inference based on variational methods. These are the two central ingredients: a flexible model of the data and a practical way to perform inference in that model. The paper positions their combination as a response to earlier generative approaches that were limited by inflexibility, inefficient computation, or difficulty scaling.

The authors report significant improvements that make generative approaches highly competitive for semi-supervised learning. The stated contribution is therefore about making this modeling strategy effective and computationally practical in the scarce-label setting. It connects advances in model representation and inference to the same goal: learning usefully when obtaining labels is much harder than collecting data.
summary.tldr: Deep generative models combined with variational Bayesian inference make generative semi-supervised learning competitive when labeled data are scarce.

title: Semi-supervised Learning with Deep Generative Models

abstract: This paper formulates the search for a set of bounding boxes (as needed in object proposal generation) as a monotone submodular maximization problem over the space of all possible bounding boxes in an image. Since the number of possible bounding boxes in an image is very large $O(#pixels^2)$, even a single linear scan to perform the greedy augmentation for submodular maximization is intractable. Thus, we formulate the greedy augmentation step as a Branch-and-Bound scheme. In order to speed up repeated application of B\&B, we propose a novel generalization of Minoux’s ‘lazy greedy’ algorithm to the B\&B tree. Theoretically, our proposed formulation provides a new understanding to the problem, and contains classic heuristic approaches such as Sliding Window+Non-Maximal Suppression (NMS) and and Efficient Subwindow Search (ESS) as special cases. Empirically, we show that our approach leads to a state-of-art performance on object proposal generation via a novel diversity measure.

Thus, we formulate the greedy augmentation step as a Branch-and-Bound scheme. paragraphs: Object proposal generation searches for bounding boxes that might contain objects in an image. This paper treats the choice of an entire collection of boxes as a monotone submodular maximization problem. That formulation makes the value of adding a box depend on the boxes already selected, providing a framework for choosing a diverse set.

The search space contains quadratically many boxes in the number of pixels, making even a full scan for one greedy addition impractical. The authors replace that scan with a branch-and-bound procedure. They also extend lazy greedy selection to the branch-and-bound tree, aiming to speed up the repeated searches required to build the collection.

The formulation includes sliding windows with non-maximal suppression and Efficient Subwindow Search as special cases, connecting established heuristics within a common framework. Using a new diversity measure, the method achieves reported state-of-the-art empirical performance on object proposal generation. Its contribution combines a set-level objective with a search procedure designed to make greedy selection feasible over a very large space of candidate boxes.
summary.tldr: SubmodBoxes combines submodular selection, branch-and-bound search, and lazy greedy updates to find diverse object proposals efficiently.

title: SubmodBoxes: Near-Optimal Search for a Set of Diverse Object Proposals

abstract: Online allocation problems have been widely studied due to their numerous practical applications (particularly to Internet advertising), as well as considerable theoretical interest. The main challenge in such problems is making assignment decisions in the face of uncertainty about future input; effective algorithms need to predict which constraints are most likely to bind, and learn the balance between short-term gain and the value of long-term resource availability. In many important applications, the algorithm designer is faced with multiple objectives to optimize. In particular, in online advertising it is fairly common to optimize multiple metrics, such as clicks, conversions, and impressions, as well as other metrics which may be largely uncorrelated such as ‘share of voice’, and ‘buyer surplus’. While there has been considerable work on multi-objective offline optimization (when the entire input is known in advance), very little is known about the online case, particularly in the case of adversarial input. In this paper, we give the first results for bi-objective online submodular optimization, providing almost matching upper and lower bounds for allocating items to agents with two submodular value functions. We also study practically relevant special cases of this problem related to Internet advertising, and obtain improved results. All our algorithms are nearly best possible, as well as being efficient and easy to implement in practice.

The paper is motivated by applications such as advertising, where clicks, conversions, impressions, and other measures can create distinct allocation priorities.

Submodularity captures diminishing returns, so the value of another allocation depends on what has already been assigned. They establish almost matching upper and lower bounds for this online problem, addressing a setting where the input may be adversarial rather than conveniently predictable.

The paper also examines special cases relevant to internet advertising and obtains improved results there. The authors describe the algorithms as efficient and straightforward to implement. The contribution is a theoretical account of what can be achieved when uncertain future arrivals and two allocation objectives must be handled together.
summary.tldr: The paper develops nearly optimal algorithms and bounds for online allocation with two submodular objectives, including advertising-related special cases.

title: Bi-Objective Online Matching and Submodular Allocations

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of maximizing continuous submodular functions that naturally arise in many learning applications such as those involving utility functions in active learning and sensing, matrix approximations and network inference. Despite the apparent lack of convexity in such functions, we prove that stochastic projected gradient methods can provide strong approximation guarantees for maximizing continuous submodular functions with convex constraints. More specifically, we prove that for monotone continuous DR-submodular functions, all fixed points of projected gradient ascent provide a factor $1/2$ approximation to the global maxima. We also study stochastic gradient methods and show that after $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations these methods reach solutions which achieve in expectation objective values exceeding $(\frac{\text{OPT}}{2}-\epsilon)$. An immediate application of our results is to maximize submodular functions that are defined stochastically, i.e. the submodular function is defined as an expectation over a family of submodular functions with an unknown distribution. We will show how stochastic gradient methods are naturally well-suited for this setting, leading to a factor $1/2$ approximation when the function is monotone. In particular, it allows us to approximately maximize discrete, monotone submodular optimization problems via projected gradient ascent on a continuous relaxation, directly connecting the discrete and continuous domains. Finally, experiments on real data demonstrate that our projected gradient methods consistently achieve the best utility compared to other continuous baselines while remaining competitive in terms of computational effort.

paragraphs: Submodular objectives express a form of diminishing returns and arise in learning tasks involving utility, sensing, and network inference. Their continuous versions need not have the convexity properties that usually make optimization straightforward. This paper shows that projected gradient methods can nevertheless provide meaningful approximation guarantees for a specified class under convex constraints.

For monotone continuous DR-submodular functions, every fixed point of projected gradient ascent achieves at least half the global optimum. With stochastic gradients, the methods reach an expected objective value above OPT/2 minus ε after O(1/ε²) iterations. The theoretical claims retain their monotonicity and diminishing-returns conditions.
summary.tldr: Projected gradient methods obtain half-optimum approximation guarantees for monotone continuous DR-submodular maximization under convex constraints.

title: Gradient Methods for Submodular Maximization

abstract: Selective classification techniques (also known as reject option) have not yet been considered in the context of deep neural networks (DNNs). These techniques can potentially significantly improve DNNs prediction performance by trading-off coverage. In this paper we propose a method to construct a selective classifier given a trained neural network. Our method allows a user to set a desired risk level. At test time, the classifier rejects instances as needed, to grant the desired risk (with high probability). Empirical results over CIFAR and ImageNet convincingly demonstrate the viability of our method, which opens up possibilities to operate DNNs in mission-critical applications. For example, using our method an unprecedented 2% error in top-5 ImageNet classification can be guaranteed with probability 99.9%, with almost 60% test coverage.

paragraphs: A classifier need not answer every input. Selective classification allows it to reject some cases in exchange for lower error on those it accepts. This paper brings that approach to trained deep neural networks, giving users a way to specify a desired risk level and control the resulting reliability–coverage trade-off.

The proposed method constructs a selective classifier from an existing trained network. At test time, it rejects instances as needed to meet the chosen risk level with high probability. Coverage is the proportion of inputs for which it returns a prediction, so a stronger error requirement can come at the cost of answering fewer cases.

Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate the method's viability. The reported ImageNet example guarantees 2% top-5 classification error with 99.9% probability while retaining almost 60% test coverage. These figures describe error on the accepted predictions together with confidence in the guarantee. The result supports the possibility of using rejection to make deep classifiers more suitable for applications that demand controlled prediction risk.
summary.tldr: A rejection mechanism lets trained neural networks meet a user-selected error target with high probability by reducing prediction coverage.

title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Deep generative models based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated impressive sample quality but in order to work they require a careful choice of architecture, parameter initialization, and selection of hyper-parameters. This fragility is in part due to a dimensional mismatch or non-overlapping support between the model distribution and the data distribution, causing their density ratio and the associated f -divergence to be undefined. We overcome this fundamental limitation and propose a new regularization approach with low computational cost that yields a stable GAN training procedure. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this regularizer accross several architectures trained on common benchmark image generation tasks. Our regularization turns GAN models into reliable building blocks for deep learning.

This fragility is in part due to a dimensional mismatch or non-overlapping support between the model distribution and the data distribution, causing their density ratio and the associated f -divergence to be undefined. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this regularizer accross several architectures trained on common benchmark image generation tasks. Our regularization turns GAN models into reliable building blocks for deep learning.

paragraphs: GANs can generate convincing samples, yet training them often requires careful choices of architecture, initialization, and hyperparameters. This paper connects part of that fragility to a mismatch between the generated and real-data distributions. In particular, the distributions may occupy spaces of different dimensions or have supports that do not overlap.

These mismatches can leave the density ratio and its associated f-divergence undefined. That creates a problem with the mathematical comparison underlying training, beyond the practical difficulty of choosing settings. The authors propose a regularization approach that overcomes this issue and yields stable training, while adding little computational cost to the procedure.

The regularizer is evaluated across several architectures on common image-generation benchmarks, where the authors demonstrate its effectiveness. Testing multiple architectures supports its usefulness beyond one particular network design. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of a source of GAN instability and a low-cost intervention with empirical support, aimed at making adversarial generative models more dependable components of deep-learning systems.
summary.tldr: A low-cost regularizer addresses distribution mismatches that can undermine GAN training and demonstrates stable behavior across several architectures.

title: Stabilizing Training of Generative Adversarial Networks through Regularization

abstract: In sequential decision making, it is often important and useful for end users to understand the underlying patterns or causes that lead to the corresponding decisions. However, typical deep reinforcement learning algorithms seldom provide such information due to their black-box nature. In this paper, we present a probabilistic model, Q-LDA, to uncover latent patterns in text-based sequential decision processes. The model can be understood as a variant of latent topic models that are tailored to maximize total rewards; we further draw an interesting connection between an approximate maximum-likelihood estimation of Q-LDA and the celebrated Q-learning algorithm. We demonstrate in the text-game domain that our proposed method not only provides a viable mechanism to uncover latent patterns in decision processes, but also obtains state-of-the-art rewards in these games.

paragraphs: The paper addresses interpretability in sequential decision making with text. A system may choose effective actions while leaving users unable to see the patterns behind those choices. Q-LDA is a probabilistic model intended to expose latent structure in these decision processes while also pursuing strong reward performance.

The model adapts latent topic modeling to the goal of maximizing total reward. This connects hidden patterns in text to the sequential decision objective, rather than treating text structure as a separate descriptive task. The authors also establish a connection between approximate maximum-likelihood estimation for Q-LDA and Q-learning, linking probabilistic model fitting with a familiar reinforcement-learning algorithm.

Experiments in text games show that the method can uncover latent patterns and achieve rewards described as state of the art. These are complementary findings: the model provides a mechanism for examining decision-related structure while remaining competitive at the task itself. The stated interpretability result concerns discovering latent patterns; it does not establish that those patterns are proven causal explanations of decisions.
summary.tldr: Q-LDA connects reward-oriented topic modeling with Q-learning to reveal latent decision patterns and achieve strong text-game rewards.

title: Q-LDA: Uncovering Latent Patterns in Text-based Sequential Decision Processes

abstract: In this paper, we propose a generative multi-column network for image inpainting. This network synthesizes different image components in a parallel manner within one stage. To better characterize global structures, we design a confidence-driven reconstruction loss while an implicit diversified MRF regularization is adopted to enhance local details. The multi-column network combined with the reconstruction and MRF loss propagates local and global information derived from context to the target inpainting regions. Extensive experiments on challenging street view, face, natural objects and scenes manifest that our method produces visual compelling results even without previously common post-processing.

To better characterize global structures, we design a confidence-driven reconstruction loss while an implicit diversified MRF regularization is adopted to enhance local details. The multi-column network combined with the reconstruction and MRF loss propagates local and global information derived from context to the target inpainting regions. Extensive experiments on challenging street view, face, natural objects and scenes manifest that our method produces visual compelling results even without previously common post-processing.

paragraphs: Image inpainting fills a missing region using the surrounding image as context. A successful completion needs both coherent overall structure and convincing small details. This paper proposes a generative multi-column convolutional network that synthesizes different image components in parallel within a single stage, addressing these requirements through a coordinated architecture.

The training objective gives global structure and local detail distinct roles. A confidence-driven reconstruction loss helps characterize the image's overall organization. An implicit diversified Markov random field regularizer encourages richer local detail. Together with the network, these losses propagate information from the visible context into the region being reconstructed.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging street views, faces, natural objects, and scenes. They report visually compelling completions even without post-processing that had commonly been used previously. The finding supports the combination of parallel synthesis and complementary training objectives: the network can bring local and global contextual information together within the inpainting process itself.
summary.tldr: A parallel multi-column network combines global reconstruction and local-detail objectives to produce compelling image completions without common post-processing.

title: Image Inpainting via Generative Multi-column Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian learning is built on an assumption that the model space contains a true reflection of the data generating mechanism. This assumption is problematic, particularly in complex data environments. Here we present a Bayesian nonparametric approach to learning that makes use of statistical models, but does not assume that the model is true. Our approach has provably better properties than using a parametric model and admits a Monte Carlo sampling scheme that can afford massive scalability on modern computer architectures. The model-based aspect of learning is particularly attractive for regularizing nonparametric inference when the sample size is small, and also for correcting approximate approaches such as variational Bayes (VB). We demonstrate the approach on a number of examples including VB classifiers and Bayesian random forests.
