paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to learn related tasks over time while managing forgetting, knowledge transfer, and model growth. Local module composition, or LMC, tackles these challenges with reusable modules. Each module has its own structural component that estimates how relevant it is to the current input.

LMC uses those local relevance scores to assemble computations layer by layer. Because selection depends on module-specific learning, the method can operate without task identities. It also tracks input distribution statistics and adds modules when it detects outliers. Experiments show favorable results on the Continual Transfer-learning Benchmark, interpolation to related unseen tasks, and the ability to combine separately trained modular networks without further fine-tuning.

The paper also tests longer sequences of 30 and 100 tasks, exposing a concrete difficulty: choosing locally among many candidate modules becomes harder. In that setting, the best-performing LMC configuration creates far fewer modules than an oracle-based baseline but reaches lower overall accuracy. The results show both the flexibility of local composition and a demonstrated challenge as the pool of modules expands.
summary.tldr: LMC composes reusable modules without task identities, but selecting among many modules becomes challenging on longer task sequences.

title: Continual Learning via Local Module Composition

abstract: Extracting structured clinical information from free-text radiology reports can enable the use of radiology report information for a variety of critical healthcare applications. In our work, we present RadGraph, a dataset of entities and relations in full-text chest X-ray radiology reports based on a novel information extraction schema we designed to structure radiology reports. We release a development dataset, which contains board-certified radiologist annotations for 500 radiology reports from the MIMIC-CXR dataset (14,579 entities and 10,889 relations), and a test dataset, which contains two independent sets of board-certified radiologist annotations for 100 radiology reports split equally across the MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert datasets. Using these datasets, we train and test a deep learning model, RadGraph Benchmark, that achieves a micro F1 of 0.82 and 0.73 on relation extraction on the MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert test sets respectively. Additionally, we release an inference dataset, which contains annotations automatically generated by RadGraph Benchmark across 220,763 MIMIC-CXR reports (around 6 million entities and 4 million relations) and 500 CheXpert reports (13,783 entities and 9,908 relations) with mappings to associated chest radiographs. Our freely available dataset can facilitate a wide range of research in medical natural language processing, as well as computer vision and multi-modal learning when linked to chest radiographs.

paragraphs: RadGraph turns information in chest X-ray reports into structured entities and relationships. The authors design an information extraction schema and release expert annotations for training and evaluation. This structure makes report content available for computational research that needs more than an unorganized passage of clinical text.

The development data contain radiologist annotations for 500 MIMIC-CXR reports. The test data contain two independent expert annotation sets for 100 reports, divided equally between MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert. A trained deep learning model achieves relation-extraction micro F1 scores of 0.82 and 0.73 on the respective test sets, providing a reference for how well the schema can be extracted automatically.

The authors then apply the model at much larger scale, producing annotations for 220,763 MIMIC-CXR reports and 500 CheXpert reports, with links to corresponding chest images. These larger annotations are model-generated, distinct from the expert-labeled development and test data. The combined resource supports medical language research and, through the image mappings, research connecting radiology text with visual information.
summary.tldr: RadGraph provides expert-labeled and automatically extracted entities and relations from chest X-ray reports, with links supporting text-and-image research.

title: RadGraph: Extracting Clinical Entities and Relations from Radiology Reports

abstract: Societal and real-world considerations such as robustness, fairness, social welfare and multi-agent tradeoffs have given rise to multi-distribution learning paradigms, such as collaborative [Blum et al. 2017], group distributionally robust [Sagawa et al. 2019], and fair federated learning [Mohri et al. 2019]. In each of these settings, a learner seeks to minimize its worstcase loss over a set of $n$ predefined distributions, while using as few samples as possible. In this paper, we establish the optimal sample complexity of these learning paradigms and give algorithms that meet this sample complexity. Importantly, our sample complexity bounds exceed that of the sample complexity of learning a single distribution only by an additive factor of $\frac{n\log(n)}{\epsilon^2}$. These improve upon the best known sample complexity of agnostic federated learning by Mohri et al. 2019 by a multiplicative factor of $n$, the sample complexity of collaborative learning by Nguyen and Zakynthinou 2018 by a multiplicative factor $\frac{\log(n)}{\epsilon^3}$, and give the first sample complexity bounds for the group DRO objective of Sagawa et al. 2019. To achieve optimal sample complexity, our algorithms learn to sample and learn from distributions on demand. Our algorithm design and analysis extends stochastic optimization techniques to solve zero-sum games in a new stochastic setting.

paragraphs: Learning across multiple populations can require protecting the population with the highest loss, rather than optimizing an overall average. This paper studies that worst-case objective over n predefined distributions. The setting encompasses collaborative learning, fair federated learning, and group distributionally robust learning, with sample efficiency as the central question.

The authors establish optimal sample complexity and give algorithms that attain it. Their bounds exceed the cost of learning from one distribution by only an additive term of n log(n)/epsilon², where epsilon is the accuracy parameter. This describes how the statistical cost of covering multiple distributions enters the guarantee.

The algorithms learn which distributions to sample and learn from on demand. Their design extends stochastic optimization techniques to zero-sum games in a new stochastic setting. The resulting bounds improve earlier guarantees for agnostic federated and collaborative learning and provide the first sample complexity bounds for the group DRO objective considered. The contribution links adaptive data collection to optimal guarantees for a shared worst-case learning goal.
summary.tldr: On-demand sampling achieves optimal sample complexity for minimizing the worst-case loss across multiple predefined distributions.

title: On-Demand Sampling: Learning Optimally from Multiple Distributions

abstract: Inspired by the great success of unsupervised learning in Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing, the Reinforcement Learning community has recently started to focus more on unsupervised discovery of skills. Most current approaches, like DIAYN or DADS, optimize some form of mutual information objective. We propose a different approach that uses reward functions encoded by neural networks. These are trained iteratively to reward more complex behavior. In high-dimensional robotic environments our approach learns a wide range of interesting skills including front-flips for Half-Cheetah and one-legged running for Humanoid. It is the first skill discovery algorithm that can learn such skills without relying on any form of feature engineering. In the pixel-based Montezuma's Revenge environment our method also works with minimal changes and it learns complex skills that involve interacting with items and visiting diverse locations.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery asks how a reinforcement learning agent can acquire useful behaviors without having each desired skill specified in advance. Many existing methods approach this through mutual-information objectives. This paper introduces a different mechanism: neural networks that represent reward functions and are trained iteratively to reward increasingly complex behavior.

The reward functions provide a changing learning signal for skill acquisition. In high-dimensional robotic environments, the approach discovers behaviors including front-flips with Half-Cheetah and one-legged running with Humanoid. The authors report that it is the first skill discovery algorithm to learn such behaviors without feature engineering, making the learned reward mechanism central to the contribution.

The same approach also operates in the pixel-based Montezuma's Revenge environment with minimal changes. There, it discovers skills involving item interactions and visits to diverse locations. These results show the method working across both robotic control and a visual game environment. They support neural reward functions as a practical basis for open-ended skill discovery in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Iteratively trained neural reward functions drive unsupervised discovery of complex robotic and game-playing skills.

title: Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning with Neural Reward Functions

abstract: Value factorisation is a useful technique for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in global reward game, however, its underlying mechanism is not yet fully understood. This paper studies a theoretical framework for value factorisation with interpretability via Shapley value theory. We generalise Shapley value to Markov convex game called Markov Shapley value (MSV) and apply it as a value factorisation method in global reward game, which is obtained by the equivalence between the two games. Based on the properties of MSV, we derive Shapley-Bellman optimality equation (SBOE) to evaluate the optimal MSV, which corresponds to an optimal joint deterministic policy. Furthermore, we propose Shapley-Bellman operator (SBO) that is proved to solve SBOE. With a stochastic approximation and some transformations, a new MARL algorithm called Shapley Q-learning (SHAQ) is established, the implementation of which is guided by the theoretical results of SBO and MSV. We also discuss the relationship between SHAQ and relevant value factorisation methods. In the experiments, SHAQ exhibits not only superior performances on all tasks but also the interpretability that agrees with the theoretical analysis. The implementation of this paper is placed on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/shapley-q-learning.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, a shared reward can make individual contributions difficult to interpret. Value factorization breaks a joint value into agent-level quantities, but the paper argues that its underlying meaning needs stronger theoretical grounding. It uses Shapley value theory to build an interpretable framework for that decomposition.

The authors generalize the Shapley value to Markov convex games, calling the result the Markov Shapley value. Through an equivalence with global reward games, they use this quantity for value factorization. They derive a Shapley-Bellman optimality equation whose optimal values correspond to an optimal joint deterministic policy, and prove that a proposed operator solves that equation.

Stochastic approximation and further transformations turn this framework into Shapley Q-learning, or SHAQ. Its implementation is guided by the theoretical properties of the value and operator. Experiments report superior performance on all tested tasks and interpretations consistent with the analysis. The paper thus links an agent-level allocation of joint value to both a learning algorithm and an explanation of what its factorized values represent.
summary.tldr: SHAQ derives interpretable multi-agent value factorization and Q-learning from a Markov extension of Shapley value theory.

title: SHAQ: Incorporating Shapley Value Theory into Multi-Agent Q-Learning

abstract: Distillation with unlabeled examples is a popular and powerful method for training deep neural networks in settings where the amount of labeled data is limited: A large “teacher” neural network is trained on the labeled data available, and then it is used to generate labels on an unlabeled dataset (typically much larger in size). These labels are then utilized to train the smaller “student” model which will actually be deployed. Naturally, the success of the approach depends on the quality of the teacher’s labels, since the student could be confused if trained on inaccurate data. This paper proposes a principled approach for addressing this issue based on a “debiasing" reweighting of the student’s loss function tailored to the distillation training paradigm. Our method is hyper-parameter free, data-agnostic, and simple to implement. We demonstrate significant improvements on popular academic datasets and we accompany our results with a theoretical analysis which rigorously justifies the performance of our method in certain settings.

paragraphs: Distillation with unlabeled data trains a large teacher on available labels, uses it to label additional examples, and then trains a smaller student for deployment. This makes abundant unlabeled data useful when labeled examples are scarce. However, errors in the teacher's generated labels can mislead the student during training.

The paper proposes a principled reweighting of the student's loss to address that problem. The weights are designed as a debiasing correction for the distillation setting, changing how training examples contribute to the learning objective. The method is described as hyperparameter-free, data-agnostic, and simple to implement, so its contribution centers on modifying the student's training loss.

Experiments on popular academic datasets show significant improvements. A theoretical analysis also rigorously supports the method's performance in certain settings. The qualification matters: the theory provides justification within its covered cases, while the experiments supply broader practical evidence on the evaluated datasets. Together, these results support treating the reliability of teacher-generated supervision as part of the student's optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A hyperparameter-free reweighting of the student loss addresses bias from teacher-generated labels and improves distillation in the reported experiments.

title: Weighted Distillation with Unlabeled Examples

abstract: Randomized experiments are widely used to estimate causal effects across many domains. However, classical causal inference approaches rely on independence assumptions that are violated by network interference, when the treatment of one individual influences the outcomes of others. All existing approaches require at least approximate knowledge of the network, which may be unavailable or costly to collect. We consider the task of estimating the total treatment effect (TTE), the average difference between the outcomes when the whole population is treated versus when the whole population is untreated. By leveraging a staggered rollout design, in which treatment is incrementally given to random subsets of individuals, we derive unbiased estimators for TTE that do not rely on any prior structural knowledge of the network, as long as the network interference effects are constrained to low-degree interactions among neighbors of an individual. We derive bounds on the variance of the estimators, and we show in experiments that our estimator performs well against baselines on simulated data. Central to our theoretical contribution is a connection between staggered rollout observations and polynomial extrapolation.

paragraphs: When one person's treatment affects someone else's outcome, standard independence assumptions for causal inference can fail. This paper targets the total treatment effect: the average outcome difference between treating the entire population and treating nobody. It asks how to estimate that quantity without knowing the network through which people influence one another.

The approach uses a staggered randomized rollout, gradually assigning treatment to random subsets of individuals. Observations from successive stages are connected to polynomial extrapolation, allowing the authors to construct unbiased estimators of the total treatment effect. The guarantee requires network interference to involve low-degree interactions among an individual's neighbors; it does not cover unrestricted forms of interference.

The authors derive variance bounds and compare their estimator with baselines on simulated data, where it performs well. The methodological value is that experimental rollout structure can support estimation even without prior structural knowledge of the network. The low-degree interaction condition remains essential to the stated unbiasedness result, while the experiments provide supporting evidence within simulated settings.
summary.tldr: Staggered randomized rollouts enable unbiased total-effect estimation without network knowledge when interference has low-degree interactions.

title: Staggered Rollout Designs Enable Causal Inference Under Interference Without Network Knowledge

abstract: We propose a few-shot learning method for feature selection that can select relevant features given a small number of labeled instances. Existing methods require many labeled instances for accurate feature selection. However, sufficient instances are often unavailable. We use labeled instances in multiple related tasks to alleviate the lack of labeled instances in a target task. To measure the dependency between each feature and label, we use the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, which is a kernel-based independence measure. By modeling the kernel functions with neural networks that take a few labeled instances in a task as input, we can encode the task-specific information to the kernels such that the kernels are appropriate for the task. Feature selection with such kernels is performed by using iterative optimization methods, in which each update step is obtained as a closed-form. This formulation enables us to directly and efficiently minimize the expected test error on features selected by a small number of labeled instances. We experimentally demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing feature selection methods.

The paper addresses this scarcity by learning from labeled data across multiple related tasks. The goal is to use that shared experience to choose relevant features for a target task with little supervision.

This formulation supports direct, efficient optimization of expected test error for features selected from small labeled samples. Experiments show better performance than existing feature-selection methods. The central contribution is to connect learning across tasks with the feature-selection objective itself: the learned kernels are designed to support selections that work well when labels are scarce.
summary.tldr: Task-adapted kernels learned across related tasks improve feature selection when only a few labeled examples are available.

title: Few-shot Learning for Feature Selection with Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion

abstract: Meticulously analysing the empirical strengths and weaknesses of reinforcement learning methods in hard (challenging) environments is essential to inspire innovations and assess progress in the field. In tabular reinforcement learning, there is no well-established standard selection of environments to conduct such analysis, which is partially due to the lack of a widespread understanding of the rich theory of hardness of environments. The goal of this paper is to unlock the practical usefulness of this theory through four main contributions. First, we present a systematic survey of the theory of hardness, which also identifies promising research directions. Second, we introduce $\texttt{Colosseum}$, a pioneering package that enables empirical hardness analysis and implements a principled benchmark composed of environments that are diverse with respect to different measures of hardness. Third, we present an empirical analysis that provides new insights into computable measures. Finally, we benchmark five tabular agents in our newly proposed benchmark. While advancing the theoretical understanding of hardness in non-tabular reinforcement learning remains essential, our contributions in the tabular setting are intended as solid steps towards a principled non-tabular benchmark. Accordingly, we benchmark four agents in non-tabular versions of $\texttt{Colosseum}$ environments, obtaining results that demonstrate the generality of tabular hardness measures.

paragraphs: Comparing reinforcement-learning methods requires environments that expose different strengths and weaknesses. Its goal is to make that theory useful for practical evaluation.

The authors survey theoretical measures of hardness and introduce Colosseum, a package for empirical analysis. Its benchmark includes environments chosen to vary across different hardness measures. The paper also studies computable measures experimentally and evaluates five tabular agents, connecting theoretical descriptions of difficulty with observed learning behavior.

The authors extend the empirical evaluation to four agents using non-tabular versions of Colosseum environments. Those results demonstrate that tabular hardness measures can have relevance beyond their original setting. At the same time, the paper explicitly recognizes that stronger theoretical understanding of non-tabular difficulty remains needed. The contribution is a principled starting point for benchmark design, together with software and experiments that help researchers examine what makes particular environments challenging.
summary.tldr: Colosseum connects reinforcement-learning hardness theory with diverse benchmarks and empirical analysis of agent performance.

title: Hardness in Markov Decision Processes: Theory and Practice

abstract: Language is an important tool for humans to share knowledge. We propose a meta-learning method that shares knowledge across supervised learning tasks using feature descriptions written in natural language, which have not been used in the existing meta-learning methods. The proposed method improves the predictive performance on unseen tasks with a limited number of labeled data by meta-learning from various tasks. With the feature descriptions, we can find relationships across tasks even when their feature spaces are different. The feature descriptions are encoded using a language model pretrained with a large corpus, which enables us to incorporate human knowledge stored in the corpus into meta-learning. In our experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves better predictive performance than the existing meta-learning methods using a wide variety of real-world datasets provided by the statistical office of the EU and Japan.

In our experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves better predictive performance than the existing meta-learning methods using a wide variety of real-world datasets provided by the statistical office of the EU and Japan.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to improve learning on a new task with few labeled examples. Sharing that experience becomes harder when tasks use different feature spaces. This paper proposes using natural-language descriptions of features to uncover relationships between tasks even when their inputs do not share the same representation.

The method encodes feature descriptions with a language model pretrained on a large text corpus. These encodings let the meta-learning system incorporate information about what features mean, alongside the supervised learning tasks themselves. The authors frame this as a way to bring human knowledge represented in the language model's training corpus into the transfer process.

Experiments use a wide variety of real-world datasets from statistical offices in the EU and Japan. The proposed method achieves better predictive performance than the compared meta-learning methods. These results support feature descriptions as a useful source of cross-task knowledge, particularly for unseen tasks with limited labels and feature spaces that differ from those encountered during meta-learning.
summary.tldr: Natural-language feature descriptions help a meta-learning model transfer knowledge between tasks with different feature spaces.

title: Sharing Knowledge for Meta-learning with Feature Descriptions

abstract: This work provides the first theoretical study on the ability of graph Message Passing Neural Networks (gMPNNs) ---such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)--- to perform inductive out-of-distribution (OOD) link prediction tasks, where deployment (test) graph sizes are larger than training graphs. We first prove non-asymptotic bounds showing that link predictors based on permutation-equivariant (structural) node embeddings obtained by gMPNNs can converge to a random guess as test graphs get larger. We then propose a theoretically-sound gMPNN that outputs structural pairwise (2-node) embeddings and prove non-asymptotic bounds showing that, as test graphs grow, these embeddings converge to embeddings of a continuous function that retains its ability to predict links OOD. Empirical results on random graphs show agreement with our theoretical results.

paragraphs: A graph model trained to predict links may later encounter graphs much larger than those used in training. This paper theoretically studies that size shift for graph message-passing neural networks. The question is whether learned structural representations retain useful information about links as the deployment graph grows.

The authors prove finite-size bounds showing that predictors based on structural embeddings of individual nodes can approach random guessing on increasingly large test graphs. The result is a possible failure of this representation strategy, rather than a statement that every node-based predictor always fails. They then propose a message-passing model that produces structural embeddings for pairs of nodes.

For the pairwise construction, the authors prove bounds showing convergence toward embeddings of a continuous function that preserves out-of-distribution link-prediction ability. Experiments on random graphs agree with the theoretical findings. The contrast identifies representation granularity as consequential: encoding a pair directly can retain predictive structure that individual-node embeddings may lose under increasing graph size.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how node-based link predictors can degrade on larger graphs and develops pairwise embeddings with theoretical generalization guarantees.

title: OOD Link Prediction Generalization Capabilities of Message-Passing GNNs in Larger Test Graphs

abstract: It has been a long-standing dream to design artificial agents that explore their environment efficiently via intrinsic motivation, similar to how children perform curious free play. Despite recent advances in intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning (RL), sample-efficient exploration in object manipulation scenarios remains a significant challenge as most of the relevant information lies in the sparse agent-object and object-object interactions. In this paper, we propose to use structured world models to incorporate relational inductive biases in the control loop to achieve sample-efficient and interaction-rich exploration in compositional multi-object environments. By planning for future novelty inside structured world models, our method generates free-play behavior that starts to interact with objects early on and develops more complex behavior over time. Instead of using models only to compute intrinsic rewards, as commonly done, our method showcases that the self-reinforcing cycle between good models and good exploration also opens up another avenue: zero-shot generalization to downstream tasks via model-based planning. After the entirely intrinsic task-agnostic exploration phase, our method solves challenging downstream tasks such as stacking, flipping, pick & place, and throwing that generalizes to unseen numbers and arrangements of objects without any additional training.

paragraphs: Learning through free play is difficult in object manipulation because useful information is concentrated in relatively sparse interactions between the agent and objects, or between objects themselves. This paper proposes structured world models that incorporate relationships among objects into the agent’s control process. The aim is to make exploration informative even before a particular task is specified.

summary.tldr: Structured world models guide curious exploration and then support object-manipulation tasks without additional training.

title: Curious Exploration via Structured World Models Yields Zero-Shot Object Manipulation

abstract: In Machine Learning, a benchmark refers to an ensemble of datasets associated with one or multiple metrics together with a way to aggregate different systems performances. They are instrumental in {\it (i)} assessing the progress of new methods along different axes and {\it (ii)} selecting the best systems for practical use. This is particularly the case for NLP with the development of large pre-trained models (\textit{e.g.} GPT, BERT) that are expected to generalize well on a variety of tasks. While the community mainly focused on developing new datasets and metrics, there has been little interest in the aggregation procedure, which is often reduced to a simple average over various performance measures. However, this procedure can be problematic when the metrics are on a different scale, which may lead to spurious conclusions. This paper proposes a new procedure to rank systems based on their performance across different tasks. Motivated by the social choice theory, the final system ordering is obtained through aggregating the rankings induced by each task and is theoretically grounded. We conduct extensive numerical experiments (on over 270k scores) to assess the soundness of our approach both on synthetic and real scores (\textit{e.g.} GLUE, EXTREM, SEVAL, TAC, FLICKR). In particular, we show that our method yields different conclusions on state-of-the-art systems than the mean-aggregation procedure while being both more reliable and robust.

paragraphs: A benchmark needs a rule for combining performance across tasks as well as datasets and metrics. This paper examines how the aggregation rule affects which language-processing systems appear best.

The authors propose ranking systems within each task and then combining those rankings into an overall ordering. Motivated by social choice theory, the procedure has a theoretical foundation. Its focus on task-level rankings changes how heterogeneous performance measures contribute to the final comparison, directly addressing problems associated with averaging scores on different scales.

The authors find that their procedure can produce different conclusions about state-of-the-art systems while being more reliable and robust than mean aggregation. The contribution shows that benchmark conclusions depend partly on how evidence across tasks is combined, making aggregation itself an important component of evaluation design.
summary.tldr: Aggregating task-level rankings offers a theoretically grounded alternative to averaging benchmark scores, with more reliable and robust reported comparisons.

title: What are the best Systems? New Perspectives on NLP Benchmarking

abstract: The cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) with permutation invariant agents framework has achieved tremendous empirical successes in real-world applications. Unfortunately, the theoretical understanding of this MARL problem is lacking due to the curse of many agents and the limited exploration of the relational reasoning in existing works. In this paper, we verify that the transformer implements complex relational reasoning, and we propose and analyze model-free and model-based offline MARL algorithms with the transformer approximators. We prove that the suboptimality gaps of the model-free and model-based algorithms are independent of and logarithmic in the number of agents respectively, which mitigates the curse of many agents. These results are consequences of a novel generalization error bound of the transformer and a novel analysis of the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) of the system dynamics with the transformer. Our model-based algorithm is the first provably efficient MARL algorithm that explicitly exploits the permutation invariance of the agents. Our improved generalization bound may be of independent interest and is applicable to other regression problems related to the transformer beyond MARL.

This paper studies a setting with permutation-invariant agents, where reordering the agents should not change the underlying problem. It examines how transformers can represent relationships among those agents and how that structure affects theoretical learning guarantees.

The authors establish transformers' ability to implement complex relational reasoning and develop both model-free and model-based offline learning algorithms using transformer approximators. Their analysis gives suboptimality bounds with different dependence on agent count: independent of that count for the model-free algorithm and logarithmic in it for the model-based algorithm. The authors identify their model-based method as the first provably efficient MARL algorithm to explicitly exploit agent permutation invariance. The generalization bound may also apply to other transformer regression problems, extending the potential relevance of the analysis beyond multi-agent learning.
summary.tldr: Transformer-based offline MARL algorithms exploit permutation invariance to obtain suboptimality bounds with mild dependence on agent count.

title: Relational Reasoning via Set Transformers: Provable Efficiency and Applications to MARL

abstract: We propose generative multitask learning (GMTL), a simple and scalable approach to causal machine learning in the multitask setting. Our approach makes a minor change to the conventional multitask inference objective, and improves robustness to target shift. Since GMTL only modifies the inference objective, it can be used with existing multitask learning methods without requiring additional training. The improvement in robustness comes from mitigating unobserved confounders that cause the targets, but not the input. We refer to them as \emph{target-causing confounders}. These confounders induce spurious dependencies between the input and targets. This poses a problem for conventional multitask learning, due to its assumption that the targets are conditionally independent given the input. GMTL mitigates target-causing confounding at inference time, by removing the influence of the joint target distribution, and predicting all targets jointly. This removes the spurious dependencies between the input and targets, where the degree of removal is adjustable via a single hyperparameter. This flexibility is useful for managing the trade-off between in- and out-of-distribution generalization. Our results on the Attributes of People and Taskonomy datasets reflect an improved robustness to target shift across four multitask learning methods.

paragraphs: Multitask learning predicts several targets from the same input. This paper examines a specific source of unreliable relationships: unobserved confounders that cause the targets but do not cause the input. Such target-causing confounders can induce spurious input-target dependencies and create problems for methods that assume targets are conditionally independent once the input is known.

The result identifies a specific causal mechanism and offers a comparatively small intervention for mitigating it, while preserving flexibility over the trade-off between in-distribution and shifted-data performance.
summary.tldr: GMTL changes multitask inference to mitigate target-causing confounding and improve robustness to target shift without retraining.

title: Generative multitask learning mitigates target-causing confounding

abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRF) have brought tremendous progress to novel view synthesis. Though NeRF enables the rendering of subtle details in a scene by learning from a dense set of images, it also reconstructs the undesired reflections when we capture images through glass. As a commonly observed interference, the reflection would undermine the visibility of the desired transmitted scene behind glass by occluding the transmitted light rays. In this paper, we aim at addressing the problem of rendering novel transmitted views given a set of reflection-corrupted images. By introducing the transmission encoder and recurring edge constraints as guidance, our neural transmitted radiance fields can resist such reflection interference during rendering and reconstruct high-fidelity results even under sparse views. The proposed method achieves superior performance from the experiments on a newly collected dataset compared with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct scenes from images so they can be rendered from new viewpoints. When the images are taken through glass, however, the reconstruction can include unwanted reflections along with the scene behind it. This paper targets the transmitted scene: the content visible through the glass that reflection interference makes harder to recover.

The proposed neural transmitted radiance field uses a transmission encoder together with recurring edge constraints to guide reconstruction. These additions are intended to help the model resist reflection interference when producing new views. The task therefore goes beyond reproducing everything visible in the input photographs; it seeks a representation that renders the desired scene despite contaminated observations.

The authors report high-fidelity reconstructions even when only sparse views are available. Experiments on a newly collected dataset show superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support incorporating transmission-oriented guidance into radiance-field reconstruction when the source images contain reflections, with the reported benefit covering both interference handling and reconstruction from limited viewpoints.
summary.tldr: Neural transmitted radiance fields use transmission guidance and recurring edges to reconstruct new views of scenes behind glass despite reflections.

title: Neural Transmitted Radiance Fields

abstract: Recent progress in scaling up large language models has shown impressive capabilities in performing few-shot learning across a wide range of natural language tasks. However, a key limitation is that these language models fundamentally lack grounding to visual perception - a crucial attribute needed to extend to real world tasks such as in visual-question answering and robotics. While prior works have largely connected image to text through pretraining or fine-tuning, learning such alignments are generally costly due to a combination of curating massive datasets and large computational burdens. In order to resolve these limitations, we propose a simple yet effective approach called Language-Quantized AutoEncoder (LQAE), a modification of VQ-VAE that learns to align text-image data in an unsupervised manner by leveraging pretrained language model denoisers (e.g., BERT). Our main idea is to encode images as sequences of text tokens by directly quantizing image embeddings using a pretrained language codebook. We then feed a masked version of the quantized embeddings into a BERT to reconstruct the original input. By doing so, LQAE learns to represent similar images with similar clusters of text tokens, thereby aligning these two modalities without the use of aligned text-image pairs. We show LQAE learns text-aligned image tokens that enable few-shot multi-modal learning with large language models, outperforming baseline methods in tasks such as image classification and VQA while requiring as few as 1-10 image-text pairs.

Building that connection commonly involves expensive image-text alignment training. Language-Quantized AutoEncoder, or LQAE, explores an unsupervised alternative that uses a pretrained language model to help organize image representations without aligned image-text pairs.

LQAE modifies a vector-quantized autoencoder by quantizing image embeddings with a pretrained language codebook. This expresses an image through a sequence of text-associated tokens. A masked version of those embeddings is then passed through a language-model denoiser such as BERT as part of reconstructing the original input. The resulting image tokens support few-shot multimodal learning with large language models. The authors report improvements over baseline methods on tasks including image classification and visual question answering, using as few as one to ten image-text pairs. These pairs belong to the few-shot use of the learned representations; the alignment approach itself does not require paired image-text training data.
summary.tldr: LQAE learns text-aligned image tokens without paired alignment data, enabling multimodal few-shot learning with as few as one to ten image-text pairs.

title: Language Quantized AutoEncoders: Towards Unsupervised Text-Image Alignment

abstract: The pursuit of controllability as a higher standard of visual content creation has yielded remarkable progress in customizable image synthesis. However, achieving controllable video synthesis remains challenging due to the large variation of temporal dynamics and the requirement of cross-frame temporal consistency. Based on the paradigm of compositional generation, this work presents VideoComposer that allows users to flexibly compose a video with textual conditions, spatial conditions, and more importantly temporal conditions. Specifically, considering the characteristic of video data, we introduce the motion vector from compressed videos as an explicit control signal to provide guidance regarding temporal dynamics. In addition, we develop a Spatio-Temporal Condition encoder (STC-encoder) that serves as a unified interface to effectively incorporate the spatial and temporal relations of sequential inputs, with which the model could make better use of temporal conditions and hence achieve higher inter-frame consistency. Extensive experimental results suggest that VideoComposer is able to control the spatial and temporal patterns simultaneously within a synthesized video in various forms, such as text description, sketch sequence, reference video, or even simply hand-crafted motions. The code and models are publicly available athttps://videocomposer.github.io.

The code and models are publicly available athttps://videocomposer.github.io.

paragraphs: Controlling generated video requires specifying both what appears and how it changes across frames. That is difficult because motion varies widely and neighboring frames must remain coherent. VideoComposer addresses this through compositional generation, allowing text, spatial information, and temporal information to jointly guide the synthesized video.

The method uses motion vectors from compressed video as an explicit signal for temporal dynamics. It also introduces a Spatio-Temporal Condition encoder that provides a shared interface for sequential inputs. This encoder incorporates relationships within and across frames, helping the model use temporal conditions more effectively and improve consistency between generated frames.

Experimental results suggest that VideoComposer can control spatial and temporal patterns simultaneously through several input forms, including text descriptions, sketch sequences, reference videos, and hand-crafted motions. The contribution is a unified way to combine these kinds of control in video synthesis. Its findings support flexible motion guidance in the evaluated settings, connecting user-supplied conditions to both visual content and how that content develops over time.
summary.tldr: VideoComposer combines text, spatial cues, and explicit motion signals to guide video content and temporal behavior together.

title: VideoComposer: Compositional Video Synthesis with Motion Controllability

abstract: Transformers have emerged as the cornerstone of state-of-the-art natural language processing models, showcasing exceptional performance across a wide range of AI applications. However, the memory demands posed by the self-attention mechanism and the large feedforward network in Transformers limit their ability to handle long sequences, thereby creating challenges for tasks involving multiple long sequences or long-term dependencies. We present a distinct approach, Blockwise Parallel Transformer (BPT), that leverages blockwise computation of self-attention and feedforward network fusion to minimize memory costs. By processing longer input sequences while maintaining memory efficiency, BPT enables training sequences 32 times longer than vanilla Transformers and up to 4 times longer than previous memory-efficient methods. Extensive experiments on language modeling and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of BPT in reducing memory requirements and improving performance.

This paper addresses the execution of these computations so that longer sequences can fit within memory.

Its contribution therefore concerns how Transformer computations are organized, with the goal of making longer training inputs practical while retaining memory efficiency.

These findings connect an implementation-level change to the ability to train with more context. The reported sequence-length comparisons describe the demonstrated gains; they do not establish an identical increase for every model or workload.
summary.tldr: BPT reduces Transformer memory use through blockwise attention and feedforward fusion, enabling substantially longer training sequences.

title: Blockwise Parallel Transformers for Large Context Models

abstract: This work proposes POMP, a prompt pre-training method for vision-language models. Being memory and computation efficient, POMP enables the learned prompt to condense semantic information for a rich set of visual concepts with over twenty-thousand classes. Once pre-trained, the prompt with a strong transferable ability can be directly plugged into a variety of visual recognition tasks including image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, to boost recognition performances in a zero-shot manner. Empirical evaluation shows that POMP achieves state-of-the-art performances on 21 datasets, e.g., 67.0% average accuracy on 10 classification datasets (+3.1% compared to CoOp) and 84.4 hIoU on open-vocabulary Pascal VOC segmentation (+6.9 compared to ZSSeg).

The paper emphasizes memory and computation efficiency as what makes training with more than twenty thousand classes feasible.

After pretraining, the prompt can be inserted directly into different visual recognition tasks. The authors consider image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, reporting improved performance in a zero-shot manner. The same pretrained prompt is therefore intended to carry useful information across multiple forms of visual recognition.

Examples include 67.0% average accuracy on ten classification datasets, reported as 3.1% above CoOp, and 84.4 hIoU on open-vocabulary Pascal VOC segmentation, 6.9 above ZSSeg. These findings support broad prompt pretraining as a reusable source of recognition improvements. The contribution combines coverage of many concepts with demonstrated transfer across tasks, rather than reporting gains for only one recognition setting.
summary.tldr: POMP efficiently pretrains prompts on over twenty thousand classes and transfers them to improve several visual recognition tasks without task-specific training.

title: Prompt Pre-Training with Twenty-Thousand Classes for Open-Vocabulary Visual Recognition

abstract: Counterfactual inference aims to answer retrospective "what if" questions and thus belongs to the most fine-grained type of inference in Pearl's causality ladder. Existing methods for counterfactual inference with continuous outcomes aim at point identification and thus make strong and unnatural assumptions about the underlying structural causal model. In this paper, we relax these assumptions and aim at partial counterfactual identification of continuous outcomes, i.e., when the counterfactual query resides in an ignorance interval with informative bounds. We prove that, in general, the ignorance interval of the counterfactual queries has non-informative bounds, already when functions of structural causal models are continuously differentiable. As a remedy, we propose a novel sensitivity model called Curvature Sensitivity Model. This allows us to obtain informative bounds by bounding the curvature of level sets of the functions. We further show that existing point counterfactual identification methods are special cases of our Curvature Sensitivity Model when the bound of the curvature is set to zero. We then propose an implementation of our Curvature Sensitivity Model in the form of a novel deep generative model, which we call Augmented Pseudo-Invertible Decoder. Our implementation employs (i) residual normalizing flows with (ii) variational augmentations. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our Augmented Pseudo-Invertible Decoder. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first partial identification model for Markovian structural causal models with continuous outcomes.

paragraphs: Counterfactual inference asks what would have happened under a different course of events. For continuous outcomes, methods seeking one identified answer can require strong assumptions about the causal model. This paper instead seeks informative intervals of possible counterfactual answers, allowing uncertainty about the underlying model to remain visible.

The authors first prove that continuous differentiability of the causal functions is generally insufficient to make those intervals informative. Their Curvature Sensitivity Model adds a bound on the curvature of the functions' level sets. This restriction enables informative bounds. Existing point-identification methods emerge as special cases when the curvature bound is zero, connecting the proposed sensitivity approach to more restrictive methods.

The paper implements the model through an Augmented Pseudo-Invertible Decoder, a deep generative model combining residual normalizing flows with variational augmentations. Empirical results demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is a route to partial counterfactual identification for continuous outcomes in Markovian structural causal models, where informative answers depend on an explicit geometric restriction rather than smoothness alone.
summary.tldr: Bounding curvature in causal models enables informative intervals for continuous counterfactual outcomes where smoothness alone is insufficient.

title: Partial Counterfactual Identification of Continuous Outcomes with a Curvature Sensitivity Model

abstract: Various gradient compression algorithms have been proposed to alleviate the communication bottleneck in distributed learning, and they have demonstrated effectiveness in terms of high compression ratios and theoretical low communication complexity. However, when it comes to practically training modern deep neural networks (DNNs), these algorithms have yet to match the inference performance of uncompressed SGD-momentum (SGDM) and adaptive optimizers (e.g.,Adam). More importantly, recent studies suggest that these algorithms actually offer no speed advantages over SGDM/Adam when used with common distributed DNN training frameworks ( e.g., DistributedDataParallel (DDP)) in the typical settings, due to heavy compression/decompression computation or incompatibility with the efficient All-Reduce or the requirement of uncompressed warmup at the early stage. For these reasons, we propose a novel 1-bit adaptive optimizer, dubbed *Bi*nary *r*andomization a*d*aptive optimiz*er* (**Birder**). The quantization of Birder can be easily and lightly computed, and it does not require warmup with its uncompressed version in the beginning. Also, we devise Hierarchical-1-bit-All-Reduce to further lower the communication volume. We theoretically prove that it promises the same convergence rate as the Adam. Extensive experiments, conducted on 8 to 64 GPUs (1 to 8 nodes) using DDP, demonstrate that Birder achieves comparable inference performance to uncompressed SGDM/Adam, with up to ${2.5 \times}$ speedup for training ResNet-50 and ${6.3\times}$ speedup for training BERT-Base. Code is publicly available at https://openi.pcl.ac.cn/c2net_optim/Birder.

paragraphs: Compressing gradients can reduce communication during distributed training, but communication savings alone do not ensure faster training. Compression overhead, compatibility with collective communication, and uncompressed warmup can erase the benefit. Birder addresses these practical obstacles with a 1-bit adaptive optimizer designed for distributed deep neural network training.

Its binary randomization scheme makes quantization lightweight and avoids an initial warmup using an uncompressed optimizer. The authors also introduce Hierarchical-1-bit-All-Reduce to reduce communication volume further. These components address both the representation of communicated information and the mechanism used to exchange it. The paper additionally proves a convergence rate matching Adam's.

Experiments use DistributedDataParallel across 8 to 64 GPUs on 1 to 8 nodes. Birder achieves inference performance comparable to uncompressed momentum SGD and Adam, with reported training speedups reaching 2.5 times for ResNet-50 and 6.3 times for BERT-Base. These maximum observed speedups support the practical value of reducing communication while keeping compression overhead low.
summary.tldr: Birder combines lightweight 1-bit adaptive updates with hierarchical communication to accelerate distributed training while maintaining comparable inference performance in reported experiments.

title: Birder: Communication-Efficient 1-bit Adaptive Optimizer for Practical Distributed DNN Training

abstract: Recently, neural heuristics based on deep reinforcement learning have exhibited promise in solving multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems (MOCOPs). However, they are still struggling to achieve high learning efficiency and solution quality. To tackle this issue, we propose an efficient meta neural heuristic (EMNH), in which a meta-model is first trained and then fine-tuned with a few steps to solve corresponding single-objective subproblems. Specifically, for the training process, a (partial) architecture-shared multi-task model is leveraged to achieve parallel learning for the meta-model, so as to speed up the training; meanwhile, a scaled symmetric sampling method with respect to the weight vectors is designed to stabilize the training. For the fine-tuning process, an efficient hierarchical method is proposed to systematically tackle all the subproblems. Experimental results on the multi-objective traveling salesman problem (MOTSP), multi-objective capacitated vehicle routing problem (MOCVRP), and multi-objective knapsack problem (MOKP) show that, EMNH is able to outperform the state-of-the-art neural heuristics in terms of solution quality and learning efficiency, and yield competitive solutions to the strong traditional heuristics while consuming much shorter time.

paragraphs: Multi-objective combinatorial optimization seeks good discrete solutions while balancing several goals. Neural heuristics have shown promise, but learning efficiently and producing strong solutions remain challenges. This paper proposes EMNH, which trains a shared starting model and then adapts it in a few steps to single-objective subproblems representing different objective tradeoffs.

During training, a multi-task architecture shares part of its structure so the meta-model can learn in parallel. A scaled symmetric sampling method for objective weight vectors stabilizes this process. These components address complementary needs: making shared training faster and improving how training explores the different weightings of the objectives.

For adaptation, a hierarchical procedure systematically handles the collection of subproblems. Experiments cover multi-objective traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and knapsack problems. EMNH outperforms the evaluated leading neural heuristics in solution quality and learning efficiency. It also produces solutions competitive with strong traditional heuristics while using substantially less time. The reported benefit is therefore both stronger learned search and a favorable quality-versus-time comparison on the tested problems.
summary.tldr: EMNH combines shared meta-training with fast hierarchical adaptation to solve multiple objective tradeoffs efficiently and with strong solution quality.

title: Efficient Meta Neural Heuristic for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) serve as one type of efficient model to process spatio-temporal patterns in time series, such as the Address-Event Representation data collected from Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS). Although convolutional SNNs have achieved remarkable performance on these AER datasets, benefiting from the predominant spatial feature extraction ability of convolutional structure, they ignore temporal features related to sequential time points. In this paper, we develop a recurrent spiking neural network (RSNN) model embedded with an advanced spiking convolutional block attention module (SCBAM) component to combine both spatial and temporal features of spatio-temporal patterns. It invokes the history information in spatial and temporal channels adaptively through SCBAM, which brings the advantages of efficient memory calling and history redundancy elimination. The performance of our model was evaluated in DVS128-Gesture dataset and other time-series datasets. The experimental results show that the proposed SRNN-SCBAM model makes better use of the history information in spatial and temporal dimensions with less memory space, and achieves higher accuracy compared to other models.

paragraphs: Event-based vision data contain patterns across both space and time. Convolutional spiking neural networks can extract spatial structure effectively, but the paper argues that they overlook temporal features connecting successive time points. The proposed model adds recurrence and attention so that past information can contribute more selectively to recognizing the current pattern.

The architecture embeds a spiking convolutional block attention module, SCBAM, in a recurrent spiking neural network. This module adaptively accesses historical information through spatial and temporal channels. Its purpose is to combine useful spatial and sequential features while removing redundant history. The memory mechanism therefore concerns both which past information is useful and how efficiently that information can be retained and recalled.

Evaluation on DVS128-Gesture and other time-series datasets finds higher accuracy than the compared models while using less memory space. The reported results also indicate better use of history across spatial and temporal dimensions. The contribution is a recurrent attention design that improves the usefulness of stored history in these experiments, linking temporal modeling with more efficient memory use.
summary.tldr: A spiking attention module helps a recurrent network use spatial and temporal history more accurately with less memory in reported experiments.

title: Enhancing Adaptive History Reserving by Spiking Convolutional Block Attention Module in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Embodied agents operate in a structured world, often solving tasks with spatial, temporal, and permutation symmetries. Most algorithms for planning and model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) do not take this rich geometric structure into account, leading to sample inefficiency and poor generalization. We introduce the Equivariant Diffuser for Generating Interactions (EDGI), an algorithm for MBRL and planning that is equivariant with respect to the product of the spatial symmetry group SE(3), the discrete-time translation group ℤ, and the object permutation group Sₙ. EDGI follows the Diffuser framework by Janner et al. (2022) in treating both learning a world model and planning in it as a conditional generative modeling problem, training a diffusion model on an offline trajectory dataset. We introduce a new SE(3) × ℤ × Sₙ-equivariant diffusion model that supports multiple representations. We integrate this model in a planning loop, where conditioning and classifier guidance let us softly break the symmetry for specific tasks as needed. On object manipulation and navigation tasks, EDGI is substantially more sample efficient and generalizes better across the symmetry group than non-equivariant models.

paragraphs: Embodied agents encounter tasks with geometric and organizational structure: scenes can be rotated or translated, trajectories shifted in time, and objects reordered. EDGI builds these spatial, temporal, and permutation symmetries into a planning model. Equivariance means that the model's behavior transforms consistently with the corresponding transformation of its inputs.

Following the Diffuser framework, EDGI treats learning a world model and planning with it as conditional generation. It trains a diffusion model on an offline collection of trajectories. The new model respects the combined symmetry group and supports multiple representations, making these structural relationships part of the generative mechanism.

Planning still needs to express task-specific goals that may favor particular positions, times, or objects. EDGI uses conditioning and classifier guidance to softly break symmetry where the task requires it. On object manipulation and navigation tasks, the authors report substantially better sample efficiency and generalization across the symmetry group than non-equivariant models. The results support encoding these regularities directly when learning plans from trajectory data.
summary.tldr: EDGI embeds spatial, temporal, and object-order symmetries into diffusion-based planning, improving sample efficiency and symmetry-related generalization in evaluated tasks.

title: EDGI: Equivariant Diffusion for Planning with Embodied Agents

abstract: Understanding comprehensive assembly knowledge from videos is critical for futuristic ultra-intelligent industry. To enable technological breakthrough, we present HA-ViD – the first human assembly video dataset that features representative industrial assembly scenarios, natural procedural knowledge acquisition process, and consistent human-robot shared annotations. Specifically, HA-ViD captures diverse collaboration patterns of real-world assembly, natural human behaviors and learning progression during assembly, and granulate action annotations to subject, action verb, manipulated object, target object, and tool. We provide 3222 multi-view and multi-modality videos), 1.5M frames, 96K temporal labels and 2M spatial labels. We benchmark four foundational video understanding tasks: action recognition, action segmentation, object detection and multi-object tracking. Importantly, we analyze their performance and the further reasoning steps for comprehending knowledge in assembly progress, process efficiency, task collaboration, skill parameters and human intention. Details of HA-ViD is available at: https://iai-hrc.github.io/ha-vid.

paragraphs: Understanding an assembly video involves more than recognizing isolated motions. A system must connect actions with objects, tools, collaborators, and the evolving procedure. HA-ViD is a dataset designed around this broader problem, with representative industrial assembly scenarios and annotations intended to support shared understanding between humans and robots.

The collection captures different collaboration patterns, natural human behavior, and changes as people learn assembly procedures. Its action annotations separate the acting subject, action verb, manipulated object, target object, and tool. The dataset includes 3,222 videos across multiple views and modalities, 1.5 million frames, 96,000 temporal labels, and two million spatial labels.

The authors benchmark action recognition, action segmentation, object detection, and multi-object tracking. They then examine how those capabilities relate to further reasoning about assembly progress, process efficiency, collaboration, skill parameters, and human intention. This makes the contribution both a labeled video resource and an analysis of the additional reasoning needed to turn basic visual predictions into more comprehensive assembly knowledge.
summary.tldr: HA-ViD provides richly annotated industrial assembly videos and benchmarks for connecting visual recognition with procedural understanding.

title: HA-ViD: A Human Assembly Video Dataset for Comprehensive Assembly Knowledge Understanding

abstract: As more non-AI experts use complex AI systems for daily tasks, there has been an increasing effort to develop methods that produce explanations of AI decision making that are understandable by non-AI experts. Towards this effort, leveraging higher-level concepts and producing concept-based explanations have become a popular method. Most concept-based explanations have been developed for classification techniques, and we posit that the few existing methods for sequential decision making are limited in scope. In this work, we first contribute a desiderata for defining ``concepts'' in sequential decision making settings. Additionally, inspired by the Protege Effect which states explaining knowledge often reinforces one's self-learning, we explore how concept-based explanations of an RL agent's decision making can in turn improve the agent's learning rate, as well as improve end-user understanding of the agent's decision making. To this end, we contribute a unified framework, State2Explanation (S2E), that involves learning a joint embedding model between state-action pairs and concept-based explanations, and leveraging such learned model to both (1) inform reward shaping during an agent's training, and (2) provide explanations to end-users at deployment for improved task performance. Our experimental validations, in Connect 4 and Lunar Lander, demonstrate the success of S2E in providing a dual-benefit, successfully informing reward shaping and improving agent learning rate, as well as significantly improving end user task performance at deployment time.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations describe decisions using higher-level ideas that people can understand. Most existing work focuses on classification, while agents making sequences of decisions pose different explanatory needs. This paper proposes criteria for defining concepts in sequential decision making and investigates whether explanations can also help the agent learn more quickly.

State2Explanation learns a shared embedding that connects state–action pairs with concept-based explanations. During training, this learned relationship informs reward shaping, which adjusts the learning signal guiding the agent. At deployment, the same model provides explanations to users. The framework therefore connects agent training and user-facing explanation through one learned representation.

The approach is inspired by the idea that explaining knowledge can reinforce learning. Experiments in Connect 4 and Lunar Lander report both faster agent learning through reward shaping and significantly improved user task performance during deployment. These findings support the proposed dual use of explanations in the evaluated environments: helping train the agent and helping people work with its decisions.
summary.tldr: State2Explanation connects actions with concepts to improve both reinforcement learning and users' task performance in two evaluated environments.

title: State2Explanation: Concept-Based Explanations to Benefit Agent Learning and User Understanding

abstract: Labeling neural network submodules with human-legible descriptions is useful for many downstream tasks: such descriptions can surface failures, guide interventions, and perhaps even explain important model behaviors. To date, most mechanistic descriptions of trained networks have involved small models, narrowly delimited phenomena, and large amounts of human labor. Labeling all human-interpretable sub-computations in models of increasing size and complexity will almost certainly require tools that can generate and validate descriptions automatically. Recently, techniques that use learned models in-the-loop for labeling have begun to gain traction, but methods for evaluating their efficacy are limited and ad-hoc. How should we validate and compare open-ended labeling tools? This paper introduces FIND (Function INterpretation and Description), a benchmark suite for evaluating the building blocks of automated interpretability methods. FIND contains functions that resemble components of trained neural networks, and accompanying descriptions of the kind we seek to generate. The functions are procedurally constructed across textual and numeric domains, and involve a range of real-world complexities, including noise, composition, approximation, and bias. We evaluate methods that use pretrained language models (LMs) to produce code-based and natural language descriptions of function behavior. Additionally, we introduce a new interactive method in which an Automated Interpretability Agent (AIA) generates function descriptions. We find that an AIA, built with an off-the-shelf LM augmented with black-box access to functions, can sometimes infer function structure—acting as a scientist by forming hypotheses, proposing experiments, and updating descriptions in light of new data. However, FIND also reveals that LM-based descriptions capture global function behavior while missing local details. These results suggest that FIND will be useful for characterizing the performance of more sophisticated interpretability methods before they are applied to real-world models.
originalAbstract: Labeling neural network submodules with human-legible descriptions is useful for many downstream tasks: such descriptions can surface failures, guide interventions, and perhaps even explain important model behaviors. To date, most mechanistic descriptions of trained networks have involved small models, narrowly delimited phenomena, and large amounts of human labor. Labeling all human-interpretable sub-computations in models of increasing size and complexity will almost certainly require tools that can generate and validate descriptions automatically. Recently, techniques that use learned models in-the-loop for labeling have begun to gain traction, but methods for evaluating their efficacy are limited and ad-hoc. How should we validate and compare open-ended labeling tools? This paper introduces FIND (Function INterpretation and Description), a benchmark suite for evaluating the building blocks of automated interpretability methods. FIND contains functions that resemble components of trained neural networks, and accompanying descriptions of the kind we seek to generate. The functions are procedurally constructed across textual and numeric domains, and involve a range of real-world complexities, including noise, composition, approximation, and bias. We evaluate methods that use pretrained language models (LMs) to produce code-based and natural language descriptions of function behavior. Additionally, we introduce a new interactive method in which an Automated Interpretability Agent (AIA) generates function descriptions. We find that an AIA, built with an off-the-shelf LM augmented with black-box access to functions, can sometimes infer function structure—acting as a scientist by forming hypotheses, proposing experiments, and updating descriptions in light of new data. However, FIND also reveals that LM-based descriptions capture global function behavior while missing local details. These results suggest that FIND will be useful for characterizing the performance of more sophisticated interpretability methods before they are applied to real-world models.

paragraphs: Automatically describing the computations inside neural networks could help identify failures and guide interventions, but evaluating such descriptions is difficult. FIND provides a benchmark for the building blocks of automated interpretability. It contains procedurally constructed functions resembling network components, paired with descriptions, across text and numerical domains. These functions include complications such as noise, composition, approximation, and bias.

The authors evaluate pretrained language models that describe function behavior using either code or natural language. They also introduce an Automated Interpretability Agent with black-box access to functions. This interactive setup allows the agent to form hypotheses, propose experiments, inspect resulting evidence, and revise its description, making the evaluation about investigation as well as initial description quality.

The agent can sometimes infer function structure, but the benchmark also reveals a recurring weakness: language-model descriptions capture broad behavior while overlooking local details. A plausible overall explanation can therefore miss important behavior in particular cases. The authors suggest using FIND to characterize more sophisticated interpretability methods before applying them to real models, where validating explanations can be harder.
summary.tldr: FIND tests automated function explanations and shows that interactive language-model agents sometimes infer structure while still missing local details.

title: FIND: A Function Description Benchmark for Evaluating Interpretability Methods

abstract: Multiobjective optimization (MOO) plays a critical role in various real-world domains. A major challenge therein is generating $K$ uniform Pareto-optimal solutions to represent the entire Pareto front. To address this issue, this paper firstly introduces \emph{fill distance} to evaluate the $K$ design points, which provides a quantitative metric for the representativeness of the design. However, directly specifying the optimal design that minimizes the fill distance is nearly intractable due to the nested $\min-\max-\min$ optimization problem. To address this, we propose a surrogate ``max-packing'' design for the fill distance design, which is easier to optimize and leads to a rate-optimal design with a fill distance at most $4\times$ the minimum value. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed paradigm efficiently produces high-quality, representative solutions and outperforms baseline methods.

paragraphs: Multiobjective optimization produces trade-offs rather than a single solution that is best on every objective. A useful summary therefore needs several Pareto-optimal solutions distributed across the available trade-offs. This paper asks how to choose K such solutions so they represent the whole Pareto front instead of concentrating in a small region.

The authors introduce fill distance as a measure of representativeness. It captures the largest gap between the front and its nearest selected design point, making uncovered regions central to evaluation. Directly minimizing this quantity creates a difficult nested optimization problem. The proposed alternative is a max-packing design, which is easier to optimize and encourages the selected solutions to spread apart.

The surrogate comes with a guarantee: its fill distance is at most four times the minimum achievable value, and the design is rate-optimal. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report efficient production of representative, high-quality solutions and improvements over baselines. The result connects a tractable selection strategy to a quantitative coverage guarantee, rather than relying only on visual impressions of uniformity.
summary.tldr: A max-packing surrogate selects representative Pareto-optimal solutions with fill distance guaranteed to be within four times the optimum.

title: Gliding over the Pareto Front with Uniform Designs

abstract: Generalization capabilities, or rather a lack thereof, is one of the most important unsolved problems in the field of robot learning, and while several large scale efforts have set out to tackle this problem, unsolved it remains. In this paper, we hypothesize that learning temporal action abstractions using latent variable models (LVMs), which learn to map data to a compressed latent space and back, is apromising direction towards low-level skills that can readily be used for new tasks. Although several works have attempted to show this, they have generally been limited by architectures that do not faithfully capture sharable representations. To address this we present Quantized Skill Transformer (QueST), which learns a larger and more flexible latent encoding that is more capable of modeling the breadth of low-level skills necessary for a variety of tasks. To make use of this extra flexibility, QueST imparts causal inductive bias from the action sequence data into the latent space, leading to more semantically useful and transferable representations. We compare to state-of-the-art imitation learning and LVM baselines and see that QueST’s architecture leads to strong performance on several multitask and few-shot learning benchmarks. Further results and videos are available at https://quest-model.github.io.
