Experimental evaluations on three benchmark tasks, namely video depth estimation, camera pose estimation, and camera intrinsics estimation, demonstrate that our 4D modeling achieves superior performance in capturing physical-scale measurements with greater global accuracy than existing methods.

paragraphs: DynamicVerse turns real-world videos into representations of three-dimensional scenes evolving over time. Its emphasis is physical scale: recovering measurements tied to the real world, rather than geometry known only up to an arbitrary scale. It also combines geometry with motion, object masks, and descriptive language, providing several complementary views of the same dynamic scene.

The framework uses large vision, geometric, and multimodal models to estimate these different components. It combines bundle adjustment within video windows with global optimization to process long sequences into a coherent 4D format. This links local geometric estimates with consistency across the full video, addressing the need to describe extended real-world activity.

The resulting dataset contains more than 100,000 videos, 800,000 annotated masks, and 10 million frames sourced from internet videos. Evaluations cover video depth, camera pose, and camera intrinsics estimation. The authors report better physical-scale measurements and greater global accuracy than existing methods. These results support the framework's ability to produce geometrically useful annotations alongside motion and semantic information for dynamic world modeling.
summary.tldr: DynamicVerse converts real-world videos into physically scaled 4D data combining geometry, motion, object masks, and descriptions.

title: DynamicVerse: A Physically-Aware Multimodal Framework for 4D World Modeling

abstract: Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDD) seeks to condense large-scale image-text datasets into compact surrogates while retaining their effectiveness for cross-modal learning. Despite recent progress, existing MDD approaches often suffer from ***Modality Collapse***, characterized by over-concentrated intra-modal representations and enlarged distributional gap across modalities. In this paper, at the first time, we identify this issue as stemming from a fundamental conflict between the over-compression behavior inherent in dataset distillation and the cross-modal supervision imposed by contrastive objectives. To alleviate modality collapse, we introduce **RepBlend**, a novel MDD framework that weakens overdominant cross-modal supervision via representation blending, thereby significantly enhancing intra-modal diversity. Additionally, we observe that current MDD methods impose asymmetric supervision across modalities, resulting in biased optimization. To address this, we propose symmetric projection trajectory matching, which synchronizes the optimization dynamics using modality-specific projection heads, thereby promoting balanced supervision and enhancing cross-modal alignment. Experiments on Flickr-30K and MS-COCO show that RepBlend consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art MDD methods, achieving significant gains in retrieval performance (e.g., +9.4 IR@10, +6.3 TR@10 under the 100-pair setting) and offering up to 6.7$\times$ distillation speedup.

Reported gains include +9.4 IR@10 and +6.3 TR@10 with 100 image-text pairs, alongside distillation speedups reaching 6.7 times. title: Beyond Modality Collapse: Representation Blending for Multimodal Dataset Distillation

abstract: The online caching problem aims to minimize cache misses when serving a sequence of requests under a limited cache size. While naive learning-augmented caching algorithms achieve ideal $1$-consistency, they lack robustness guarantees. Existing robustification methods either sacrifice $1$-consistency or introduce excessive computational overhead. In this paper, we introduce Guard, a lightweight robustification framework that enhances the robustness of a broad class of learning-augmented caching algorithms to $2H_{k-1} + 2$, while preserving their $1$-consistency. Guard achieves the current best-known trade-off between consistency and robustness, with only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ additional per-request overhead, thereby maintaining the original time complexity of the base algorithm. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets and prediction models validate the effectiveness of Guard in practice.

paragraphs: A cache has limited space, so it must choose what to retain as requests arrive. Predictions can improve those choices, but a prediction-guided algorithm may perform poorly when its advice is unreliable. This paper addresses the challenge of adding worst-case protection while preserving the best-case benefit of accurate predictions.

The proposed Guard framework applies to a broad class of learning-augmented caching algorithms. It preserves 1-consistency, the ideal guarantee associated with correct predictions, while providing a robustness bound of 2H_{k-1} + 2. Here, the bound depends on cache size through a harmonic-number expression. The authors describe this as the best-known consistency–robustness tradeoff.

Guard adds only constant computational overhead per request, so it maintains the original time complexity of the underlying algorithm. This is central to its contribution because earlier robustification approaches either weakened consistency or introduced excessive computation. Experiments across multiple real-world datasets and prediction models support its practical effectiveness. The result is a lightweight way to retain the advantages of prediction-based caching while placing a theoretical bound on behavior when predictions are unreliable.
summary.tldr: Guard adds robustness guarantees to prediction-guided caching while preserving 1-consistency and constant additional work per request.

title: Robustifying Learning-Augmented Caching Efficiently without Compromising 1-Consistency

abstract: Learning transferable data representations from abundant unlabeled data remains a central challenge in machine learning. Although numerous self-supervised learning methods have been proposed to address this challenge, a significant class of these approaches aligns the covariance or correlation matrix with the identity matrix. Despite impressive performance across various downstream tasks, these methods often suffer from biased sample risk, leading to substantial optimization shifts in mini-batch settings and complicating theoretical analysis. In this paper, we introduce a novel \underline{\bf Adv}ersarial \underline{\bf S}elf-\underline{\bf S}upervised Representation \underline{\bf L}earning (Adv-SSL) for unbiased transfer learning with no additional cost compared to its biased counterparts. Our approach not only outperforms the existing methods across multiple benchmark datasets but is also supported by comprehensive end-to-end theoretical guarantees. Our analysis reveals that the minimax optimization in Adv-SSL encourages representations to form well-separated clusters in the embedding space, provided there is sufficient upstream unlabeled data. As a result, our method achieves strong classification performance even with limited downstream labels, shedding new light on few-shot learning.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning aims to extract useful representations from unlabeled examples so that later tasks need fewer labels. This paper examines methods that push a representation's covariance or correlation matrix toward the identity matrix. The authors identify a problem with these objectives: estimates computed from finite samples can be biased, shifting what the model optimizes when training uses small batches.

Adv-SSL replaces this approach with an adversarial, minimax formulation designed to support unbiased transfer learning. The authors report that it does so without additional cost relative to the biased alternatives they consider. Their contribution combines a training method with theoretical guarantees connecting representation learning to subsequent classification.

The analysis shows that the minimax objective encourages distinct clusters in representation space when sufficiently much unlabeled training data is available. That condition matters: the clustering conclusion depends on adequate upstream data. Experiments report improvements over existing methods across multiple benchmarks, alongside strong classification with few downstream labels. Together, these findings connect a correction to the learning objective with representations that transfer effectively.
summary.tldr: Adv-SSL uses adversarial optimization to address biased self-supervised objectives and supports effective transfer with few labels.

title: Adv-SSL: Adversarial Self-Supervised Representation Learning with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Blind-spot denoising (BSD) method is a powerful paradigm for zero-shot image denoising by training models to predict masked target pixels from their neighbors. However, they struggle with real-world noise exhibiting strong local correlations, where efforts to suppress noise correlation often weaken pixel-value dependencies, adversely affecting denoising performance. This paper presents a theoretical analysis quantifying the impact of replacing masked pixels with observations exhibiting weaker noise correlation but potentially reduced similarity, revealing a trade-off that impacts the statistical risk of the estimation. Guided by this insight, we propose a computational scheme that replaces masked pixels with distant ones of similar appearance and lower noise correlation. This strategy improves the prediction by balancing noise suppression and structural consistency. Experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method, outperforming existing zero-shot BSD methods.

paragraphs: Blind-spot denoising learns to predict hidden image pixels from surrounding observations. Real-world noise complicates this approach when nearby pixels have strongly correlated noise. Attempts to weaken that correlation can also disrupt useful relationships among pixel values, creating a trade-off between removing shared noise and preserving the image structure needed for accurate prediction.

The paper analyzes this trade-off theoretically by considering replacements with weaker noise correlation but potentially lower similarity. It quantifies how both factors affect statistical estimation risk. Guided by that analysis, the proposed method refills masked locations using distant pixels with similar appearances and lower noise correlation, balancing the two properties in its computational scheme.

The authors report that this strategy outperforms existing zero-shot blind-spot denoising methods in experiments. Its significance lies in treating replacement-pixel selection as a balance between statistical and visual compatibility. A useful replacement should reduce the influence of correlated noise while retaining enough similarity to preserve the dependencies that help reconstruct the underlying image.
summary.tldr: The method improves blind-spot denoising by refilling masked pixels with distant, similar observations that have less-correlated noise.

title: Zero-Shot Blind-Spot Image Denoising via Cross-Scale Non-Local Pixel Refilling

abstract: Understanding what and how neural networks memorize during training is crucial, both from the perspective of unintentional memorization of potentially sensitive information and from the standpoint of effective knowledge acquisition for real-world, knowledge-intensive tasks. While previous studies primarily investigate memorization within a single modality, such as text memorization in large language models or image memorization in diffusion models, unified multimodal models are becoming increasingly prevalent in practical applications. In this work, we focus on the unique characteristics of cross-modality memorization and conduct a systematic study centered on vision-language models. To facilitate controlled experiments, we first introduce a synthetic persona dataset comprising diverse synthetic person images and textual descriptions. We quantify factual knowledge memorization and cross-modal transferability by training models on a single modality and evaluating their performance in the other. Our results reveal that facts learned in one modality transfer to the other, but a significant gap exists between recalling information in the source and target modalities. Furthermore, we observe that this gap exists across various scenarios, including more capable models, machine unlearning, and the multi-hop case. At the end, we propose a baseline method to mitigate this challenge. We hope our study can inspire future research on developing more robust multimodal learning techniques to enhance cross-modal transferability.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may learn a fact through one modality without recalling it equally well through another. This paper studies that cross-modality gap directly. The question matters both for useful knowledge acquisition and for understanding how memorized, potentially sensitive information can be accessed through different kinds of input.

The authors create a synthetic persona dataset containing generated person images and textual descriptions. This gives them a controlled setting for teaching facts through one modality and testing recall through the other. The design separates how well the model remembers information in its original modality from how well that knowledge transfers across modalities.

The experiments show that transfer does occur, but recall in the target modality trails recall in the source modality by a substantial margin. The gap also appears with more capable models, in machine-unlearning settings, and in multi-hop cases. The authors propose a baseline approach to mitigate it. The findings identify cross-modal accessibility as a distinct concern when evaluating what a multimodal model has learned.
summary.tldr: Controlled persona experiments show that memorized facts transfer between vision and language, but recall remains substantially weaker across modalities.

title: Quantifying Cross-Modality Memorization in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a predominant technique to align language models (LMs) with human preferences or promote outputs which are deemed to be desirable by a given reward function. Standard RL approaches optimize average reward, while methods explicitly focused on reducing the probability of undesired outputs typically come at a cost to average-case performance. To improve this tradeoff, we introduce RePULSe, a new training method that augments the standard RL loss with an additional loss that uses learned proposals to guide sampling low-reward outputs, and then reduces those outputs’ probability. We run experiments demonstrating that RePULSe produces a better tradeoff of expected reward versus the probability of undesired outputs and is more adversarially robust, compared to standard RL alignment approaches and alternatives.

To improve this tradeoff, we introduce RePULSe, a new training method that augments the standard RL loss with an additional loss that uses learned proposals to guide sampling low-reward outputs, and then reduces those outputs’ probability. We run experiments demonstrating that RePULSe produces a better tradeoff of expected reward versus the probability of undesired outputs and is more adversarially robust, compared to standard RL alignment approaches and alternatives.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly aligns language models by maximizing average reward. That objective does not directly express how often the model produces low-reward outputs. Existing approaches that explicitly suppress undesirable outputs can reduce average-case performance, creating a tradeoff between typical quality and the probability of unwanted behavior.

RePULSe adds a targeted loss to the standard reinforcement learning objective. Learned proposals guide the sampling process toward low-reward outputs, and the added loss reduces their probability. This gives training a mechanism for locating and discouraging undesirable responses while retaining the usual objective that promotes high expected reward. Undesirability here is tied to the reward function used for alignment.

The experiments show a better tradeoff between expected reward and the probability of undesirable outputs than standard reinforcement learning alignment methods and the alternatives evaluated. They also report greater adversarial robustness. The findings support targeted sampling as a way to improve this balance, rather than establishing that unwanted outputs disappear entirely or that average performance must be sacrificed to reduce them.
summary.tldr: RePULSe targets sampled low-reward responses during training, improving the tradeoff between average reward and undesirable-output probability.

title: Reducing the Probability of Undesirable Outputs in Language Models Using Probabilistic Inference

abstract: Recent studies on Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shifted from the end-to-end action-generation paradigm toward a pipeline involving task planning followed by action generation, demonstrating improved performance on various complex, long-horizon manipulation tasks. However, existing approaches vary significantly in terms of network architectures, planning paradigms, representations, and training data sources, making it challenging for researchers to identify the precise sources of performance gains and determine which component is more difficult to learn. To systematically investigate the impacts of different planning paradigms and representations isolating from network architectures and training data, in this paper, we introduce \name, a unified VLA architecture suite capable of various task planning paradigms, and design a comprehensive suite of controlled experiments across diverse object categories (rigid and deformable), visual modalities (2D and 3D), environments (simulation and real-world), and end-effectors (grippers and dexterous hands). Our results demonstrate that: 1) visually grounded planning representations are generally better than language planning representations; 2) the Hierarchical-VLA paradigm generally achieves superior performance than other paradigms, albeit at the cost of slower training and inference speeds.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action systems increasingly plan a task before generating actions, with reported improvements on complex, long-horizon manipulation. Comparing those approaches is difficult because their architectures, planning formats, and training data often differ simultaneously. VLA-OS provides a unified architecture suite to study planning choices while isolating them from architecture and data differences.

The controlled experiments cover rigid and deformable objects, 2D and 3D visual inputs, simulated and real environments, and both grippers and dexterous hands. This range lets the study examine planning representations and paradigms across varied manipulation settings rather than tying the comparison to a single type of robot interaction.

Two main findings emerge. Planning representations grounded in visual information generally outperform language-based representations. Hierarchical-VLA also generally performs better than the other paradigms, but requires slower training and inference. The study therefore offers evidence about which planning choices help and identifies a concrete speed tradeoff, while preserving that these are general tendencies in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: VLA-OS isolates planning choices and finds that visual grounding and hierarchical planning generally help, with hierarchical planning costing additional time.

title: VLA-OS: Structuring and Dissecting Planning Representations and Paradigms in Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Machine learning models are often vulnerable to inference attacks that expose sensitive information from their training data. Shadow model technique is commonly employed in such attacks, like membership inference. However, the need for a large number of shadow models leads to high computational costs, limiting their practical applicability. Such inefficiency mainly stems from the independent training and use of these shadow models. To address this issue, we present a novel shadow pool training framework SHAPOOL, which constructs multiple shared models and trains them jointly within a single process. In particular, we leverage the Mixture-of-Experts mechanism as the shadow pool to interconnect individual models, enabling them to share some sub-networks and thereby improving efficiency. To ensure the shared models closely resemble independent models and serve as effective substitutes, we introduce three novel modules: path-choice routing, pathway regularization, and pathway alignment. These modules guarantee random data allocation for pathway learning, promote diversity among shared models, and maintain consistency with target models. We evaluate SHAPOOL in the context of various membership inference attacks and show that it significantly reduces the computational cost of shadow model construction while maintaining comparable attack performance.

paragraphs: Inference attacks can expose information about a model's training data, including whether a particular example was used. Such attacks often depend on many shadow models, whose independent training is computationally expensive. SHAPOOL reduces this cost by constructing shared models and training them jointly in one process.

The framework uses a mixture-of-experts structure so that different models can share subnetworks. Sharing must still preserve the properties that make separate shadow models useful. Path-choice routing, pathway regularization, and pathway alignment address this through random data allocation for pathway learning, diversity among shared models, and consistency with target models.

The authors evaluate SHAPOOL across several membership inference attacks and report significantly lower shadow-model construction costs with comparable attack performance. The result supports shared training as a substitute for independently constructing every shadow model in the evaluated attacks. The key contribution is making that substitution efficient while explicitly addressing the diversity and target resemblance that sharing could otherwise undermine.
summary.tldr: SHAPOOL shares subnetworks across jointly trained shadow models to reduce membership-inference attack costs while maintaining comparable effectiveness.

title: Toward Efficient Inference Attacks: Shadow Model Sharing via Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Video object removal has achieved advanced performance due to the recent success of video generative models. However, when addressing the side effects of objects, \textit{e.g.,} their shadows and reflections, existing works struggle to eliminate these effects for the scarcity of paired video data as supervision. This paper presents \method, termed \textbf{R}emove \textbf{O}bjects with \textbf{S}ide \textbf{E}ffects, a framework that systematically studies the object's effects on environment, which can be categorized into five common cases: shadows, reflections, light, translucency and mirror. Given the challenges of curating paired videos exhibiting the aforementioned effects, we leverage a 3D rendering engine for synthetic data generation. We carefully construct a fully-automatic pipeline for data preparation, which simulates a large-scale paired dataset with diverse scenes, objects, shooting angles, and camera trajectories. ROSE is implemented as an video inpainting model built on diffusion transformer. To localize all object-correlated areas, the entire video is fed into the model for reference-based erasing. Moreover, additional supervision is introduced to explicitly predict the areas affected by side effects, which can be revealed through the differential mask between the paired videos. To fully investigate the model performance on various side effect removal, we presents a new benchmark, dubbed ROSE-Bench, incorporating both common scenarios and the five special side effects for comprehensive evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that \method achieves superior performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios.

paragraphs: Removing an object from a video also requires removing its effects on the surrounding scene. A shadow or reflection can reveal the object even after its visible body disappears. ROSE studies five categories of these effects: shadows, reflections, light, translucency, and mirrors. A central obstacle is the scarcity of paired videos that can supervise their removal.

The authors build an automatic synthetic-data pipeline using a 3D rendering engine. It produces paired videos across varied scenes, objects, camera angles, and camera trajectories. ROSE itself is a diffusion-transformer video inpainting model that receives the whole video for reference-based erasing. Additional supervision teaches it to predict affected regions using difference masks derived from the paired videos.

The paper also introduces ROSE-Bench, covering ordinary removal scenarios and the five effect categories. Experiments show superior performance to existing video object-erasing models and good generalization to real-world videos. The approach links deliberately constructed supervision with explicit localization of environmental effects, helping the model treat removal as a scene-wide editing problem.
summary.tldr: ROSE uses synthetic paired videos and explicit effect-region supervision to remove objects together with their shadows, reflections, and other visual effects.

title: ROSE: Remove Objects with Side Effects in Videos

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced in reasoning tasks through reinforcement learning (RL) optimization, achieving impressive capabilities across various challenging benchmarks. However, our empirical analysis reveals a critical drawback: reasoning-oriented RL fine-tuning significantly increases the prevalence of hallucinations. We theoretically analyze the RL training dynamics, identifying high-variance gradient, entropy-induced randomness, and susceptibility to spurious local optima as key factors leading to hallucinations. To address this drawback, we propose Factuality-aware Step-wise Policy Optimization (FSPO), an innovative RL fine-tuning algorithm incorporating explicit factuality verification at each reasoning step. FSPO leverages automated verification against given evidence to dynamically adjust token-level advantage values, incentivizing factual correctness throughout the reasoning process. Experiments across mathematical reasoning and hallucination benchmarks using Qwen2.5 and Llama models demonstrate that FSPO effectively reduces hallucinations while enhancing reasoning accuracy, substantially improving both reliability and performance.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve language-model reasoning, but the paper reports an accompanying problem: reasoning-oriented fine-tuning increases hallucinations in its empirical analysis. The authors examine the training dynamics and identify high-variance gradients, randomness induced by entropy, and susceptibility to spurious local optima as factors contributing to this behavior.

Their proposed algorithm, Factuality-aware Step-wise Policy Optimization, introduces factual verification throughout the reasoning sequence. It automatically checks each step against supplied evidence and uses those checks to adjust token-level advantage values. These values influence which generated tokens training encourages, making factual correctness part of the learning signal during reasoning rather than leaving it implicit.

Experiments with Qwen2.5 and Llama models cover mathematical reasoning and hallucination benchmarks. The reported results show reduced hallucinations alongside improved reasoning accuracy. The findings support adding evidence-based feedback at intermediate steps, rather than treating reasoning performance as sufficient evidence of reliability. Because verification operates against given evidence, that evidence is an explicit part of how the proposed training method assesses factual correctness.
summary.tldr: FSPO checks reasoning steps against supplied evidence and adjusts reinforcement-learning feedback to reduce hallucinations while improving reasoning.

title: Reasoning Models Hallucinate More: Factuality-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models

abstract: To enhance the generalization ability of graph neural networks (GNNs) in learning and simulation physical dynamics, a series of equivariant GNNs have been developed to incorporate the symmetric inductive bias. However, the existing methods do not take into account the non-stationarity nature of physical dynamics, where the joint distribution changes over time. Moreover, previous approaches for modeling non-stationary time series typically involve normalizing the data, which disrupts the symmetric assumption inherent in physical dynamics. To model the non-stationary physical dynamics while preserving the symmetric inductive bias, we introduce a Non-Stationary Equivariant Graph Neural Network (NS-EGNN) to capture the non-stationarity in physical dynamics while preserving the symmetric property of the model. Specifically, NS-EGNN employs Fourier Transform on segments of physical dynamics to extract time-varying frequency information from the trajectories. It then uses the first and second-order differences to mitigate non-stationarity, followed by pooling for future predictions. Through capturing varying frequency characteristics and alleviate the linear and quadric trend in the raw physical dynamics, NS-EGNN better models the temporal dependencies in the physical dynamics. NS-EGNN has been applied on various types of physical dynamics, including molecular, motion and protein dynamics. In various scenario, NS-EGNN consistently surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art algorithms, underscoring its effectiveness. The implementation of NS-EGNN is available at https://github.com/MaojiWEN/NS-EGNN.

abstract: Harmful fine-tuning attack introduces significant security risks to the fine-tuning services. Main-stream defenses aim to vaccinate the model such that the later harmful fine-tuning attack is less effective. However, our evaluation results show that such defenses are fragile-- with a few fine-tuning steps, the model still can learn the harmful knowledge. To this end, we do further experiment and find that an embarrassingly simple solution-- adding purely random perturbations to the fine-tuned model, can recover the model from harmful behaviors, though it leads to a degradation in the model’s fine-tuning performance. To address the degradation of fine-tuning performance, we further propose \methodname, which optimizes an adaptive perturbation that will be applied to the model after fine-tuning. \methodname maintains model's safety alignment performance without compromising downstream fine-tuning performance. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on different harmful ratios, fine-tuning tasks and mainstream LLMs, where the average harmful scores are reduced by up-to 21.2%, while maintaining fine-tuning performance. As a by-product, we analyze the adaptive perturbation and show that different layers in various LLMs have distinct safety coefficients. Source code available at https://github.com/w-yibo/Panacea.

This paper evaluates defenses intended to protect models before such tuning and finds that harmful knowledge can still be learned within a few training steps. It then investigates whether changing the model after fine-tuning can restore safer behavior.

An initial experiment finds that purely random perturbations can reduce the harmful behavior, but also damage performance on the intended fine-tuning task. Panacea develops this observation into an adaptive perturbation optimized for application after fine-tuning. Its purpose is to retain the safety benefit while avoiding the loss of useful task performance seen with random changes.

Experiments vary the proportion of harmful data, fine-tuning tasks, and language models. The authors report reductions in average harmful scores of up to 21.2% while maintaining fine-tuning performance. Their analysis also finds distinct safety coefficients across layers in different models. The results support post-fine-tuning perturbation as a way to address the evaluated attacks while preserving the task adaptation that motivated fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: Panacea applies an optimized perturbation after fine-tuning to reduce harmful behavior while preserving task performance in the reported experiments.

title: Panacea: Mitigating Harmful Fine-tuning for Large Language Models via Post-fine-tuning Perturbation

abstract: Machine learning (ML) is transforming modeling and control in the physical, engineering, and biological sciences. However, rapid development has outpaced the creation of standardized, objective benchmarks—leading to weak baselines, reporting bias, and inconsistent evaluations across methods. This undermines reproducibility, misguides resource allocation, and obscures scientific progress. To address this, we propose a Common Task Framework (CTF) for scientific machine learning. The CTF features a curated set of datasets and task-specific metrics spanning forecasting, state reconstruction, and generalization under realistic constraints, including noise and limited data. Inspired by the success of CTFs in fields like natural language processing and computer vision, our framework provides a structured, rigorous foundation for head-to-head evaluation of diverse algorithms. As a first step, we benchmark methods on two canonical nonlinear systems: Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Lorenz. These results illustrate the utility of the CTF in revealing method strengths, limitations, and suitability for specific classes of problems and diverse objectives. Next, we are launching a competition around a global real world sea surface temperature dataset with a true holdout dataset to foster community engagement. Our long-term vision is to replace ad hoc comparisons with standardized evaluations on hidden test sets that raise the bar for rigor and reproducibility in scientific ML.

paragraphs: Scientific machine learning needs comparisons that reveal which methods work for which problems. This paper argues that weak baselines, selective reporting, and inconsistent evaluations make that difficult. Its proposed Common Task Framework gives competing algorithms shared datasets and task-specific metrics, making their results easier to compare directly.

The framework covers forecasting, reconstructing system states, and generalizing under realistic conditions such as noisy observations and limited data. Its initial benchmarks use the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Lorenz systems. The authors present these evaluations as demonstrations of how common tasks can expose different methods’ strengths, limitations, and suitability for particular objectives.

The broader contribution is an evaluation structure intended to replace ad hoc comparisons with reproducible assessments on hidden test data, helping researchers judge progress and allocate resources more meaningfully.
summary.tldr: A shared benchmarking framework aims to make scientific machine learning comparisons more rigorous and reproducible.

title: Common Task Framework For a Critical Evaluation of Scientific Machine Learning Algorithms

abstract: Integration is affected by the curse of dimensionality and quickly becomes intractable as the dimensionality of the problem grows. We propose a randomized algorithm that, with high probability, gives a constant-factor approximation of a general discrete integral defined over an exponentially large set. This algorithm relies on solving only a small number of instances of a discrete combinatorial optimization problem subject to randomly generated parity constraints used as a hash function. As an application, we demonstrate that with a small number of MAP queries we can efficiently approximate the partition function of discrete graphical models, which can in turn be used, for instance, for marginal computation or model selection.

paragraphs: A discrete integral adds contributions across a set of possibilities. When that set grows exponentially with the number of variables, direct summation quickly becomes impractical. This paper proposes a randomized method that approximates a general discrete integral within a constant factor with high probability, addressing the cost of reasoning over such enormous spaces.

The algorithm uses a small number of discrete combinatorial optimization problems with randomly generated parity constraints. These constraints act as a hash function, organizing the original space through randomized restrictions. The approach turns an integration task into a limited collection of constrained optimization tasks, connecting the ability to find good configurations with the ability to estimate an aggregate over configurations.

As an application, the authors approximate the partition function of a discrete graphical model using a small number of maximum a posteriori queries. The partition function normalizes the model's probabilities and can support marginal computation or model selection. The stated guarantee is a high-probability constant-factor approximation, giving a precise form of approximate integration rather than an exact sum.
summary.tldr: Random parity constraints turn a small number of optimization queries into a high-probability constant-factor approximation of discrete integrals.

title: Taming the Curse of Dimensionality: Discrete Integration by Hashing and Optimization

abstract: Much research in Bayesian modeling has been done to elicit a prior distribution that incorporates domain knowledge. We present a novel and more direct approach by imposing First-Order Logic (FOL) rules on the posterior distribution. Our approach unifies FOL and Bayesian modeling under the regularized Bayesian framework. In addition, our approach automatically estimates the uncertainty of FOL rules when they are produced by humans, so that reliable rules are incorporated while unreliable ones are ignored. We apply our approach to latent topic modeling tasks and demonstrate that by combining FOL knowledge and Bayesian modeling, we both improve the task performance and discover more structured latent representations in unsupervised and supervised learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian models often incorporate domain knowledge through a prior distribution. This paper offers a more direct route: express knowledge as first-order logic rules and impose those rules on the posterior distribution. The regularized Bayesian framework provides the machinery for combining logical statements with probabilistic learning.

Human-provided rules can differ in reliability, so the method also estimates their uncertainty automatically. Reliable rules are incorporated, while unreliable ones are ignored. This selective treatment matters because the model should benefit from useful knowledge without giving every supplied statement the same influence. Reliability assessment is therefore part of the proposed integration of logic and Bayesian modeling.

The authors apply the approach to latent topic modeling in both unsupervised and supervised learning. They report improved task performance and more structured latent representations from combining the two sources of information. These findings suggest that logical knowledge can influence both prediction-related outcomes and the organization of hidden topics when its reliability is assessed within the framework.
summary.tldr: Robust RegBayes incorporates reliable logical rules into Bayesian posteriors while estimating and filtering unreliable human-provided knowledge.

title: Robust RegBayes: Selectively Incorporating First-Order Logic Domain Knowledge into Bayesian Models

abstract: Many problems of practical interest rely on Continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) defined over combinatorial state spaces, rendering the computation of transition probabilities, and hence probabilistic inference, difficult or impossible with existing methods. For problems with countably infinite states, where classical methods such as matrix exponentiation are not applicable, the main alternative has been particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods imputing both the holding times and sequences of visited states. We propose a particle-based Monte Carlo approach where the holding times are marginalized analytically. We demonstrate that in a range of realistic inferential setups, our scheme dramatically reduces the variance of the Monte Carlo approximation and yields more accurate parameter posterior approximations given a fixed computational budget. These experiments are performed on both synthetic and real datasets, drawing from two important examples of CTMCs having combinatorial state spaces: string-valued mutation models in phylogenetics and nucleic acid folding pathways.

paragraphs: Continuous-time Markov chains can describe systems whose possible states form enormous combinatorial spaces. Computing transition probabilities in these spaces can be difficult or infeasible. For countably infinite state spaces, the abstract identifies particle Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative to classical matrix-exponentiation methods.

Existing particle approaches impute both the sequence of visited states and the holding times spent in those states. This paper proposes analytically marginalizing the holding times within a particle-based Monte Carlo method. The holding times are therefore accounted for through calculation instead of being explicitly sampled along with the state sequence.

Across the tested inference settings, this change dramatically reduces the variance of the Monte Carlo approximation. With the same computational budget, the method also produces more accurate approximations to parameter posterior distributions. The experiments include synthetic and real data from string-valued mutation models in phylogenetics and nucleic acid folding pathways. These findings demonstrate the practical value of integrating out part of a complex stochastic trajectory when that calculation is available.
summary.tldr: Analytically integrating out holding times improves particle-based inference for continuous-time Markov chains in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Continuous-Time Markov Chain Estimation

abstract: Applications of machine learning methods increasingly deal with graph structured data through kernels. Most existing graph kernels compare graphs in terms of features defined on small subgraphs such as walks, paths or graphlets, adopting an inherently local perspective. However, several interesting properties such as girth or chromatic number are global properties of the graph, and are not captured in local substructures. This paper presents two graph kernels defined on unlabeled graphs which capture global properties of graphs using the celebrated Lovász number and its associated orthonormal representation. We make progress towards theoretical results aiding kernel choice, proving a result about the separation margin of our kernel for classes of graphs. We give empirical results on classification of synthesized graphs with important global properties as well as established benchmark graph datasets, showing that the accuracy of our kernels is better than or competitive to existing graph kernels.

paragraphs: Graph kernels let learning algorithms compare graph-structured objects. Many existing kernels build this comparison from small pieces such as walks, paths, or graphlets. The paper argues that this local perspective misses important global properties, including girth and chromatic number, motivating comparisons that account for the graph as a whole.

The authors introduce two kernels for unlabeled graphs using the Lovász number and its associated orthonormal representation. These mathematical constructions provide a geometric way to capture global graph properties. The paper also proves a result about the kernel's separation margin for classes of graphs, offering theoretical support relevant to choosing a kernel.

Evaluation includes synthetic graphs designed around important global properties and established graph benchmark datasets. The reported classification accuracy is better than or competitive with existing graph kernels. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support global geometric representations as a useful basis for graph comparison, with competitive performance across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Two graph kernels use geometric representations to capture global structure and achieve better or competitive classification accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Global graph kernels using geometric embeddings

abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian networks and neural networks with stochastic hidden units are commonly perceived as two separate types of models. We show that either of these types of models can often be transformed into an instance of the other, by switching between centered and differentiable non-centered parameterizations of the latent variables. The choice of parameterization greatly influences the efficiency of gradient-based posterior inference; we show that they are often complementary to eachother, we clarify when each parameterization is preferred and show how inference can be made robust. In the non-centered form, a simple Monte Carlo estimator of the marginal likelihood can be used for learning the parameters. Theoretical results are supported by experiments.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Bayesian networks and neural networks with stochastic hidden units are often treated as separate model families. This paper shows that they can often be expressed as instances of one another. The connection comes from changing how latent variables are parameterized, specifically by switching between centered and differentiable non-centered forms.

This change of representation matters computationally. The authors show that the choice can substantially affect the efficiency of gradient-based posterior inference. The two forms are often complementary, and the paper clarifies when each is preferable and how to make inference robust. The result supports choosing a parameterization according to the inference problem rather than assuming one form is always better.

In the non-centered form, a simple Monte Carlo estimator of marginal likelihood can also be used to learn model parameters. The paper therefore connects model representation to both posterior inference and parameter learning. Experiments support its theoretical results. Its central contribution is the ability to move between useful formulations and exploit their different computational properties, with transformations described as available often rather than universally.
summary.tldr: Switching latent-variable parameterizations often connects Bayesian and stochastic neural networks and can improve gradient-based inference.

title: Efficient Gradient-Based Inference through Transformations between Bayes Nets and Neural Nets

abstract: We propose Significance-Offset Convolutional Neural Network, a deep convolutional network architecture for regression of multivariate asynchronous time series. The model is inspired by standard autoregressive (AR) models and gating mechanisms used in recurrent neural networks. It involves an AR-like weighting system, where the final predictor is obtained as a weighted sum of adjusted regressors, while the weights are data-dependent functions learnt through a convolutional network. The architecture was designed for applications on asynchronous time series and is evaluated on such datasets: a hedge fund proprietary dataset of over 2 million quotes for a credit derivative index, an artificially generated noisy autoregressive series and UCI household electricity consumption dataset. The proposed architecture achieves promising results as compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression for multivariate asynchronous time series, where several observed quantities need not arrive on a shared schedule. It introduces the Significance-Offset Convolutional Neural Network, an architecture designed for this setting. The design combines ideas from autoregressive models with the gating mechanisms used in recurrent neural networks.

Its final prediction is a weighted sum of adjusted regressors. This resembles an autoregressive predictor, but the weights are learned functions of the data, computed by a convolutional network. Consequently, the architecture can vary how much different inputs contribute to a prediction instead of using one fixed set of weights for every situation.

The authors evaluate the model on a proprietary financial dataset containing over two million credit derivative index quotes, a synthetic noisy autoregressive series, and household electricity consumption data. They report promising results compared with convolutional and recurrent networks. These findings support the proposed combination of adaptive weighting and adjusted inputs as a useful architecture for asynchronous time-series regression in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A convolutional architecture predicts asynchronous time series through data-dependent weights applied to adjusted regressors.

title: Autoregressive Convolutional Neural Networks for Asynchronous Time Series

abstract: We introduce SCAL, an algorithm designed to perform efficient exploration-exploration in any unknown weakly-communicating Markov Decision Process (MDP) for which an upper bound c on the span of the optimal bias function is known. For an MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and $\Gamma \leq S$ possible next states, we prove a regret bound of $O(c\sqrt{\Gamma SAT})$, which significantly improves over existing algorithms (e.g., UCRL and PSRL), whose regret scales linearly with the MDP diameter $D$. In fact, the optimal bias span is finite and often much smaller than $D$ (e.g., $D=+\infty$ in non-communicating MDPs). A similar result was originally derived by Bartlett and Tewari (2009) for REGAL.C, for which no tractable algorithm is available. In this paper, we relax the optimization problem at the core of REGAL.C, we carefully analyze its properties, and we provide the first computationally efficient algorithm to solve it. Finally, we report numerical simulations supporting our theoretical findings and showing how SCAL significantly outperforms UCRL in MDPs with large diameter and small span.

paragraphs: SCAL addresses exploration and exploitation in unknown, weakly communicating Markov Decision Processes. Its key requirement is a known upper bound c on the span of the optimal bias function. This quantity offers an alternative to the MDP diameter, which can be much larger and can even be infinite in noncommunicating cases.

For S states, A actions, and at most Γ possible next states, the authors prove regret of order c√(ΓSAT). The significance is the dependence on the bias-span bound rather than a linear dependence on diameter, as in the cited existing algorithms. This can yield a substantially better guarantee when the span is small relative to the diameter.

A similar theoretical result existed for REGAL.C without a tractable algorithm. The paper relaxes its central optimization problem and supplies a computationally efficient solution. Simulations support the analysis and show SCAL significantly outperforming UCRL in large-diameter, small-span environments, connecting the favorable theoretical dependence to observed performance in that setting.
summary.tldr: SCAL efficiently explores unknown weakly communicating MDPs using a known bias-span bound, improving guarantees when diameter is large relative to span.

title: Efficient Bias-Span-Constrained Exploration-Exploitation in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) is a widely used algorithm for recovering sparse high dimensional vectors in linear regression models. The optimal performance of OMP requires a priori knowledge of either the sparsity of regression vector or noise statistics. Both these statistics are rarely known a priori and are very difficult to estimate. In this paper, we present a novel technique called residual ratio thresholding (RRT) to operate OMP without any a priori knowledge of sparsity and noise statistics and establish finite sample and large sample support recovery guarantees for the same. Both analytical results and numerical simulations in real and synthetic data sets indicate that RRT has a performance comparable to OMP with a priori knowledge of sparsity and noise statistics.

The optimal performance of OMP requires a priori knowledge of either the sparsity of regression vector or noise statistics. Both these statistics are rarely known a priori and are very difficult to estimate. In this paper, we present a novel technique called residual ratio thresholding (RRT) to operate OMP without any a priori knowledge of sparsity and noise statistics and establish finite sample and large sample support recovery guarantees for the same. Both analytical results and numerical simulations in real and synthetic data sets indicate that RRT has a performance comparable to OMP with a priori knowledge of sparsity and noise statistics.

paragraphs: Orthogonal matching pursuit recovers sparse, high-dimensional regression vectors, where only a limited number of entries are nonzero. The paper identifies a practical obstacle to its optimal performance: it requires advance knowledge of either the vector's sparsity or the noise statistics. Those quantities are often unavailable and difficult to estimate before recovery begins.

The proposed residual ratio thresholding technique allows OMP to operate without either kind of prior knowledge. Its purpose is to remove this information requirement while retaining effective sparse recovery. The authors establish support-recovery guarantees in both finite-sample and large-sample settings; support recovery concerns identifying which entries of the regression vector are nonzero.

Analytical results and numerical simulations using real and synthetic datasets indicate performance comparable to OMP supplied with the sparsity or noise information in advance. This comparison addresses the method's central practical question: how much recovery quality can be retained when the usual side information is missing? The reported evidence supports residual ratio thresholding as a way to make OMP usable under that uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Residual ratio thresholding lets OMP recover sparse regression support without prior sparsity or noise statistics, with guarantees and comparable reported performance.

title: Signal and Noise Statistics Oblivious Orthogonal Matching Pursuit

abstract: We present a VAE architecture for encoding and generating high dimensional sequential data, such as video or audio. Our deep generative model learns a latent representation of the data which is split into a static and dynamic part, allowing us to approximately disentangle latent time-dependent features (dynamics) from features which are preserved over time (content). This architecture gives us partial control over generating content and dynamics by conditioning on either one of these sets of features. In our experiments on artificially generated cartoon video clips and voice recordings, we show that we can convert the content of a given sequence into another one by such content swapping. For audio, this allows us to convert a male speaker into a female speaker and vice versa, while for video we can separately manipulate shapes and dynamics. Furthermore, we give empirical evidence for the hypothesis that stochastic RNNs as latent state models are more efficient at compressing and generating long sequences than deterministic ones, which may be relevant for applications in video compression.

Our deep generative model learns a latent representation of the data which is split into a static and dynamic part, allowing us to approximately disentangle latent time-dependent features (dynamics) from features which are preserved over time (content). This architecture gives us partial control over generating content and dynamics by conditioning on either one of these sets of features. In our experiments on artificially generated cartoon video clips and voice recordings, we show that we can convert the content of a given sequence into another one by such content swapping. For audio, this allows us to convert a male speaker into a female speaker and vice versa, while for video we can separately manipulate shapes and dynamics. Furthermore, we give empirical evidence for the hypothesis that stochastic RNNs as latent state models are more efficient at compressing and generating long sequences than deterministic ones, which may be relevant for applications in video compression.

paragraphs: Video and audio contain both properties that persist through a sequence and properties that change over time. This paper introduces a variational autoencoder that represents these two kinds of information separately. Its latent representation contains a static part for content and a dynamic part for temporal behavior.

The separation is approximate, giving partial control over generation by conditioning on one set of features or the other. In experiments with generated cartoon clips and voice recordings, the authors demonstrate content swapping between sequences. The reported examples include converting voices between male and female speakers and separately changing video shapes and dynamics.

The paper also examines how latent temporal states should be modeled. Its experiments support the hypothesis that stochastic recurrent networks compress and generate long sequences more efficiently than deterministic ones. The authors identify possible relevance to video compression. Together, these results connect a structured latent representation with controllable generation and provide empirical support for stochastic models of long sequences.
summary.tldr: A sequential variational autoencoder approximately separates persistent content from changing dynamics, enabling partial control and content swapping.

title: Disentangled Sequential Autoencoder

abstract: We propose a new concept named adaptive submodularity ratio to study the greedy policy for sequential decision making. While the greedy policy is known to perform well for a wide variety of adaptive stochastic optimization problems in practice, its theoretical properties have been analyzed only for a limited class of problems. We narrow the gap between theory and practice by using adaptive submodularity ratio, which enables us to prove approximation guarantees of the greedy policy for a substantially wider class of problems. Examples of newly analyzed problems include important applications such as adaptive influence maximization and adaptive feature selection. Our adaptive submodularity ratio also provides bounds of adaptivity gaps. Experiments confirm that the greedy policy performs well with the applications being considered compared to standard heuristics.

paragraphs: Sequential decision problems often require choosing an action, observing what happens, and then choosing again. Greedy policies make each choice based on its immediate value given the information currently available. Although this approach works well in many adaptive stochastic optimization problems, earlier theory explained its performance for only a limited class.

The paper introduces the adaptive submodularity ratio as a way to broaden that analysis. Using this quantity, the authors prove approximation guarantees for greedy policies in a substantially wider range of problems. The contribution is a framework for establishing performance guarantees beyond the previously analyzed class, connecting practical success with a more flexible theoretical treatment.

The newly covered applications include adaptive influence maximization and adaptive feature selection. The ratio also yields bounds on adaptivity gaps, which describe the value of allowing decisions to respond to observations. Experiments show that greedy policies perform well against standard heuristics on the considered applications. These empirical findings complement the guarantees, whose applicability is established through the proposed ratio.
summary.tldr: The adaptive submodularity ratio extends theoretical guarantees for greedy sequential decisions to a broader class of adaptive optimization problems.

title: Beyond Adaptive Submodularity: Approximation Guarantees of Greedy Policy with Adaptive Submodularity Ratio

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental task in unsupervised machine learning. Lloyd’s 1957 algorithm for k-means clustering remains one of the most widely used due to its speed and simplicity, but the greedy approach is sensitive to initialization and often falls short at a poor solution. This paper explores an alternative to Lloyd’s algorithm that retains its simplicity and mitigates its tendency to get trapped by local minima. Called power k-means, our method embeds the k-means problem in a continuous class of similar, better behaved problems with fewer local minima. Power k-means anneals its way toward the solution of ordinary k-means by way of majorization-minimization (MM), sharing the appealing descent property and low complexity of Lloyd’s algorithm. Further, our method complements widely used seeding strategies, reaping marked improvements when used together as demonstrated on a suite of simulated and real data examples.

paragraphs: Ordinary k-means is commonly optimized using Lloyd's algorithm, whose speed and simplicity make it attractive. Its greedy updates, however, can lead to poor local solutions and sensitivity to the initial cluster centers. Power k-means seeks to reduce this difficulty while preserving the computational qualities that make the standard approach useful.

The method places the k-means objective within a continuous family of related problems that have fewer local minima. It then gradually moves through that family toward ordinary k-means. A majorization-minimization procedure drives this annealing process, retaining a descent property and low computational complexity comparable to Lloyd's algorithm.

The approach also works alongside existing strategies for choosing initial cluster centers. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show marked improvements when power k-means and those seeding strategies are combined. The result supports changing the optimization path as a complement to choosing better starting points. The method mitigates trapping in local minima; the stated contribution does not require a guarantee of finding the global optimum.
summary.tldr: Power k-means gradually approaches the ordinary k-means objective through easier related problems, reducing local-minimum difficulties while retaining efficient updates.

title: Power k-Means Clustering

abstract: We investigate the connections between neural networks and simple building blocks in kernel space. In particular, using well established feature space tools such as direct sum, averaging, and moment lifting, we present an algebra for creating “compositional” kernels from bags of features. We show that these operations correspond to many of the building blocks of “neural tangent kernels (NTK)”. Experimentally, we show that there is a correlation in test error between neural network architectures and the associated kernels. We construct a simple neural network architecture using only 3x3 convolutions, 2x2 average pooling, ReLU, and optimized with SGD and MSE loss that achieves 96% accuracy on CIFAR10, and whose corresponding compositional kernel achieves 90% accuracy. We also use our constructions to investigate the relative performance of neural networks, NTKs, and compositional kernels in the small dataset regime. In particular, we find that compositional kernels outperform NTKs and neural networks outperform both kernel methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to build kernels compositionally from bags of features. It uses established feature-space operations, including direct sums, averaging, and moment lifting, to form an algebra of kernel construction. The authors show that these operations correspond to many building blocks of neural tangent kernels, connecting neural architectures with simpler constructions in kernel space.

One network built from 3×3 convolutions, 2×2 average pooling, and ReLU reaches 96% accuracy on CIFAR10 when trained with stochastic gradient descent and mean squared error. Its corresponding compositional kernel reaches 90%, illustrating both a connection and a performance gap.

The authors also compare neural networks, neural tangent kernels, and compositional kernels when datasets are small. In those experiments, compositional kernels outperform neural tangent kernels, while neural networks outperform both. The construction thus provides a useful framework for examining architecture-related kernel behavior, with the reported comparisons also showing that the associated kernels do not reproduce the networks’ full performance.
summary.tldr: A compositional kernel algebra connects feature-space operations to neural architectures and supports empirical comparisons with neural tangent kernels and networks.

title: Neural Kernels Without Tangents

abstract: 0-1 knapsack is of fundamental importance across many fields. In this paper, we present a game-theoretic method to solve 0-1 knapsack problems (KPs) where the number of items (products) is large and the values of items are not predetermined but decided by an external value assignment function (e.g., a neural network in our case) during the optimization process. While existing papers are interested in predicting solutions with neural networks for classical KPs whose objective functions are mostly linear functions, we are interested in solving KPs whose objective functions are neural networks. In other words, we choose a subset of items that maximize the sum of the values predicted by neural networks. Its key challenge is how to optimize the neural network-based non-linear KP objective with a budget constraint. Our solution is inspired by game-theoretic approaches in deep learning, e.g., generative adversarial networks. After formally defining our two-player game, we develop an adaptive gradient ascent method to solve it. In our experiments, our method successfully solves two neural network-based non-linear KPs and conventional linear KPs with 1 million items.

paragraphs: A knapsack problem asks which items to select while staying within a budget. In the classical version, each item has a fixed value. This paper studies a different setting: an external function, such as a neural network, determines item values during optimization. The objective is to select a subset that maximizes the sum of those predicted values.

This changes the role of the neural network. Rather than using a network to predict a solution to a conventional knapsack problem, the researchers make the network part of the objective being optimized. The resulting nonlinear objective must still respect the budget constraint. They formulate a two-player game, drawing inspiration from game-theoretic methods in deep learning, and develop an adaptive gradient ascent method to solve it.

The experiments report successful solutions for two nonlinear knapsack problems with neural network objectives and for conventional linear problems containing one million items. These findings demonstrate the method on both the proposed setting and a large classical setting; they do not establish universal optimality for arbitrary neural objectives.
summary.tldr: A two-player game and adaptive gradient ascent tackle budget-constrained item selection when neural networks determine item values.

title: A Novel Method to Solve Neural Knapsack Problems

abstract: While designing inductive bias in neural architectures has been widely studied, we hypothesize that transformer networks are flexible enough to learn inductive bias from suitable generic tasks. Here, we replace architecture engineering by encoding inductive bias in the form of datasets. Inspired by Peirce’s view that deduction, induction, and abduction are the primitives of reasoning, we design three synthetic tasks that are intended to require the model to have these three abilities. We specifically design these tasks to be synthetic and devoid of mathematical knowledge to ensure that only the fundamental reasoning biases can be learned from these tasks. This defines a new pre-training methodology called "LIME" (Learning Inductive bias for Mathematical rEasoning). Models trained with LIME significantly outperform vanilla transformers on four very different large mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Unlike dominating the computation cost as traditional pre-training approaches, LIME requires only a small fraction of the computation cost of the typical downstream task. The code for generating LIME tasks is available at https://github.com/tonywu95/LIME.

paragraphs: An inductive bias encourages a model to learn certain kinds of patterns or solutions. This paper hypothesizes that transformers can acquire useful reasoning biases from suitable generic training tasks. It develops LIME, a pretraining method that encodes these biases in synthetic datasets, shifting the design effort toward the tasks used to prepare the model.

The authors construct three tasks intended to require deduction, induction, and abduction. They deliberately exclude mathematical knowledge from these tasks so that pretraining targets fundamental reasoning tendencies rather than mathematical subject matter. This design tests whether preparation on abstract reasoning primitives can benefit later mathematical learning.

Models pretrained with LIME significantly outperform vanilla transformers on four different large mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The pretraining requires only a small fraction of the computation typically spent on the downstream task. These findings support the practical value of the proposed synthetic preparation and the hypothesis that suitable datasets can teach useful biases, without establishing that the tasks universally confer the three reasoning abilities.
summary.tldr: LIME uses inexpensive synthetic reasoning pretraining to improve transformer performance on four mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

title: LIME: Learning Inductive Bias for Primitives of Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: We propose a general approach for distance based clustering, using the gradient of the cost function that measures clustering quality with respect to cluster assignments and cluster center positions. The approach is an iterative two step procedure (alternating between cluster assignment and cluster center updates) and is applicable to a wide range of functions, satisfying some mild assumptions. The main advantage of the proposed approach is a simple and computationally cheap update rule. Unlike previous methods that specialize to a specific formulation of the clustering problem, our approach is applicable to a wide range of costs, including non-Bregman clustering methods based on the Huber loss. We analyze the convergence of the proposed algorithm, and show that it converges to the set of appropriately defined fixed points, under arbitrary center initialization. In the special case of Bregman cost functions, the algorithm converges to the set of centroidal Voronoi partitions, which is consistent with prior works. Numerical experiments on real data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Distance-based clustering methods often depend on a particular choice of clustering cost. This paper develops a more general procedure that uses the gradient of the cost to guide clustering. It alternates between assigning data points to clusters and updating the positions of cluster centers, with a simple and computationally inexpensive update rule.

The framework applies to a broad range of cost functions satisfying mild assumptions. Its scope includes costs outside the Bregman family, such as clustering formulations based on Huber loss. This flexibility matters because changing the measure of clustering quality need not require developing an entirely separate optimization procedure for each formulation.

The authors prove convergence to an appropriately defined set of fixed points from arbitrary center initializations. For Bregman costs, the limiting set consists of centroidal Voronoi partitions, consistent with previous results for that setting. The guarantee identifies stable outcomes of the procedure rather than asserting global optimality. Experiments on real data demonstrate the method’s effectiveness, complementing the convergence analysis and supporting the usefulness of the general update approach.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a cheap gradient-based clustering procedure that supports varied costs and converges to defined fixed-point sets.

title: Gradient Based Clustering

abstract: What matters for contrastive learning? We argue that contrastive learning heavily relies on informative features, or “hard” (positive or negative) features. Early works include more informative features by applying complex data augmentations and large batch size or memory bank, and recent works design elaborate sampling approaches to explore informative features. The key challenge toward exploring such features is that the source multi-view data is generated by applying random data augmentations, making it infeasible to always add useful information in the augmented data. Consequently, the informativeness of features learned from such augmented data is limited. In response, we propose to directly augment the features in latent space, thereby learning discriminative representations without a large amount of input data. We perform a meta learning technique to build the augmentation generator that updates its network parameters by considering the performance of the encoder. However, insufficient input data may lead the encoder to learn collapsed features and therefore malfunction the augmentation generator. A new margin-injected regularization is further added in the objective function to avoid the encoder learning a degenerate mapping. To contrast all features in one gradient back-propagation step, we adopt the proposed optimization-driven unified contrastive loss instead of the conventional contrastive loss. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: MetAug addresses how contrastive learning can obtain informative positive and negative features. Randomly augmenting input data does not always add useful information, which can limit the representations learned from the resulting views. The paper proposes augmenting features directly in latent space to learn discriminative representations without requiring a large amount of input data.

A meta-learning procedure trains the feature-augmentation generator by considering the encoder’s performance. This makes the generator responsive to how well its augmentations support representation learning. However, limited input data can cause the encoder to collapse to uninformative features, which also undermines the generator. The method adds a margin-based regularizer to discourage this degenerate mapping.

MetAug also introduces a unified contrastive loss designed to contrast all features within one gradient back-propagation step. The generator, regularizer, and loss address different parts of the same learning process: creating informative features, keeping representations useful, and training with those features together. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets.
summary.tldr: MetAug learns feature-space augmentations through meta-learning and combines them with anti-collapse regularization and a unified contrastive loss.

title: MetAug: Contrastive Learning via Meta Feature Augmentation

abstract: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART; Chipman et al., 2010) have gained great popularity as a flexible nonparametric function estimation and modeling tool. Nearly all existing BART models rely on decision tree weak learners with axis-parallel univariate split rules to partition the Euclidean feature space into rectangular regions. In practice, however, many regression problems involve features with multivariate structures (e.g., spatial locations) possibly lying in a manifold, where rectangular partitions may fail to respect irregular intrinsic geometry and boundary constraints of the structured feature space. In this paper, we develop a new class of Bayesian additive multivariate decision tree models that combine univariate split rules for handling possibly high dimensional features without known multivariate structures and novel multivariate split rules for features with multivariate structures in each weak learner. The proposed multivariate split rules are built upon stochastic predictive spanning tree bipartition models on reference knots, which are capable of achieving highly flexible nonlinear decision boundaries on manifold feature spaces while enabling efficient dimension reduction computations. We demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method using simulation data and a Sacramento housing price data set.
