paragraphs: Bayesian additive regression trees estimate flexible relationships by combining many decision trees. Most existing versions divide feature space using one variable at a time, producing rectangular regions. This geometry can be poorly suited to structured inputs such as spatial locations, where valid regions may have irregular boundaries or lie on a manifold.

BAMDT combines two kinds of splits within each tree. Ordinary single-variable splits handle features without a known multivariate structure, including potentially high-dimensional inputs. New multivariate splits handle features whose joint geometry matters. These splits use stochastic spanning-tree bipartitions built on reference points, allowing flexible nonlinear boundaries while supporting efficient dimension-reduction computations.

This combination matters because one regression problem can contain both structured and unstructured features. The model can account for their different properties within the same ensemble instead of forcing every feature through rectangular partitions. Experiments with simulated data and Sacramento housing prices report superior performance for the proposed method. Those findings support the value of making tree boundaries responsive to the geometry of the structured inputs in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: BAMDT combines ordinary and geometry-aware tree splits to model regression problems containing both unstructured and jointly structured features.

title: BAMDT: Bayesian Additive Semi-Multivariate Decision Trees for Nonparametric Regression

abstract: With a variety of local feature attribution methods being proposed in recent years, follow-up work suggested several evaluation strategies. To assess the attribution quality across different attribution techniques, the most popular among these evaluation strategies in the image domain use pixel perturbations. However, recent advances discovered that different evaluation strategies produce conflicting rankings of attribution methods and can be prohibitively expensive to compute. In this work, we present an information-theoretic analysis of evaluation strategies based on pixel perturbations. Our findings reveal that the results are strongly affected by information leakage through the shape of the removed pixels as opposed to their actual values. Using our theoretical insights, we propose a novel evaluation framework termed Remove and Debias (ROAD) which offers two contributions: First, it mitigates the impact of the confounders, which entails higher consistency among evaluation strategies. Second, ROAD does not require the computationally expensive retraining step and saves up to 99% in computational costs compared to the state-of-the-art. We release our source code at https://github.com/tleemann/road_evaluation.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods assign importance to parts of an input, but judging those assignments is itself difficult. In image tasks, popular evaluations perturb pixels and examine the consequences. Different versions of these evaluations can disagree about which attribution method is best, and some require expensive model retraining.

This paper analyzes pixel-perturbation evaluations using information theory. It identifies a confounding signal: the shape formed by the removed pixels can leak information, independently of the pixel values being assessed. Consequently, an evaluation may partly measure information conveyed by the removal pattern, weakening its ability to isolate the quality of the attribution.

The proposed Remove and Debias framework, ROAD, uses this analysis to reduce the influence of those confounders. The authors report greater consistency across evaluation strategies and computational savings of up to 99% relative to the state of the art, because ROAD avoids retraining. The contribution therefore concerns both the credibility of attribution comparisons and the practical cost of carrying them out.
summary.tldr: ROAD makes attribution evaluations more consistent and cheaper by reducing information leakage from pixel-removal patterns and avoiding retraining.

title: A Consistent and Efficient Evaluation Strategy for Attribution Methods

abstract: The application of an ensemble of neural networks is becoming an imminent tool for advancing state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithms. However, training these large numbers of neural networks in the ensemble has an exceedingly high computation cost which may become a hindrance in training large-scale systems. In this paper, we propose DNS: a Determinantal Point Process based Neural Network Sampler that specifically uses k-DPP to sample a subset of neural networks for backpropagation at every training step thus significantly reducing the training time and computation cost. We integrated DNS in REDQ for continuous control tasks and evaluated on MuJoCo environments. Our experiments show that DNS augmented REDQ matches the baseline REDQ in terms of average cumulative reward and achieves this using less than 50% computation when measured in FLOPS. The code is available at https://github.com/IntelLabs/DNS

paragraphs: Ensembles of neural networks can strengthen deep reinforcement learning methods, but training many networks makes each update expensive. DNS addresses this cost by changing which ensemble members receive backpropagation at each training step. The approach retains an ensemble while selectively spending computation on a subset of its networks.

The selection mechanism uses a k-determinantal point process, or k-DPP, to sample that subset. The central intervention is therefore in the training procedure: the method does not backpropagate through every ensemble member at every step. The authors propose this sampler as a way to reduce both training time and computational expense in ensemble reinforcement learning.

They integrate DNS into REDQ and evaluate it on continuous-control tasks in MuJoCo environments. In those experiments, DNS-augmented REDQ matches baseline REDQ’s average cumulative reward while using less than half the computation measured in floating-point operations. This result shows that selective ensemble updates can preserve the reported control performance while substantially reducing arithmetic work in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: DNS samples ensemble members for backpropagation, matching REDQ’s reported reward with less than half its floating-point computation.

title: DNS: Determinantal Point Process Based Neural Network Sampler for Ensemble Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) and invariant risk minimization (IRM) are two popular methods proposed to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization performance of machine learning models. While effective for small models, it has been observed that these methods can be vulnerable to overfitting with large overparameterized models. This work proposes a principled method, Model Agnostic samPLe rEweighting (MAPLE), to effectively address OOD problem, especially in overparameterized scenarios. Our key idea is to find an effective reweighting of the training samples so that the standard empirical risk minimization training of a large model on the weighted training data leads to superior OOD generalization performance. The overfitting issue is addressed by considering a bilevel formulation to search for the sample reweighting, in which the generalization complexity depends on the search space of sample weights instead of the model size. We present theoretical analysis in linear case to prove the insensitivity of MAPLE to model size, and empirically verify its superiority in surpassing state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

paragraphs: Methods intended to improve generalization under distribution shifts can themselves overfit when used with large, overparameterized models. This paper focuses on that difficulty for distributionally robust optimization and invariant risk minimization. It proposes MAPLE, which changes the importance assigned to training examples so that ordinary weighted training produces better out-of-distribution performance.

The key mechanism is a bilevel optimization problem that searches for useful sample weights. One level concerns training the predictive model on weighted data, while the other concerns selecting the weights. In the proposed formulation, generalization complexity depends on the space of possible sample weights rather than directly on the size of the predictive model.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis in the linear setting that establishes MAPLE's insensitivity to model size. Experiments also report large improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The theory's stated scope is the linear case, while the empirical results support the broader practical motivation: controlling how training data influence learning can help address distribution shifts even when the model itself has many parameters.
summary.tldr: MAPLE searches for training-sample weights that improve out-of-distribution generalization, with linear-case theory separating generalization complexity from model size.

title: Model Agnostic Sample Reweighting for Out-of-Distribution Learning

abstract: Iterative methods are ubiquitous in large-scale scientific computing applications, and a number of approaches based on meta-learning have been recently proposed to accelerate them. However, a systematic study of these approaches and how they differ from meta-learning is lacking. In this paper, we propose a framework to analyze such learning-based acceleration approaches, where one can immediately identify a departure from classical meta-learning. We theoretically show that this departure may lead to arbitrary deterioration of model performance, and at the same time, we identify a methodology to ameliorate it by modifying the loss objective, leading to a novel training method for learning-based acceleration of iterative algorithms. We demonstrate the significant advantage and versatility of the proposed approach through various numerical applications.

However, a systematic study of these approaches and how they differ from meta-learning is lacking. In this paper, we propose a framework to analyze such learning-based acceleration approaches, where one can immediately identify a departure from classical meta-learning. We theoretically show that this departure may lead to arbitrary deterioration of model performance, and at the same time, we identify a methodology to ameliorate it by modifying the loss objective, leading to a novel training method for learning-based acceleration of iterative algorithms. We demonstrate the significant advantage and versatility of the proposed approach through various numerical applications.

paragraphs: Iterative numerical methods solve problems through repeated updates, making their speed important in large-scale scientific computing. Learning-based approaches try to accelerate that process using experience across problems. This paper develops a framework for analyzing such methods and examines how their setup differs from classical meta-learning, despite the close connection between the two.

The authors identify a departure from the classical formulation and prove that it can lead to arbitrarily severe deterioration in model performance. This is a possibility established by the analysis, rather than a claim that every learning-based accelerator behaves badly. It shows why a training formulation needs to be evaluated in the context of the iterative method it is intended to improve.

The proposed remedy modifies the loss objective, producing a new training method for learned acceleration. Across several numerical applications, the authors report substantial advantages and versatility. The work therefore connects a theoretical diagnosis to a concrete change in training: analyzing the mismatch guides the objective used to learn the accelerator, and numerical demonstrations show the usefulness of that correction.
summary.tldr: An analysis of learned numerical acceleration exposes a potentially severe training mismatch and motivates an improved loss objective.

title: Principled Acceleration of Iterative Numerical Methods Using Machine Learning

abstract: Self-distillation (SD) is the process of first training a "teacher" model and then using its predictions to train a "student" model that has the same architecture. Specifically, the student’s loss is $\big(\xi*\ell(\text{teacher’s predictions}, \text{ student’s predictions}) + (1-\xi)*\ell(\text{given labels}, \text{ student’s predictions})\big)$, where $\ell$ is the loss function and $\xi$ is some parameter $\in [0,1]$. SD has been empirically observed to provide performance gains in several settings. In this paper, we theoretically characterize the effect of SD in two supervised learning problems with noisy labels . We first analyze SD for regularized linear regression and show that in the high label noise regime, the optimal value of $\xi$ that minimizes the expected error in estimating the ground truth parameter is surprisingly greater than 1. Empirically, we show that $\xi > 1$ works better than $\xi \leq 1$ even with the cross-entropy loss for several classification datasets when 50% or 30% of the labels are corrupted. Further, we quantify when optimal SD is better than optimal regularization. Next, we analyze SD in the case of logistic regression for binary classification with random label corruption and quantify the range of label corruption in which the student outperforms the teacher (w.r.t. accuracy). To our knowledge, this is the first result of its kind for the cross-entropy loss.

paragraphs: Self-distillation trains a teacher and then trains a student with the same architecture using both teacher predictions and given labels. A parameter xi controls their relative contributions to the student's loss, conventionally between zero and one. This paper studies how that process behaves when labels are noisy, providing theoretical analyses for two supervised learning problems.

For regularized linear regression with high label noise, the authors show that the xi minimizing expected ground-truth parameter estimation error exceeds one. This extends beyond an ordinary weighted average: the coefficient on the given-label loss becomes negative. Classification experiments with cross-entropy also favor xi above one on several datasets with 30% or 50% corrupted labels. The paper additionally quantifies when optimal self-distillation improves on optimal regularization.

A second analysis considers binary logistic regression with random label corruption. It identifies a range of corruption levels where the student has higher accuracy than the teacher. Together, the results explain specific conditions under which distillation can improve learning from noisy labels, while distinguishing theoretical conclusions for the analyzed models from the broader classification experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when self-distillation helps with noisy labels, including a high-noise regression regime where the optimal teacher-loss weight exceeds one.

title: Understanding Self-Distillation in the Presence of Label Noise

abstract: Uncertainty estimation is a key factor that makes deep learning reliable in practical applications. Recently proposed evidential neural networks explicitly account for different uncertainties by treating the network’s outputs as evidence to parameterize the Dirichlet distribution, and achieve impressive performance in uncertainty estimation. However, for high data uncertainty samples but annotated with the one-hot label, the evidence-learning process for those mislabeled classes is over-penalized and remains hindered. To address this problem, we propose a novel method, Fisher Information-based Evidential Deep Learning ($\mathcal{I}$-EDL). In particular, we introduce Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to measure the informativeness of evidence carried by each sample, according to which we can dynamically reweight the objective loss terms to make the network more focus on the representation learning of uncertain classes. The generalization ability of our network is further improved by optimizing the PAC-Bayesian bound. As demonstrated empirically, our proposed method consistently outperforms traditional EDL-related algorithms in multiple uncertainty estimation tasks, especially in the more challenging few-shot classification settings.

The proposed Fisher Information-based Evidential Deep Learning method measures how informative each sample’s evidence is using the Fisher Information Matrix. It then dynamically reweights terms in the training objective, directing more attention toward learning representations of uncertain classes. The authors additionally optimize a PAC-Bayesian bound to improve generalization.

Across multiple uncertainty-estimation tasks, the method consistently outperforms traditional evidential-learning approaches in the reported experiments. The gains are especially apparent in few-shot classification, where only a small number of examples are available. The contribution connects the treatment of ambiguous training evidence to the reliability of uncertainty estimates: rather than applying the same balance of penalties to every sample, the objective adapts according to the informativeness of its evidence.
summary.tldr: Fisher-information-based loss reweighting improves evidential uncertainty estimation in reported experiments, particularly for few-shot classification.

title: Uncertainty Estimation by Fisher Information-based Evidential Deep Learning

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) for Graph neural networks (GNNs), called NAS-GNNs, has achieved significant performance over manually designed GNN architectures. However, these methods inherit issues from the conventional NAS methods, such as high computational cost and optimization difficulty. More importantly, previous NAS methods have ignored the uniqueness of GNNs, where GNNs possess expressive power without training. With the randomly-initialized weights, we can then seek the optimal architecture parameters via the sparse coding objective and derive a novel NAS-GNNs method, namely neural architecture coding (NAC). Consequently, our NAC holds a no-update scheme on GNNs and can efficiently compute in linear time. Empirical evaluations on multiple GNN benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach leads to state-of-the-art performance, which is up to $200\times$ faster and $18.8%$ more accurate than the strong baselines.

paragraphs: Searching for a graph neural network architecture can produce strong models, but the search itself can be computationally expensive and difficult to optimize. This paper builds on a useful property of graph neural networks: they already possess expressive power with randomly initialized weights. That makes their untrained representations relevant to architecture selection.

The proposed method, neural architecture coding or NAC, keeps the graph network weights fixed and searches for architecture parameters using a sparse coding objective. It therefore avoids updating those network weights during its architecture-search procedure. The authors describe the resulting computation as linear time, making the no-update strategy central to its efficiency.

Evaluations on multiple graph neural network benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, with improvements of up to 200 times in speed and 18.8% in accuracy over strong baselines. These are reported upper-end experimental gains, not uniform improvements across every task. The broader finding is that useful architecture choices can be obtained by exploiting the expressive structure already present in randomly initialized graph networks.
summary.tldr: NAC searches graph neural network architectures using fixed random weights and sparse coding, with substantial reported speed and accuracy gains.

title: Do Not Train It: A Linear Neural Architecture Search of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We consider a class of structured fractional minimization problems, in which the numerator part of the objective is the sum of a differentiable convex function and a convex non-smooth function, while the denominator part is a convex or concave function. This problem is difficult to solve since it is non-convex. By exploiting the structure of the problem, we propose two Coordinate Descent (CD) methods for solving this problem. The proposed methods iteratively solve a one-dimensional subproblem globally , and they are guaranteed to converge to coordinate-wise stationary points. In the case of a convex denominator, under a weak locally bounded non-convexity condition , we prove that the optimality of coordinate-wise stationary point is stronger than that of the standard critical point and directional point. Under additional suitable conditions, CD methods converge Q-linearly to coordinate-wise stationary points. In the case of a concave denominator, we show that any critical point is a global minimum, and CD methods converge to the global minimum with a sublinear convergence rate. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed methods to some machine learning and signal processing models. Our experiments on real-world data have shown that our method significantly and consistently outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies objectives written as a ratio. The numerator combines a differentiable convex function with a potentially nonsmooth convex function, while the denominator may be convex or concave. Despite that structure, the overall optimization problem is nonconvex, so familiar guarantees for convex minimization do not automatically apply.

The authors propose two coordinate descent methods that globally solve a one-dimensional subproblem at each iteration. Both converge to coordinate-wise stationary points. For a convex denominator, a weak local bounded-nonconvexity condition makes this stationarity notion stronger than the standard critical-point and directional-point notions considered in the paper. Additional suitable conditions yield Q-linear convergence to such points.

The concave-denominator case gives a stronger conclusion: every critical point is a global minimum, and the methods reach a global minimum at a sublinear rate. These distinctions explain why denominator structure matters for what the algorithms can guarantee. Applications to machine learning and signal processing, with experiments on real-world data, report significant and consistent accuracy improvements over existing methods.
summary.tldr: Two coordinate descent methods exploit ratio-objective structure to obtain convergence guarantees that depend on the denominator and additional conditions.

title: Coordinate Descent Methods for Fractional Minimization

abstract: In large language model training, input documents are typically concatenated together and then split into sequences of equal length to avoid padding tokens. Despite its efficiency, the concatenation approach compromises data integrity—it inevitably breaks many documents into incomplete pieces, leading to excessive truncations that hinder the model from learning to compose logically coherent and factually consistent content that is grounded on the complete context. To address the issue, we propose Best-fit Packing, a scalable and efficient method that packs documents into training sequences through length-aware combinatorial optimization. Our method completely eliminates unnecessary truncations while retaining the same training efficiency as concatenation. Empirical results from both text and code pre-training show that our method achieves superior performance (e.g., +4.7% on reading comprehension; +16.8% in context following; and +9.2% on program synthesis), and reduces closed-domain hallucination effectively by up to 58.3%.

paragraphs: Language-model training commonly joins documents together and cuts the resulting text into equal-length sequences. This avoids wasting space on padding, but it also splits many documents into incomplete fragments. The paper examines how those avoidable cuts interfere with learning content that is coherent, factually consistent, and grounded in the complete context.

The proposed method, Best-fit Packing, uses document lengths in a combinatorial optimization procedure to arrange documents into training sequences. The authors report that it eliminates unnecessary truncations while maintaining the training efficiency of concatenation. This makes the organization of training data itself the intervention, preserving more complete document context without giving up efficient sequence packing.

Experiments on text and code pre-training report gains of 4.7% in reading comprehension, 16.8% in context following, and 9.2% in program synthesis. Closed-domain hallucination is reduced by up to 58.3%. These results indicate that preserving document integrity during sequence construction can materially affect what a language model learns, even when the reported training efficiency remains the same.
summary.tldr: Best-fit Packing preserves document context without sacrificing training efficiency, improving text and code performance and reducing closed-domain hallucination.

title: Fewer Truncations Improve Language Modeling

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has recently gained much interest in fine-tuning foundation models. It effectively reduces the number of trainable parameters by incorporating low-rank matrices $A$ and $B$ to represent the weight change, i.e., $\Delta W=BA$. Despite LoRA’s progress, it faces storage challenges when handling extensive customization adaptations or larger base models. In this work, we aim to further compress trainable parameters by enjoying the powerful expressiveness of the Fourier transform. Specifically, we introduce FourierFT, which treats $\Delta W$ as a matrix in the spatial domain and learns only a small fraction of its spectral coefficients. With the trained spectral coefficients, we implement the inverse discrete Fourier transform to recover $\Delta W$. Empirically, our FourierFT method shows comparable or better performance with fewer parameters than LoRA on various tasks, including natural language understanding, natural language generation, instruction tuning, and image classification. For example, when performing instruction tuning on the LLaMA2-7B model, FourierFT surpasses LoRA with only 0.064M trainable parameters, compared to LoRA’s 33.5M. Our code is released at this link.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a foundation model can require storing a separate weight update for each customization. LoRA compresses those updates into products of low-rank matrices, but storage remains a concern when models or collections of customizations grow. This paper proposes FourierFT as another way to represent a weight update using very few trainable values.

FourierFT treats the update as a matrix in the spatial domain and learns only a small subset of its Fourier coefficients. An inverse discrete Fourier transform reconstructs the weight-update matrix from those trained coefficients. The trainable representation therefore lives in the spectral domain, while the recovered matrix supplies the change applied to the model's weights.

Experiments cover natural language understanding, generation, instruction tuning, and image classification. Across these tasks, FourierFT achieves comparable or better performance than LoRA with fewer parameters. In the reported LLaMA2-7B instruction-tuning example, it surpasses LoRA using 0.064 million trainable parameters versus 33.5 million. This illustrates the substantial compression that the spectral representation achieves in that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: FourierFT learns a small subset of Fourier coefficients to represent weight updates, matching or beating LoRA with fewer trainable parameters in the reported experiments.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning with Discrete Fourier Transform

abstract: Score-based diffusion models have proven effective in image generation and have gained widespread usage; however, the underlying factors contributing to the performance disparity between stochastic and deterministic (i.e., the probability flow ODEs) sampling schemes remain unclear. We introduce a novel formulation of diffusion models using Feynman’s path integral, which is a formulation originally developed for quantum physics. We find this formulation providing comprehensive descriptions of score-based generative models, and demonstrate the derivation of backward stochastic differential equations and loss functions. The formulation accommodates an interpolating parameter connecting stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes, and we identify this parameter as a counterpart of Planck’s constant in quantum physics. This analogy enables us to apply the Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB) expansion, a well-established technique in quantum physics, for evaluating the negative log-likelihood to assess the performance disparity between stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models can generate images using stochastic sampling or deterministic probability-flow differential equations. These sampling choices can differ in performance, and the paper seeks a mathematical framework for understanding that disparity. It introduces a formulation based on Feynman's path integral, a technique originating in quantum physics.

Within this formulation, the authors derive backward stochastic differential equations and loss functions for diffusion models. A parameter connects the stochastic and deterministic sampling schemes, allowing both to be studied within the same description. The paper identifies this parameter as analogous to Planck's constant, establishing a mathematical connection that makes tools from quantum physics applicable.

The authors use that connection to apply the Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin expansion when evaluating negative log-likelihood. This supplies a way to assess the performance difference between the sampling schemes. The contribution is a unified analytical viewpoint and an associated approximation technique for studying diffusion sampling, with the physics analogy serving as a route to the mathematical analysis.
summary.tldr: A path-integral formulation connects stochastic and deterministic diffusion sampling and enables a quantum-physics approximation for analyzing their performance difference.

title: Understanding Diffusion Models by Feynman’s Path Integral

abstract: We argue that representations in AI models, particularly deep networks, are converging. First, we survey many examples of convergence in the literature: over time and across multiple domains, the ways by which different neural networks represent data are becoming more aligned. Next, we demonstrate convergence across data modalities: as vision models and language models get larger, they measure distance between datapoints in a more and more alike way. We hypothesize that this convergence is driving toward a shared statistical model of reality, akin to Plato's concept of an ideal reality. We term such a representation the platonic representation and discuss several possible selective pressures toward it. Finally, we discuss the implications of these trends, their limitations, and counterexamples to our analysis.

paragraphs: Different neural networks can organize information in increasingly similar ways despite differences in their training or inputs. This position paper argues that such representational convergence is a broad trend. It surveys examples from the literature across domains and over time, focusing on how models' internal representations become more aligned.

The authors also demonstrate convergence between vision and language models: as the models become larger, their assessments of distances between data points become more alike. This comparison concerns the relationships models assign among examples. It provides evidence that models working with different kinds of data can develop increasingly similar representational organization.

The larger hypothesis is that these trends point toward a shared statistical representation of reality, which the authors call a platonic representation. They discuss possible pressures that could favor convergence, along with implications, limitations, and counterexamples. The observed alignment and the proposed destination remain distinct claims: the paper presents evidence of convergence while treating a common model of reality as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that model representations are converging and hypothesizes a shared statistical representation of reality.

title: Position: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis

abstract: Tabular biomedical data poses challenges in machine learning because it is often high-dimensional and typically low-sample-size (HDLSS). Previous research has attempted to address these challenges via local feature selection, but existing approaches often fail to achieve optimal performance due to their limitation in identifying globally important features and their susceptibility to the co-adaptation problem. In this paper, we propose ProtoGate, a prototype-based neural model for feature selection on HDLSS data. ProtoGate first selects instance-wise features via adaptively balancing global and local feature selection. Furthermore, ProtoGate employs a non-parametric prototype-based prediction mechanism to tackle the co-adaptation problem, ensuring the feature selection results and predictions are consistent with underlying data clusters. We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate the performance and interpretability of ProtoGate on synthetic and real-world datasets. The results show that ProtoGate generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods in prediction accuracy by a clear margin while providing high-fidelity feature selection and explainable predictions. Code is available at https://github.com/SilenceX12138/ProtoGate.

paragraphs: Biomedical tables often contain many features but relatively few examples. Choosing useful features is therefore central to learning from them. Methods that select features separately for each example can overlook features that matter across the dataset, and the selection and prediction components can suffer from co-adaptation.

ProtoGate balances global and local feature selection adaptively to choose features for individual examples. It then makes predictions through a non-parametric prototype mechanism. The design aims to address co-adaptation while keeping selected features and predictions consistent with the clusters present in the data.

The authors evaluate both predictive performance and interpretability using synthetic and real-world datasets. ProtoGate generally exceeds state-of-the-art prediction accuracy by a clear margin and provides high-fidelity feature selections and explainable predictions. The qualified finding is that it generally performs better across these evaluations. Its contribution connects two forms of explanation—identifying relevant features and using prototypes for prediction—within a model designed for data with many dimensions and few samples.
summary.tldr: ProtoGate combines adaptive global-to-local feature selection with prototype-based prediction to improve accuracy and interpretability on small, high-dimensional biomedical datasets.

title: ProtoGate: Prototype-based Neural Networks with Global-to-local Feature Selection for Tabular Biomedical Data

abstract: Pretrained deep-learning models are the go-to solution for images or text. However, for tabular data the standard is still to train tree-based models. Indeed, transfer learning on tables hits the challenge of data integration: finding correspondences, correspondences in the entries (entity matching) where different words may denote the same entity, correspondences across columns (schema matching), which may come in different orders, names... We propose a neural architecture that does not need such correspondences. As a result, we can pretrain it on background data that has not been matched. The architecture –CARTE for Context Aware Representation of Table Entries– uses a graph representation of tabular (or relational) data to process tables with different columns, string embedding of entries and columns names to model an open vocabulary, and a graph-attentional network to contextualize entries with column names and neighboring entries. An extensive benchmark shows that CARTE facilitates learning, outperforming a solid set of baselines including the best tree-based models. CARTE also enables joint learning across tables with unmatched columns, enhancing a small table with bigger ones. CARTE opens the door to large pretrained models for tabular data.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between tables is difficult because their entries and columns may not line up. The same entity can have different names, and columns can differ in naming, order, or availability. CARTE addresses this integration problem with a neural architecture that does not require those correspondences to be established first.

The method represents tabular or relational data as a graph. String embeddings represent both entries and column names, allowing an open vocabulary. A graph-attention network then interprets entries using their column names and neighboring entries. This contextual representation allows the model to process tables with different columns and to pretrain on background data that has not been matched.

An extensive benchmark finds that CARTE outperforms a strong collection of baselines, including leading tree-based models. The architecture also supports joint learning across tables with unmatched columns, allowing larger tables to help learning on a smaller one. The broader significance is a practical route toward pretrained tabular models that reduces the need for explicit data alignment before knowledge can be shared.
summary.tldr: CARTE enables pretraining and transfer across tables without first matching their entities or columns.

title: CARTE: Pretraining and Transfer for Tabular Learning

abstract: How would randomly shuffling feature vectors among nodes from the same class affect graph neural networks (GNNs)? The feature shuffle, intuitively, perturbs the dependence between graph topology and features (A-X dependence) for GNNs to learn from. Surprisingly, we observe a consistent and significant improvement in GNN performance following the feature shuffle. Having overlooked the impact of A-X dependence on GNNs, the prior literature does not provide a satisfactory understanding of the phenomenon. Thus, we raise two research questions. First, how should A-X dependence be measured, while controlling for potential confounds? Second, how does A-X dependence affect GNNs? In response, we (i) propose a principled measure for A-X dependence, (ii) design a random graph model that controls A-X dependence, (iii) establish a theory on how A-X dependence relates to graph convolution, and (iv) present empirical analysis on real-world graphs that align with the theory. We conclude that A-X dependence mediates the effect of graph convolution, such that smaller dependence improves GNN-based node classification.
originalAbstract: How would randomly shuffling feature vectors among nodes from the same class affect graph neural networks (GNNs)? The feature shuffle, intuitively, perturbs the dependence between graph topology and features (A-X dependence) for GNNs to learn from. Surprisingly, we observe a consistent and significant improvement in GNN performance following the feature shuffle. Having overlooked the impact of A-X dependence on GNNs, the prior literature does not provide a satisfactory understanding of the phenomenon. Thus, we raise two research questions. First, how should A-X dependence be measured, while controlling for potential confounds? Second, how does A-X dependence affect GNNs? In response, we (i) propose a principled measure for A-X dependence, (ii) design a random graph model that controls A-X dependence, (iii) establish a theory on how A-X dependence relates to graph convolution, and (iv) present empirical analysis on real-world graphs that align with the theory. We conclude that A-X dependence mediates the effect of graph convolution, such that smaller dependence improves GNN-based node classification.

paragraphs: This paper begins with a surprising observation: randomly exchanging feature vectors among nodes belonging to the same class consistently and substantially improves graph neural network performance in the authors' observations. The shuffle changes how features are arranged across the graph while keeping each exchanged vector within its class. That points to the relationship between connectivity and features as an important influence.

The authors call this relationship A-X dependence. They develop a measure designed to account for potential confounding factors and construct a random graph model in which the dependence can be controlled. They then establish a theoretical connection between this dependence and the effect of graph convolution, supported by analysis of real-world graphs.

Their conclusion is that A-X dependence mediates how graph convolution affects node classification, with smaller dependence improving performance in the analysis presented. The work adds a specific explanatory factor to understanding GNN behavior: the arrangement of features on the topology matters, beyond considering the graph and the feature values separately.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how dependence between graph structure and node features influences graph convolution and node classification performance.

title: Feature Distribution on Graph Topology Mediates the Effect of Graph Convolution: Homophily Perspective

abstract: We study the performance of stochastic first-order methods for finding saddle points of convex-concave functions. A notorious challenge faced by such methods is that the gradients can grow arbitrarily large during optimization, which may result in instability and divergence. In this paper, we propose a simple and effective regularization technique that stabilizes the iterates and yields meaningful performance guarantees even if the domain and the gradient noise scales linearly with the size of the iterates (and is thus potentially unbounded). Besides providing a set of general results, we also apply our algorithm to a specific problem in reinforcement learning, where it leads to performance guarantees for finding near-optimal policies in an average-reward MDP without prior knowledge of the bias span.

paragraphs: Saddle-point optimization involves minimizing a function in some variables while maximizing it in others. This paper studies stochastic first-order methods for convex-concave problems, where updates use noisy gradient information. A central difficulty is that gradients can become arbitrarily large as optimization proceeds, causing unstable updates or even divergence.

The authors propose a regularization technique that stabilizes the sequence of iterates. Their analysis provides performance guarantees in settings that allow an unbounded domain and gradient noise that grows linearly with the size of the iterates. This matters because the analysis accommodates potentially increasing noise instead of depending on a fixed bound that may fail during optimization.

The paper also applies the method to reinforcement learning with an average-reward Markov decision process. In that setting, it provides guarantees for finding nearly optimal policies without advance knowledge of the bias span. The contribution therefore includes both general optimization results and a concrete learning application in which the method removes a prior-knowledge requirement.
summary.tldr: A regularization method stabilizes stochastic saddle-point optimization with potentially unbounded gradients and supports average-reward reinforcement learning guarantees.

title: Dealing With Unbounded Gradients in Stochastic Saddle-point Optimization

abstract: Neural models are equivalent to dynamic systems from a physics-inspired view, implying that computation on neural networks can be interpreted as the dynamical interactions between neurons. However, existing work models neuronal interaction as a weight-based linear transformation, and the nonlinearity comes from the nonlinear activation functions, which leads to limited nonlinearity and data-fitting ability of the whole neural model. Inspired by Riemannian geometry, we interpret neural structures by projecting neurons onto the Riemannian neuronal state space and model neuronal interaction with Riemannian metric (${\it RieM}$), which provides a more efficient neural representation with higher parameter efficiency. With ${\it RieM}$, we further design a novel data-free neural compression mechanism that does not require additional fine-tuning with real data. Using backbones like ResNet and Vision Transformer, we conduct extensive experiments on datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, and COCO object detection. Empirical results show that, under equal compression rates and computational complexity, models compressed with ${\it RieM}$ achieve superior inference accuracy compared to existing data-free compression methods.

summary.tldr: RieM uses geometry-based neuronal interactions to compress networks without real-data fine-tuning, improving accuracy over compared data-free methods at matched resource levels.

title: Data-free Neural Representation Compression with Riemannian Neural Dynamics

abstract: Private everlasting prediction (PEP), recently introduced by Naor et al. [2023], is a model for differentially private learning in which the learner never publicly releases a hypothesis. Instead, it provides black-box access to a "prediction oracle" that can predict the labels of an endless stream of unlabeled examples drawn from the underlying distribution. Importantly, PEP provides privacy both for the initial training set and for the endless stream of classification queries. We present two conceptual modifications to the definition of PEP, as well as new constructions exhibiting significant improvements over prior work. Specifically, we incorporate robustness against poisoning attacks into the definition of PEP; we present a relaxed privacy definition, suitable for PEP, that allows us to disconnect the privacy parameter $\delta$ from the number of total time steps $T$; and we present new constructions for axis-aligned rectangles and decision-stumps exhibiting improved sample complexity and runtime.

paragraphs: Private everlasting prediction provides access to a prediction service without publicly releasing its learned hypothesis. The service labels an endless stream of examples drawn from the underlying distribution while protecting both the original training data and the incoming queries. This paper revises that framework and develops improved constructions within it.

One change incorporates robustness to poisoning attacks into the definition, making malicious interference part of the prediction problem. Another introduces a relaxed privacy definition suited to this setting. Under that definition, the privacy parameter delta can be disconnected from the total number of time steps. This distinction matters for a service intended to keep answering indefinitely, and the relaxation is part of the resulting claim.

The authors also provide new constructions for axis-aligned rectangles and decision stumps, reporting improvements in sample complexity and runtime over earlier work. These are specific prediction classes for which the framework receives concrete algorithms. The overall contribution combines a revised account of privacy and robustness with more efficient methods for maintaining a private prediction oracle over an unending query stream.
summary.tldr: The paper extends everlasting private prediction with poisoning robustness, a relaxed privacy definition, and more efficient constructions for two prediction classes.

title: Private Truly-Everlasting Robust-Prediction

abstract: This paper studies the causal relations from subsampled time series, in which measurements are sparse and sampled at a coarser timescale than the causal timescale of the underlying system. In such data, because there are numerous missing time-slices (i.e., cross-sections at each time point) between two consecutive measurements, conventional causal discovery methods designed for standard time series data would produce significant errors. To learn causal relations from subsampled time series, a typical solution is to conduct different interventions and then make a comparison. However, full interventions are often expensive, unethical, or even infeasible, particularly in fields such as health and social science. In this paper, we first explore how readily available two-time-slices data can replace intervention data to improve causal ordering, and propose a novel Descendant Hierarchical Topology algorithm with Conditional Independence Test (DHT-CIT) to learn causal relations from subsampled time series using only two time-slices. Specifically, we develop a conditional independence criterion that can be applied iteratively to test each node from time series and identify all of its descendant nodes. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our DHT-CIT algorithm.

paragraphs: When measurements arrive more slowly than the causal processes operating in a system, many intermediate states go unobserved. Conventional time-series causal discovery methods can then make substantial errors. One response is to compare interventions, but interventions may be costly, unethical, or infeasible in settings such as health and social science.

This paper investigates how data from only two time slices can replace intervention data to improve causal ordering. It proposes DHT-CIT, a Descendant Hierarchical Topology algorithm using conditional independence tests. The central technical ingredient is a criterion applied repeatedly to each node to identify its descendants, meaning the nodes downstream of it in the causal structure.

By organizing discovery around descendant relationships, the method extracts causal information despite the missing intermediate measurements. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior performance for DHT-CIT. The contribution is therefore a specific algorithm for learning from coarsely sampled observations, supported by a conditional-independence criterion and empirical results, with two time slices providing the observations used by the method.
summary.tldr: DHT-CIT uses conditional independence tests on two time slices to learn causal relationships from coarsely sampled time series.

title: Learning Causal Relations from Subsampled Time Series with Two Time-Slices

abstract: Towards energy-efficient artificial intelligence similar to the human brain, the bio-inspired spiking neural networks (SNNs) have advantages of biological plausibility, event-driven sparsity, and binary activation. Recently, large-scale language models exhibit promising generalization capability, making it a valuable issue to explore more general spike-driven models. However, the binary spikes in existing SNNs fail to encode adequate semantic information, placing technological challenges for generalization. This work proposes the first fully spiking mechanism for general language tasks, including both discriminative and generative ones. Different from previous spikes with 0,1 levels, we propose a more general spike formulation with bi-directional, elastic amplitude, and elastic frequency encoding, while still maintaining the addition nature of SNNs. In a single time step, the spike is enhanced by direction and amplitude information; in spike frequency, a strategy to control spike firing rate is well designed. We plug this elastic bi-spiking mechanism in language modeling, named SpikeLM. It is the first time to handle general language tasks with fully spike-driven models, which achieve much higher accuracy than previously possible. SpikeLM also greatly bridges the performance gap between SNNs and ANNs in language modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xingrun-Xing/SpikeLM.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer sparse, event-driven computation, making them attractive for energy-efficient artificial intelligence. Their usual binary signals, however, can struggle to encode enough semantic information for general language tasks. This paper develops a richer spiking mechanism intended to address that representational bottleneck.

SpikeLM uses elastic bi-spiking, adding direction and flexible amplitude to individual spikes while also controlling firing frequency. These changes increase the information represented within a time step and across repeated spikes. The mechanism preserves the addition-based character of spiking computation while expanding beyond the conventional zero-or-one signal.

The authors apply this mechanism to fully spike-driven models for both discriminative and generative language tasks. They report much higher accuracy than previously achieved with such models and a substantial narrowing of the performance gap between spiking and conventional artificial neural networks. The result supports richer spike encoding as a route toward broader language capabilities. Energy efficiency motivates the work, while the stated findings emphasize accuracy and the ability to handle general language tasks.
summary.tldr: SpikeLM enriches spike direction, amplitude, and frequency to improve fully spike-driven models across discriminative and generative language tasks.

title: SpikeLM: Towards General Spike-Driven Language Modeling via Elastic Bi-Spiking Mechanisms

abstract: Pruning has recently been widely adopted to reduce the parameter scale and improve the inference efficiency of Large Language Models (LLMs). Mainstream pruning techniques often rely on uniform layerwise pruning strategies, which can lead to severe performance degradation at high sparsity levels. Recognizing the varying contributions of different layers in LLMs, recent studies have shifted their focus toward non-uniform layerwise pruning. However, these approaches often rely on pre-defined values, which can result in suboptimal performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel method called Dynamic Layerwise Pruning (DLP). This approach adaptively determines the relative importance of each layer by integrating model weights with input activation information, assigning pruning rates accordingly. Experimental results show that DLP effectively preserves model performance at high sparsity levels across multiple LLMs. Specifically, at 70% sparsity, DLP reduces the perplexity of LLaMA2-7B by 7.79 and improves the average accuracy by 2.7% compared to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, DLP is compatible with various existing LLM compression techniques and can be seamlessly integrated into Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT). We release the code[The code is available at: https://github.com/ironartisan/DLP.] to facilitate future research.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model's parameter count by removing selected weights. Applying the same pruning rate to every layer can damage performance when sparsity is high, because layers contribute differently to the model's behavior. Earlier non-uniform approaches address this imbalance but often depend on values fixed in advance.

Dynamic Layerwise Pruning estimates relative layer importance using both model weights and input activations. It then assigns pruning rates based on those estimates. The key change is to let information about the model and its response to inputs determine how pruning is distributed, rather than committing to a uniform or predefined allocation.

Experiments across multiple language models show that DLP preserves performance effectively at high sparsity. At 70% sparsity on LLaMA2-7B, the authors report a perplexity reduction of 7.79 and an average accuracy improvement of 2.7% over state-of-the-art methods. They also report compatibility with existing compression techniques and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These findings make layerwise allocation an important part of the compression strategy, alongside the choice of which individual weights to remove.
summary.tldr: DLP uses weights and input activations to assign layer-specific pruning rates, improving performance retention at high sparsity.

title: DLP: Dynamic Layerwise Pruning in Large Language Models

abstract: In the differentially private partition selection problem (a.k.a. set union, key discovery), users hold subsets of items from an unbounded universe. The goal is to output as many items as possible from the union of the users’ sets while maintaining user-level differential privacy. Solutions to this problem are a core building block for many privacy-preserving ML applications including vocabulary extraction in a private corpus, computing statistics over categorical data and learning embeddings over user-provided items. We propose an algorithm for this problem, MaxAdaptiveDegree (MAD), which adaptively reroutes weight from items with weight far above the threshold needed for privacy to items with smaller weight, thereby increasing the probability that less frequent items are output. Our algorithm can be efficiently implemented in massively parallel computation systems allowing scalability to very large datasets. We prove that our algorithm stochastically dominates the standard parallel algorithm for this problem. We also develop a two-round version of our algorithm, MAD2R, where results of the computation in the first round are used to bias the weighting in the second round to maximize the number of items output. In experiments, our algorithms provide the best results among parallel algorithms and scale to datasets with hundreds of billions of items, up to three orders of magnitude larger than those analyzed in prior works.

paragraphs: Private partition selection aims to release as many distinct items as possible from users' sets while maintaining user-level differential privacy. The item universe is unbounded. This problem appears in tasks such as extracting vocabulary from private text, reporting categorical statistics, and learning embeddings from user-provided items.

MaxAdaptiveDegree, or MAD, reallocates weight to improve which items can be released. Items with weight well above the privacy threshold give up some weight to items with less support, increasing the probability of releasing less frequent items. The method can run efficiently in massively parallel systems, and the authors prove stochastic dominance over the standard parallel algorithm.

The paper also introduces MAD2R, a two-round version that uses first-round results to guide second-round weighting toward releasing more items. Experiments report the best results among the parallel algorithms considered. The methods scale to datasets containing hundreds of billions of items, up to three orders of magnitude larger than those studied in prior work. The contribution combines a formal improvement over a standard approach with evidence of large-scale practicality.
summary.tldr: MAD adaptively shifts excess item weight toward less frequent items, improving private partition selection while scaling to hundreds of billions of items.

title: Scalable Private Partition Selection via Adaptive Weighting

abstract: The emergence of multimodal large models has advanced artificial intelligence, introducing unprecedented levels of performance and functionality. However, optimizing these models remains challenging due to historically isolated paths of model-centric and data-centric developments, leading to suboptimal outcomes and inefficient resource utilization. In response, we present a new sandbox suite tailored for integrated data-model co-development. This sandbox provides a feedback-driven experimental platform, enabling cost-effective iteration and guided refinement of both data and models. Our proposed “Probe-Analyze-Refine” workflow, validated through practical use cases on multimodal tasks such as image-text pre-training with CLIP, image-to-text generation with LLaVA-like models, and text-to-video generation with DiT-based models, yields transferable and notable performance boosts, such as topping the VBench leaderboard. A comprehensive set of over 100 experiments demonstrated the suite’s usability and extensibility, while also uncovering insights into the interplay between data quality, diversity, model behavior, and computational costs. All codes, datasets, and models are open-sourced to foster future research and applications that would otherwise be infeasible due to the lack of a dedicated co-development infrastructure.

paragraphs: Improving multimodal models involves choices about both the model and its training data. The paper argues that developing these separately can produce weaker results and waste resources. Data-Juicer Sandbox provides an experimental environment in which observations about model behavior can guide data changes, and data experiments can inform further model development.

Its Probe-Analyze-Refine workflow organizes this feedback into repeated experimentation and refinement. The authors apply it to image-text pre-training with CLIP, image-to-text generation with LLaVA-like models, and text-to-video generation with DiT-based models. These applications show how the same development infrastructure can support different relationships between visual and textual information.

Across more than 100 experiments, the authors report usability, extensibility, and transferable performance improvements, including topping the VBench leaderboard. The experiments also reveal relationships among data quality, diversity, model behavior, and computational cost. The stated contribution combines practical infrastructure with evidence that coordinating data and model decisions can improve outcomes. The code, datasets, and models are open-sourced to support further work using this integrated workflow.
summary.tldr: Data-Juicer Sandbox links data and model refinement through a feedback-driven workflow validated across several multimodal tasks.

title: Data-Juicer Sandbox: A Feedback-Driven Suite for Multimodal Data-Model Co-development

abstract: Endowing large language models (LLMs) with continual learning (CL) capacities is practically important, which enables them to dynamically acquire new knowledge over time. Although many effective methods have been proposed for CL of LLMs, they did not consider online scenarios, thereby sharing a common problem: information leakage (IL), where the task-related information of learned tasks is accessed or reused again. IL not only imposes potential risks on data privacy protection but also significantly hinders the deployment of LLMs in real-world scenarios. To avoid IL while maintaining outstanding CL performance, we propose a novel CL method for LLMs, which first characterizes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) block by a presentative feature distribution, and then dynamically selects the appropriate PEFT blocks for each instance based on its similarity with the presentative feature distributions. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our method on the CL of LLM, showcasing its potential to enhance both privacy and adaptability in practical applications.

paragraphs: Continual learning allows a language model to acquire knowledge as new tasks arrive. The paper focuses on online use, where revisiting information associated with previously learned tasks can create a problem. It calls this access or reuse information leakage and identifies both privacy concerns and practical deployment difficulties.

The proposed method organizes parameter-efficient fine-tuning blocks through feature distributions that characterize them. For each incoming instance, it compares that instance with the distributions and dynamically selects suitable blocks. This makes the characterization of each block central to deciding which learned adaptation should handle a particular input.

The authors propose this selection mechanism to avoid the identified leakage while retaining strong continual-learning performance. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness for language-model continual learning and suggest potential benefits for privacy and adaptability. The privacy claim is tied to avoiding the specific reuse problem described in the paper. The broader significance is an instance-dependent way to select existing adaptations as a model continues acquiring knowledge over time.
summary.tldr: Feature-distribution-based selection of fine-tuning blocks supports continual language-model learning while addressing reuse of prior task information.

title: Exploiting Presentative Feature Distributions for Parameter-Efficient Continual Learning of Large Language Models

abstract: Recent advancements in foundation models have improved autonomous tool usage and reasoning, but their capabilities in map-based reasoning remain underexplored. To address this, we introduce MapEval, a benchmark designed to assess foundation models across three distinct tasks—textual, API-based, and visual reasoning—through 700 multiple-choice questions spanning 180 cities and 54 countries, covering spatial relationships, navigation, travel planning, and real-world map interactions. Unlike prior benchmarks that focus on simple location queries, MapEval requires models to handle long-context reasoning, API interactions and visual map analysis, making it the most comprehensive evaluation framework for geospatial AI. On evaluation of 30 foundation models, including Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, none surpasses 67% accuracy, with open-source models performing significantly worse and all models lagging over 20% behind human performance. These results expose critical gaps in spatial inference, as models struggle with distances, directions, route planning, and place-specific reasoning, highlighting the need for better geospatial AI to bridge the gap between foundation models and real-world navigation.

paragraphs: Map-based reasoning involves more than recognizing a place name. A model may need to compare distances, follow directions, plan a route, or combine information from map tools. MapEval is designed to test these capabilities across textual reasoning, API interactions, and visual map analysis, including tasks that require handling long contexts.

The benchmark contains 700 multiple-choice questions covering 180 cities in 54 countries. Its questions address spatial relationships, navigation, travel planning, and interactions with real-world maps. This scope connects several forms of input and tool use within one evaluation, allowing researchers to examine geospatial reasoning beyond simple location queries.

Across 30 evaluated foundation models, none exceeds 67% accuracy. The authors report substantially worse performance from open-source models and a gap of more than 20% behind human performance for every tested model. Difficulties include distances, directions, route planning, and reasoning about particular places. These findings identify weaknesses in the evaluated models’ ability to turn map information into correct answers, despite broader progress in reasoning and autonomous tool use.
summary.tldr: MapEval tests geospatial reasoning through text, APIs, and maps, finding substantial gaps between 30 foundation models and human performance.

title: MapEval: A Map-Based Evaluation of Geo-Spatial Reasoning in Foundation Models

abstract: Message-Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing and analyzing graph-structured data. However, their effectiveness is often hindered by phenomena such as over-squashing, where long-range dependencies or interactions are inadequately captured and expressed in the MPNN output. This limitation mirrors the challenges of the Effective Receptive Field (ERF) in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), where the theoretical receptive field is underutilized in practice. In this work, we show and theoretically explain the limited ERF problem in MPNNs. Furthermore, inspired by recent advances in ERF augmentation for CNNs, we propose an Interleaved Multiscale Message-Passing Neural Networks (IM-MPNN) architecture to address these problems in MPNNs. Our method incorporates a hierarchical coarsening of the graph, enabling message-passing across multiscale representations and facilitating long-range interactions without excessive depth or parameterization. Through extensive evaluations on benchmarks such as the Long-Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB), we demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline MPNNs in capturing long-range dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: A message-passing neural network exchanges information along graph connections, but distant nodes may have little influence on its final output. Even when the architecture theoretically permits long-range information flow, that capacity can be underused. The paper identifies and theoretically explains this limited effective receptive field, connecting it to similar behavior in convolutional networks.

The proposed Interleaved Multiscale Message-Passing Neural Network builds a hierarchy of coarser graph representations. Messages pass across these different scales, enabling information to travel through broader representations of the graph. This gives the model a way to support long-range interactions without relying on excessive depth or a large increase in parameters. The design is motivated by approaches that expand effective receptive fields in convolutional models.

Evaluations include the Long-Range Graph Benchmark and show substantial improvements over baseline message-passing networks in capturing distant dependencies while maintaining computational efficiency. The findings suggest that access to multiple graph scales can make more of the graph meaningfully influence predictions, addressing the gap between theoretical connectivity and effective information use.
summary.tldr: IM-MPNN uses hierarchical graph scales to improve long-range information use without excessive network depth or parameterization.

title: Improving the Effective Receptive Field of Message-Passing Neural Networks

abstract: Modern neural-network-based Image Quality Assessment (IQA) metrics are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which can be exploited to manipulate search engine rankings, benchmark results, and content quality assessments, raising concerns about the reliability of IQA metrics in critical applications. This paper presents the first comprehensive study of IQA defense mechanisms in response to adversarial attacks on these metrics to pave the way for safer use of IQA metrics. We systematically evaluated 30 defense strategies, including purification, training-based, and certified methods — and applied 14 adversarial attacks in adaptive and non-adaptive settings to compare these defenses on 9 no-reference IQA metrics. Our proposed benchmark aims to guide the development of IQA defense methods and is open to submissions; the latest results and code are at https://msu-video-group.github.io/adversarial-defenses-for-iqa/.

paragraphs: Neural image-quality metrics can be manipulated by adversarial attacks. This matters when their scores influence search rankings, benchmark comparisons, or judgments about content quality: an altered score can undermine the reliability of the assessment. The paper studies defenses for these metrics through a broad, systematic benchmarking effort.

The evaluation includes thirty defense strategies spanning purification, training-based approaches, and certified methods. It tests them against fourteen attacks on nine no-reference image-quality metrics. Both adaptive and non-adaptive attack settings are included, allowing defenses to be examined under different relationships between the attack and the protection being evaluated.

The main contribution described is the comparative benchmark itself. Its coverage brings multiple defense families, attack settings, and quality metrics into a shared evaluation effort, providing a basis for assessing protective methods across combinations of conditions. The benchmark also accepts submissions to support further development. The abstract establishes the scope and intended use of this resource without identifying a winning defense or claiming that the evaluated protections eliminate adversarial vulnerability.
summary.tldr: This benchmark evaluates thirty defenses against fourteen attacks on nine neural image-quality metrics.

title: Guardians of Image Quality: Benchmarking Defenses Against Adversarial Attacks on Image Quality Metrics

abstract: Pretraining large language models (LLMs) is resource-intensive, often requiring months of training time even with high-end GPU clusters. There are two approaches of mitigating such computational demands: reusing smaller models to train larger ones (upcycling), and training computationally efficient models like mixture-of-experts (MoE). In this paper, we study the upcycling of LLMs to MoE models, of which the scaling behavior remains underexplored. Through extensive experiments, we identify empirical scaling laws that describe how performance depends on dataset size and model configuration. Particularly, we show that, while scaling these factors improves performance, there is a novel interaction term between the dense and upcycled training dataset that limits the efficiency of upcycling at large computational budgets. Based on these findings, we provide guidance to scale upcycling, and establish conditions under which upcycling outperforms from-scratch trainings within budget constraints.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to reuse an existing dense language model when building a mixture-of-experts model. Reusing a smaller model, called upcycling, can reduce the need to start training from scratch. Mixture-of-experts models provide another route to computational efficiency, making their combination an appealing subject for studying training budgets.

Through extensive experiments, the authors derive empirical scaling laws relating performance to dataset size and model configuration. They identify an interaction between the data used for dense-model training and the data used during upcycling. Although increasing these factors improves performance, their interaction limits the efficiency advantage of upcycling at large computational budgets.

The findings provide guidance for scaling the approach and establish conditions under which upcycling outperforms training from scratch within a budget. The practical message is conditional: reuse can be beneficial, but its value depends on how earlier training, subsequent data, and model configuration fit together. The scaling analysis makes those dependencies part of the budget-allocation decision.
summary.tldr: Empirical scaling laws identify when converting dense models into mixture-of-experts models is more efficient than training from scratch.

title: Scaling Laws for Upcycling Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

abstract: As a leading unsupervised classification algorithm in artificial intelligence, multi-view subspace clustering segments unlabeled data from different subspaces. Recent works based on the anchor have been proposed to decrease the computation complexity for the datasets with large scales in multi-view clustering. The major differences among these methods lie on the objective functions they define. Despite considerable success, these works pay few attention to guaranting the robustness of learned consensus anchors via effective manner for efficient multi-view clustering and investigating the specific local distribution of cluster in the affine subspace. Besides, the robust consensus anchors as well as the common cluster structure shared by different views are not able to be simultaneously learned. In this paper, we propose Robust Consensus anchors learning for efficient multi-view Subspace Clustering (RCSC). We first show that if the data are sufficiently sampled from independent subspaces, and the objective function meets some conditions, the achieved anchor graph has the block-diagonal structure. As a special case, we provide a model based on Frobenius norm, non-negative and affine constraints in consensus anchors learning, which guarantees the robustness of learned consensus anchors for efficient multi-view clustering and investigates the specific local distribution of cluster in the affine subspace. While it is simple, we theoretically give the geometric analysis regarding the formulated RCSC. The union of these three constraints is able to restrict how each data point is described in the affine subspace with specific local distribution of cluster for guaranting the robustness of learned consensus anchors. RCSC takes full advantages of correlation among consensus anchors, which encourages the grouping effect and groups highly correlated consensus anchors together with the guidance of view-specific projection. The anchor graph construction, partition and robust anchor learning are jointly integrated into a unified framework. It ensures the mutual enhancement for these procedures and helps lead to more discriminative consensus anchors as well as the cluster indicator. We then adopt an alternative optimization strategy for solving the formulated problem. Experiments performed on eight multi-view datasets confirm the superiority of RCSC based on the effectiveness and efficiency.
