paragraphs: Multi-view subspace clustering groups unlabeled samples using multiple representations of the same data. Anchors reduce computational cost, but their quality and robustness affect the resulting groups. RCSC jointly learns shared anchors, the graph connecting samples to them, and the graph partition, so these components can improve one another during optimization.

The paper first establishes a conditional structural result: with sufficiently sampled independent subspaces and suitable objective-function conditions, the learned anchor graph is block diagonal. Its concrete model combines a Frobenius-norm objective with nonnegative and affine constraints. A geometric analysis explains how these ingredients restrict sample representations according to local cluster distributions in affine subspaces.

RCSC also uses correlations among consensus anchors to encourage related anchors to group together, guided by projections specific to each view. An alternating optimization strategy solves the unified objective. Experiments on eight multi-view datasets report superior effectiveness and efficiency. The theoretical result explains when cleanly separated graph structure can arise, while the empirical findings support jointly learning robust anchors and clusters on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: RCSC jointly learns robust shared anchors and clusters, with conditional guarantees for separated graph structure and strong results on eight datasets.

title: Robust Consensus Anchor Learning for Efficient Multi-view Subspace Clustering

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant popularity due to their remarkable capabilities in text understanding and generation. However, despite their widespread deployment in inference services such as ChatGPT, concerns about the potential leakage of sensitive user data have arisen. Existing solutions primarily rely on privacy-enhancing technologies to mitigate such risks, facing the trade-off among efficiency, privacy, and utility. To narrow this gap, we propose Cape, a context-aware prompt perturbation mechanism based on differential privacy, to enable efficient inference with an improved privacy-utility trade-off. Concretely, we introduce a hybrid utility function that better captures the token similarity. Additionally, we propose a bucketized sampling mechanism to handle large sampling space, which might lead to long-tail phenomenons. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets, along with ablation studies, demonstrate that Cape achieves a better privacy-utility trade-off compared to prior state-of-the-art works.

paragraphs: Prompts sent to language model services can contain sensitive user information. Privacy protection must therefore balance how much it changes the input against whether the resulting prompt remains useful and efficient to process. Cape addresses this balance through a context-aware prompt perturbation mechanism based on differential privacy.

The mechanism introduces a hybrid utility function intended to capture token similarity more effectively. That similarity assessment guides perturbation toward alternatives that retain useful aspects of the prompt. Cape also uses bucketized sampling to manage a large space of possible selections. This component addresses the long-tail behavior that can arise when sampling from many candidates, making the selection process another central part of the design.

Experiments across multiple datasets, together with ablation studies, show a better privacy-utility trade-off than the prior state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The stated result concerns the balance between protecting information and preserving usefulness, rather than eliminating that trade-off. Cape's contribution is to improve this balance by considering both contextual similarity and how perturbation candidates are sampled.
summary.tldr: Cape combines context-aware token similarity and bucketized sampling to improve the privacy-utility trade-off in prompt perturbation.

title: Cape: Context-Aware Prompt Perturbation Mechanism with Differential Privacy

abstract: Neurons in large language models often exhibit polysemanticity, simultaneously encoding multiple unrelated concepts and obscuring interpretability. Instead of relying on post-hoc methods, we present MoE-X, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model designed to be intrinsically interpretable. Our approach is motivated by the observation that, in language models, wider networks with sparse activations are more likely to capture interpretable factors. however, directly training such large sparse networks is computationally prohibitive. MoE architectures offer a scalable alternative by activating only a subset of experts for any given input, inherently aligning with interpretability objectives. In MoE-X, we establish this connection by rewriting the MoE layer as an equivalent sparse, large MLP. This approach enables efficient scaling of the hidden size while maintaining sparsity. To further enhance interpretability, we enforce sparse activation within each expert and redesign the routing mechanism to prioritize experts with the highest activation sparsity. These designs ensure that only the most salient features are routed and processed by the experts. We evaluate MoE-X on chess and natural language tasks, showing that it achieves performance comparable to dense models while significantly improving interpretability. MoE-X achieves a perplexity better than GPT-2, with interpretability surpassing even sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based approaches.

paragraphs: Language model neurons can encode several unrelated concepts, making their behavior difficult to interpret. MoE-X addresses this through the model’s architecture. Its motivation is that wide networks with sparse activations are more likely to capture interpretable factors, but directly training very large sparse networks can be computationally prohibitive.

The authors express a mixture-of-experts layer as an equivalent large, sparse multilayer perceptron. Because only some experts activate for an input, this provides a scalable way to increase hidden size while preserving sparsity. MoE-X further encourages sparse activity within each expert and changes routing to favor experts with the highest activation sparsity, directing computation toward salient features.

Evaluations on chess and natural language tasks show performance comparable to dense models with substantially better interpretability. The paper also reports better perplexity than GPT-2 and stronger interpretability than sparse-autoencoder-based approaches. These findings support incorporating interpretability objectives into the model’s computation itself. They connect the architectural choices about width, expert activity, and routing to the observed ability to identify more interpretable features.
summary.tldr: MoE-X builds sparsity into expert activations and routing to improve intrinsic interpretability while retaining competitive language-model performance.

title: Mixture of Experts Made Intrinsically Interpretable

abstract: Due to the dynamics of underlying physics and external influences, the uncertainty of time series often varies over time. However, existing Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) often fail to capture this non-stationary nature, constrained by their constant variance assumption from the additive noise model (ANM). In this paper, we innovatively utilize the Location-Scale Noise Model (LSNM) to relax the fixed uncertainty assumption of ANM. A diffusion-based probabilistic forecasting framework, termed Non-stationary Diffusion (NsDiff), is designed based on LSNM that is capable of modeling the changing pattern of uncertainty. Specifically, NsDiff combines a denoising diffusion-based conditional generative model with a pre-trained conditional mean and variance estimator, enabling adaptive endpoint distribution modeling. Furthermore, we propose an uncertainty-aware noise schedule, which dynamically adjusts the noise levels to accurately reflect the data uncertainty at each step and integrates the time-varying variances into the diffusion process. Extensive experiments conducted on nine real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the superior performance of NsDiff compared to existing approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/wwy155/NsDiff.

paragraphs: A time series can become more or less uncertain as its underlying conditions change. The paper argues that diffusion forecasting approaches based on a constant-variance additive noise model can struggle to represent this behavior. It proposes modeling changing uncertainty explicitly as part of probabilistic forecasting.

Non-stationary Diffusion, or NsDiff, uses a location-scale noise model that relaxes the fixed-uncertainty assumption. It combines a conditional diffusion generator with pretrained estimators of conditional mean and variance. These estimates support an adaptive endpoint distribution, allowing the diffusion framework to incorporate information about both the expected value and the uncertainty associated with the data.

NsDiff also introduces an uncertainty-aware noise schedule that adjusts noise levels and incorporates time-varying variances into the diffusion process. Across nine real-world and synthetic datasets, the authors report superior performance over existing approaches. The contribution connects uncertainty estimation to multiple parts of generation, so changing variability influences the forecast distribution rather than being represented through a single fixed noise scale.
summary.tldr: NsDiff incorporates time-varying uncertainty into diffusion forecasting through adaptive distributions and uncertainty-aware noise scheduling.

title: Non-stationary Diffusion For Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models provides an effective solution to alleviate the label scarcity problem in cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) detection using electrocardiogram (ECG). However, as the pre-trained models scale up, the computational costs for fine-tuning and inference become unaffordable on low-level devices deployed for clinical applications. Additionally, maintaining the model performance under low budgets in computational resources remains a significant challenge. However, a comprehensive study that can address them in a joint framework is still lacking. Here, we propose a holistic method (H-Tuning) for low-cost and efficient fine-tuning of pre-trained models on downstream datasets. Then, the inference costs of the models fine-tuned by H-Tuning are further reduced significantly using a knowledge distillation technique. Experiments on four ECG datasets demonstrate that H-Tuning reduces the GPU memory consumption during fine-tuning by 6.34 times while achieving comparable CVDs detection performance to standard fine-tuning. With the knowledge distillation technique, the model inference latency and the memory consumption are reduced by 4.52 times and 19.83 times. As such, the proposed joint framework allows for the utilization of pre-trained models with high computation efficiency and robust performance, exploring a path toward low-cost and efficient CVDs detection. Code is available at https://github.com/KAZABANA/H-Tuning

paragraphs: Pretrained models can help detect cardiovascular disease from electrocardiograms when labeled data are scarce. Their size, however, makes both adaptation and subsequent prediction expensive on devices with limited resources. H-Tuning addresses these two stages together, aiming to retain useful detection performance while reducing the computational demands of using pretrained models.

The framework first applies H-Tuning to adapt a pretrained model to a downstream ECG dataset at lower cost. It then uses knowledge distillation to reduce the cost of running the resulting model. Treating fine-tuning and inference as separate targets within one framework matters because saving resources during training alone does not resolve deployment costs.

Experiments on four ECG datasets report a 6.34-fold reduction in fine-tuning GPU memory use with detection performance comparable to standard fine-tuning. With distillation, inference latency and memory consumption fall by factors of 4.52 and 19.83, respectively. These results demonstrate substantial computational savings in the evaluated settings and support a route toward ECG detection models that fit tighter resource budgets.
summary.tldr: H-Tuning combines efficient adaptation and knowledge distillation to reduce ECG model training and inference costs while retaining comparable detection performance.

title: H-Tuning: Toward Low-Cost and Efficient ECG-based Cardiovascular Disease Detection with Pre-Trained Models

abstract: Reasoning-intensive retrieval is increasingly important for downstream applications, requiring more than lexical overlap or coarse semantic matching. While prior work mainly relies on Language Models (LMs) to synthesize reasoning-oriented supervision, we posit that it is already latent in LM-based retrievers but suppressed by contrastive overfitting. To elicit this latent reasoning, we introduce ElicitR, a retriever–LM framework with generative regularization that captures nuanced relationships among a query and its candidate documents beyond binary relevance. Concretely, alongside contrastive learning, we regularize the retriever by co-training a small LM on query–positive–negative batches. Next token prediction (NTP) for each text is conditioned on its prefix and the other in-batch texts, with cross-text conditioning weighted by retriever-computed similarities. Using MS MARCO as the only paired query-document supervision and a 135M LM for generative regularization with unlabeled raw-text initialization, ElicitR consistently improves BRIGHT by 16-29% relative across 0.1B–3B retriever scales while maintaining performance on BEIR. At 3B, ElicitR reaches an nDCG@10 of 23.1, substantially outperforming larger models trained with far more curated pairs and proprietary APIs. Further analyses show that ElicitR prevents overfitting, improves retrieval calibration, and remains robust to batch sizes, supporting its practicality.

paragraphs: Retrieval that requires reasoning must capture relationships beyond shared words or broad semantic similarity. ElicitR starts from the hypothesis that language-model-based retrievers already contain useful reasoning capabilities, but contrastive training can suppress them through overfitting. The proposed solution supplements relevance training with a generative learning objective.

A small language model is co-trained on batches containing queries, positive documents, and negative documents. When predicting the next token of a text, it uses both that text’s prefix and other texts in the batch. The retriever’s similarity scores determine the weight of this cross-text information. This gives the retriever a training signal about nuanced relationships that binary relevance labels alone do not express.

Using only MS MARCO for paired query–document supervision and a 135M language model for regularization, ElicitR improves BRIGHT results by 16–29% relative across retriever sizes from 0.1B to 3B parameters while maintaining BEIR performance. The 3B retriever reaches 23.1 nDCG@10. Additional analyses report reduced overfitting, better calibration, and robustness to batch size, supporting the practical value of the generative objective.
summary.tldr: ElicitR adds cross-text generative regularization to retriever training, improving reasoning-intensive retrieval while maintaining broader retrieval performance.

title: ElicitR: Unlocking Latent Reasoning in Dense Retrievers via Generative Regularization

abstract: Approximation of a target probability distribution using a finite set of points is a problem of fundamental importance in numerical integration. Several authors have proposed to select points by minimising a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), but the non-convexity of this objective typically precludes global minimisation. Instead, we consider the concept of stationary points of the MMD which, in contrast to points globally minimising the MMD, can be accurately computed. Our main contributions are two-fold and theoretical in nature. We first prove the (perhaps surprising) result that, for integrands in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the numerical integration error of stationary MMD points vanishes faster than the MMD. Motivated by this super-convergence property, we consider MMD gradient flows as a practical strategy for computing stationary points of the MMD. We then prove that MMD gradient flow can indeed compute stationary MMD points, based on a refined convergence analysis that establishes a novel non-asymptotic finite-particle error bound.

We then prove that MMD gradient flow can indeed compute stationary MMD points, based on a refined convergence analysis that establishes a novel non-asymptotic finite-particle error bound.

paragraphs: Numerical integration often represents a probability distribution using a finite collection of points. One way to choose those points is to minimize maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, between their distribution and the target. Because this objective is non-convex, finding its global minimum is generally difficult.

This paper studies stationary configurations of the MMD objective, which can be computed accurately even when global minimization is impractical. Its first theoretical result shows that, for integrands belonging to the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, integration error vanishes faster than the MMD itself. This super-convergence result gives stationary configurations a stronger justification than their discrepancy value alone might suggest.

The second contribution concerns how to obtain those configurations. The authors analyze MMD gradient flow and prove that it can compute stationary MMD points. Their refined analysis includes a non-asymptotic finite-particle error bound. Together, the results link an attainable optimization target to favorable integration behavior, with the super-convergence claim applying to the stated class of integrands.
summary.tldr: Stationary MMD point sets can deliver integration error that vanishes faster than their discrepancy, and gradient flow can compute them.

title: Stationary MMD Points

abstract: Features of the same sample generated by different pretrained models often exhibit inherently distinct feature distributions. Learning invariant representations from large-scale unlabeled visual data in a fully unsupervised transfer manner remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we propose a multiview self-representation learning (MSRL) method in which invariant representations are learned by exploiting the self-representation property of features across heterogeneous views. The features are derived from large-scale unlabeled visual data through transfer learning with various pretrained models and are referred to as heterogeneous multiview data. We introduce an information-passing mechanism that relies on self-representation learning to support feature aggregation over the outputs of the linear model. Moreover, an assignment probability distribution consistency scheme is presented to guide multiview self-representation learning by exploiting complementary information across different views. Consequently, representation invariance across different linear models is enforced through this scheme. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the assignment probability distribution consistency and the incremental views. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed MSRL method consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches.

Multiview Self-Representation Learning addresses this problem using heterogeneous views extracted from large collections of unlabeled visual data.

The method exploits self-representation relationships within features across the views. An information-passing mechanism uses those relationships to support aggregation of linear-model outputs. A second mechanism encourages consistency between assignment probability distributions across views. This shared assignment structure guides learning toward representations that remain invariant across the different linear models while drawing on complementary information.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of assignment-distribution consistency and incremental views, alongside extensive experiments. The method consistently outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches in those evaluations. Its contribution is an unsupervised way to organize outputs from multiple pretrained models around shared structure. Rather than requiring the original feature distributions to match, the learning process uses consistency in their assignments to help establish an invariant representation.
summary.tldr: MSRL learns invariant visual representations from heterogeneous pretrained features through self-representation and cross-view assignment consistency.

title: Multiview Self-Representation Learning across Heterogeneous Views

abstract: Embodied 3D object detection is a fundamental perceptual capability for embodied agents, in which observations are partial, heavily occluded, and sequential, requiring modeling of temporal continuity. However, existing benchmarks and methods are primarily designed for fully reconstructed global scenes and fail to capture temporal observation context and instance evolution in first-person perception. We introduce Embodied-Det, a new benchmark for embodied 3D object detection that evaluates detection accuracy, temporal stability, and consistency under egocentric sequential views. Building on this benchmark, we propose Embodied-DETR, an end-to-end temporal detection framework that models scene-level context and instance-level consistency through two complementary temporal modules, Scene-aware Feature Aggregation and Instance-aware Query Embedding. Experiments on Embodied-Det show that existing methods suffer substantial performance degradation in egocentric temporal settings, while Embodied-DETR achieves superior accuracy and temporal consistency, demonstrating the effectiveness of temporal modeling for embodied 3D perception. Codes are available at https://github.com/UniPerceptor/UniPerceptor.

paragraphs: An embodied agent observes its surroundings through a sequence of partial first-person views. Objects may be hidden, only partly visible, or seen differently over time. This makes three-dimensional detection a temporal problem. The paper argues that benchmarks built around fully reconstructed global scenes do not adequately test this observation process or the evolution of individual object instances.

The authors introduce Embodied-Det, a benchmark that measures detection accuracy together with temporal stability and consistency. They also propose Embodied-DETR, an end-to-end detector with two complementary temporal modules. Scene-aware Feature Aggregation models context across the scene, while Instance-aware Query Embedding supports consistency for individual objects. Together, these modules address temporal information at both the scene and object levels.

On the new benchmark, existing methods show substantial performance drops under sequential egocentric observations. Embodied-DETR achieves better accuracy and temporal consistency in the reported experiments. The findings support evaluating embodied perception across sequences and explicitly modeling temporal continuity, rather than judging detection solely through reconstructed scene representations.
summary.tldr: Embodied-DETR combines scene and object temporal modeling to improve 3D detection across partial first-person views.

title: Embodied-DETR: End-to-End Temporal 3D Object Detection in Egocentric Views

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a strong alternative to autoregressive language models (AR-LMs), due to their comparable accuracy and faster inference speed via parallel decoding. However, standard DLM decoding strategies, which rely on unmasking only high-confidence tokens, encounter an inherent information-theoretic bottleneck that restricts decoding progress and ultimately slows down generation. We demonstrate this through an information-theoretic lower bound that the number of decoding rounds must grow linearly with the sample’s total information and inversely with the per-round information budget, establishing a bits-to-rounds principle. Motivated by this theory, we propose Explore-Then-Exploit (ETE), a training-free decoding strategy that maximizes information throughput and decoding efficiency. ETE combines cross-block decoding with targeted exploration of high-uncertainty tokens to reshape the conditional distribution and trigger cascades of confident predictions. Experiments across diverse benchmarks verify our theoretical bounds and demonstrate that ETE consistently reduces the number of decoding rounds compared to confidence-only baselines without compromising generation quality. Furthermore, ETE integrates efficiently with KV caching, translating these algorithmic gains into improved tokens-per-second throughput.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can fill multiple token positions in parallel, yet choosing only highly confident predictions can restrict progress. This paper analyzes that restriction through an information-theoretic lower bound. The required decoding rounds grow with the sample’s total information and shrink as the amount of information obtainable per round increases.

The proposed Explore-Then-Exploit strategy uses this observation to change decoding without additional training. It combines decoding across blocks with targeted exploration of uncertain tokens. Resolving selected uncertain positions can reshape the conditional distribution and make other positions easier to predict, triggering cascades of confident token decisions.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks support the theoretical bounds and show fewer decoding rounds than confidence-only baselines without compromising generation quality. The method also works efficiently with KV caching, turning the reduction in rounds into higher tokens-per-second throughput. Its contribution is to treat uncertainty as something the decoder can selectively explore to unlock progress, rather than relying exclusively on positions that are already easy to predict.
summary.tldr: Explore-Then-Exploit speeds diffusion language decoding by resolving selected uncertain tokens that unlock further confident predictions.

title: From Bits to Rounds: Parallel Decoding with Exploration for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Pretraining produces a learned parameter vector that is typically treated as a starting point for further iterative adaptation. In this work, we instead view the outcome of pretraining as a distribution over parameter vectors, whose support already contains task-specific experts. We show that in smaller or insufficiently trained models such expert solutions occupy a negligible fraction of the volume of this distribution, making their discovery reliant on structured optimization methods such as gradient descent. In contrast, in large, well-pretrained models the density of task-experts increases dramatically, so that diverse specialists populate a substantial fraction of the neighborhood around the pretrained weights. Motivated by this perspective, we explore a simple, fully parallel post-training method that samples $N$ parameter vectors at random, selects the top $K$, and ensembles them via majority vote to combine complementary expertise. Despite its simplicity, this approach is competitive with standard post-training methods such as PPO, GRPO, and ES for contemporary large-scale models.

paragraphs: Pretrained weights are usually treated as the starting point for further optimization. This paper instead views pretraining as producing a distribution over parameter vectors that already contains task-specific experts. The central question becomes how densely useful specialists populate the neighborhood around the pretrained model.

The authors show that expert solutions occupy a negligible fraction of this distribution for smaller or insufficiently trained models. In that setting, finding them relies on structured optimization such as gradient descent. For large, well-pretrained models, they find a much higher density: diverse specialists occupy a substantial portion of the nearby parameter space.

Motivated by this distinction, the paper explores sampling N parameter vectors randomly, selecting the best K, and combining their predictions by majority vote. Sampling is fully parallel, and the vote brings together complementary expertise. For contemporary large-scale models, the approach is competitive with PPO, GRPO, and ES. The finding ties this simple post-training strategy to the density of experts associated with model scale and pretraining quality.
summary.tldr: Large, well-pretrained models contain dense nearby task experts that can be sampled, selected, and ensembled competitively with standard post-training methods.

title: Neural Thickets: Diverse Task Experts Are Dense Around Pretrained Weights

abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) has the potential to enable effective decision-making over long timescales. Existing approaches, while promising, have yet to realize the benefits of large-scale training. In this work, we identify and solve several key challenges in scaling online hierarchical RL to high-throughput environments. We propose Scalable Option Learning (SOL), a highly scalable hierarchical policy gradient algorithm which achieves a 35x higher throughput compared to existing hierarchical methods. To demonstrate SOL’s performance and scalability, we train hierarchical agents using 30 billion frames of experience on the complex game of NetHack, significantly surpassing flat agents and demonstrating positive scaling trends. We also validate SOL on MiniHack and Mujoco environments, showcasing its general applicability.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning aims to organize decisions over longer timescales, but existing methods have struggled to benefit fully from large-scale training. This paper focuses on the practical challenges of running online hierarchical learning in environments that can generate experience quickly. Its proposed algorithm is Scalable Option Learning, or SOL.

SOL is a hierarchical policy-gradient method designed for high throughput. The authors report processing experience 35 times faster than existing hierarchical methods. This matters because a promising decision-making structure must also train efficiently enough to use large experience budgets; otherwise, its computational overhead can restrict the scale at which it is tested.

The researchers train hierarchical agents on 30 billion frames of NetHack experience. Those agents substantially outperform flat agents and show positive scaling trends in the reported experiments. Evaluations on MiniHack and Mujoco provide evidence that SOL applies beyond the main game setting. The combined contribution is an algorithm that makes large-scale hierarchical training practical and empirical evidence that hierarchy can benefit from that scale.
summary.tldr: SOL scales hierarchical reinforcement learning to 30 billion NetHack frames with 35-fold higher throughput than existing hierarchical methods.

title: Scalable Option Learning in High-Throughput Environments

abstract: Computation overhead has emerged as a critical bottleneck in Federated Learning (FL). Coreset selection tackles this challenge by constructing an informative subset to represent the full dataset. However, existing approaches optimize coreset construction solely at the data level and enforce a uniform retention ratio across all clients, ignoring client heterogeneity and introducing detrimental fragmented clients. In this paper, we first introduce a gradient projection Shapley value (GPSV) to evaluate client contributions. GPSV captures both the directional and magnitude information of client updates and enables exact Shapley value calculation with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per-coalition evaluation. Building on GPSV, we then propose ShapCCS, the first client-level coreset selection strategy for FL. ShapCCS prioritizes clients with high GPSV scores while excluding fragmented clients with negligible or even negative GPSV. As a client-level coreset selection strategy, ShapCCS can be integrated with a data-level selection approach, and additionally reduces communication costs, an advantage unattainable by data-level methods alone. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of ShapCCS on model performance and robustness to noise. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ShapCCS-5CBB.

paragraphs: Federated learning can reduce computation by training on informative subsets of data. Existing coreset methods, however, may retain the same fraction of data at every client despite differences in client usefulness. ShapCCS moves selection to the client level, addressing the paper’s concern that uniform retention can leave fragmented clients with negligible or harmful contributions.

The method introduces a gradient projection Shapley value that uses both the direction and magnitude of client updates to assess contribution. It enables exact Shapley calculation with constant-time evaluation per coalition; that statement concerns each coalition evaluation, not the entire calculation. ShapCCS prioritizes clients with high scores and excludes fragmented clients whose scores are negligible or negative.

Client selection can be combined with data-level coreset construction, allowing both approaches to operate together. It also reduces communication costs, an advantage the authors distinguish from data-only selection. Experiments report superior model performance and robustness to noise. The findings support accounting for client heterogeneity when deciding which participants should represent the wider federated dataset.
summary.tldr: ShapCCS selects informative federated-learning clients using gradient-based Shapley contributions, reducing communication while improving reported performance and noise robustness.

title: ShapCCS: Shapley-Driven Client Coreset Selection in Federated Learning

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful deep learning approach for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) in the physical sciences, yet their behavior remains largely opaque and is typically understood through failure mode analyses rather than explicit interpretability. To address this issue, we introduce PINNfluence, a training data attribution framework for interpreting PINNs based on influence functions. By extending influence functions to composite physics-informed training objectives, we enable fine-grained attribution between predictions, loss components, and training data points. Through benchmark experiments across various PDEs, we demonstrate that influence patterns provide granular diagnostics that distinguish structural characteristics across well-trained and poorly-trained PINNs. PINNfluence thus opens a new avenue for understanding and improving the reliability of PINNs through the lens of their data.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by training with objectives that incorporate physical constraints. Although they can be powerful scientific tools, their behavior is difficult to interpret. This paper introduces PINNfluence to connect their predictions and training losses back to the data points used during learning.

The framework adapts influence functions to the composite objectives used by physics-informed networks. These objectives contain multiple components, so attribution must account for more than a single undifferentiated training loss. PINNfluence provides fine-grained relationships among individual data points, loss components, and predictions, offering a structured way to examine how training information affects the learned solution.

Experiments across several partial differential equations show that influence patterns distinguish structural characteristics of well-trained and poorly trained networks. This turns attribution into a diagnostic tool for examining successful and unsuccessful training behavior. The contribution is an explicit interpretation framework grounded in training data, providing a route toward understanding and improving reliability beyond analyzing failures only after they appear.
summary.tldr: PINNfluence adapts influence functions to physics-informed networks, linking predictions and loss components to training points for detailed diagnostics.

title: PINNfluence: Interpreting PINNs through Influence Functions

abstract: Text-to-video generation has advanced rapidly, but existing methods typically output only the final composited video and lack editable layered representations, limiting their use in professional workflows. We propose LayerT2V, a unified multi-layer video generation framework that produces multiple semantically consistent outputs in a single inference pass: the full video, an independent background layer, and multiple foreground RGB layers with corresponding alpha mattes. Our key insight is that recent video generation backbones use high compression in both time and space, enabling us to serialize multiple layer representations along the temporal dimension and jointly model them on a shared generation trajectory. This turns cross-layer consistency into an intrinsic objective, improving semantic alignment and temporal coherence. To mitigate layer ambiguity and conditional leakage, we augment a shared DiT backbone with LayerAdaLN and layer-aware cross-attention modulation. LayerT2V is trained in three stages: alpha mask VAE adaptation, joint multi-layer learning, and multi-foreground extension. We also introduce VidLayer, the first large-scale dataset for multi-layer video generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerT2V substantially outperforms prior methods in visual fidelity, temporal consistency, and cross-layer coherence. To facilitate future research, we will release the code and dataset upon publication.

paragraphs: Generated videos usually arrive as finished composites, making their individual visual elements difficult to edit. LayerT2V instead generates the complete video alongside a separate background and multiple foreground color layers with alpha mattes. Those mattes describe how foreground content combines with other layers, providing the components needed for layered editing.

The framework uses the strong spatial and temporal compression of recent video backbones to arrange layer representations along the temporal dimension. It generates them jointly through a shared trajectory, making consistency across layers part of the modeling objective. LayerAdaLN and layer-aware cross-attention modulation address ambiguity between layers and leakage of conditioning information.

Training proceeds through alpha-mask VAE adaptation, joint multilayer learning, and extension to multiple foregrounds. The authors also introduce VidLayer, a large-scale dataset for this task. Experiments report substantial gains over prior methods in visual fidelity, temporal consistency, and coherence between layers. The result is an approach that couples editable outputs with joint generation of their visual relationships.
summary.tldr: LayerT2V jointly generates a complete video and consistent background, foreground, and transparency layers in one inference pass.

title: LayerT2V: A Unified Multi-Layer Video Generation Framework

abstract: How can we learn the laws underlying the dynamics of stochastic systems when their trajectories are sampled sparsely in time? Existing methods either require temporally resolved high-frequency observations, or rely on geometric arguments that apply only to conservative systems, limiting the range of dynamics they can recover. Here, we present a new framework that reconciles these two perspectives by reformulating inference as a stochastic control problem. Our method uses geometry-driven path augmentation, guided by structure in the system’s invariant density to reconstruct likely trajectories and infer the underlying dynamics without assuming specific parametric models. Applied to overdamped Langevin systems, our approach accurately recovers stochastic dynamics even from severely undersampled data, outperforming existing methods in synthetic benchmarks. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating geometric inductive biases into stochastic system identification methods, with broad applications across physics, biology, and control.

paragraphs: Learning a stochastic system’s dynamics is difficult when observations are separated by large time gaps. Much of the motion between measurements is unseen. The paper addresses a gap between methods that require frequent measurements and geometric approaches whose arguments apply only to conservative systems, seeking to recover dynamics from sparse observations.

The authors reformulate inference as a stochastic control problem. Their method augments the observed data with likely intervening paths, using structure in the invariant density to guide that reconstruction. This density describes where the system tends to be found over time. Its geometry supplies information about plausible paths without requiring a specific parametric model of the underlying dynamics.

Applied to overdamped Langevin systems, the framework accurately recovers stochastic dynamics from severely undersampled data and outperforms existing methods on synthetic benchmarks. The findings show how geometric information can assist inference when temporal information is scarce. The paper presents this combination of trajectory reconstruction and geometric guidance as useful for stochastic system identification, with potential applications across physics, biology, and control.
summary.tldr: A stochastic-control framework uses invariant-density geometry to reconstruct likely paths and recover Langevin dynamics from sparsely sampled observations.

title: From geometry to dynamics: Learning overdamped Langevin dynamics from sparse observations with geometric constraints

abstract: Ensembles of neural networks typically outperform individual networks but incur large computational costs, whereas weight aggregation produces less costly, yet also less accurate, aggregate models. We introduce partial fusion of networks, which interpolates between ensembles and weight aggregation and thus allows for a flexible tradeoff between computational cost and performance. A direct way to achieve this is to extend existing weight aggregation methods based on neuron-level similarity between different networks, where partial fusion then only aggregates weights of neurons which are most similar. We showcase one particular method to jointly identify which neurons are most similar and match them via partial optimal transport. Further, we consider the more general perspective of weight aggregation and partial fusion as generalized pruning of ensemble models, where neurons cannot just be deleted, but also linearly combined. Finally, we show that generalized pruning applied to a single network yields similar benefits as partial fusion by allowing for a tradeoff between isolating, deleting, and linearly combining neurons based on similarity.

paragraphs: An ensemble runs several neural networks to gain predictive performance, but that benefit comes with additional computation. Combining their weights into a single aggregate model reduces cost while typically sacrificing accuracy. Partial fusion introduces intermediate choices, allowing some neurons to be merged while others remain separate.

The guiding principle is similarity: neurons that behave most similarly across networks are candidates for aggregation. The authors present a method based on partial optimal transport that jointly identifies these similarities and matches the neurons to merge. This provides a way to adjust the balance between keeping the ensemble’s distinct components and reducing repeated computation through shared components.

The paper also interprets partial fusion as a broader form of pruning. Under this view, neurons can be deleted or linearly combined, expanding the available operations beyond removal alone. Applying this generalized pruning to a single network produces similar benefits, with tradeoffs among retaining separate neurons, deleting them, and combining them according to similarity. The contribution is a flexible framework connecting ensemble compression, weight aggregation, and network pruning.
summary.tldr: Partial fusion merges similar neurons while retaining others, creating flexible efficiency–performance tradeoffs between full ensembles and weight aggregation.

title: Partial Fusion of Neural Networks: Efficient Tradeoffs Between Ensembles and Weight Aggregation

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

paragraphs: A language model can encode the correct answer internally yet still choose the wrong option on a multiple-choice question. This paper studies that mismatch as a knowledge-prediction gap. The distinction matters because an incorrect response may reflect a failure to use available information, rather than an absence of that information in the model.

The authors first measure how prevalent and substantial the gap is across models and datasets. They then analyze the residual stream, the internal representations through which information passes across the model. Their geometric account identifies separate subspaces associated with knowledge and prediction, giving a concrete representation-level description of how the two can become misaligned.

KAPPA is a lightweight intervention applied during inference that aligns these subspaces within the residual stream. The reported results show that it reduces the gap across multiple-choice benchmarks and models, with generalization to free-form settings. The contribution combines an interpretable account of the mismatch with a practical intervention aimed at making outputs more faithful to information already represented internally.
summary.tldr: KAPPA aligns internal knowledge and prediction subspaces to help language models use answers they already encode.

title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions

abstract: While deep learning-based weather forecasting paradigms have made significant strides, addressing extreme weather diagnostics remains a formidable challenge. This gap exists primarily because the diagnostic process demands sophisticated multi-step logical reasoning, dynamic tool invocation, and expert-level prior judgment. Although agents possess inherent advantages in task decomposition and autonomous execution, current architectures are still hampered by critical bottlenecks: inadequate expert knowledge integration, a lack of professional-grade iterative reasoning loops, and the absence of fine-grained validation and evaluation systems for complex workflows under extreme conditions. To this end, we propose HVR-Met, a multi-agent meteorological diagnostic system characterized by the deep integration of expert knowledge. Its central innovation is the “Hypothesis-Verification-Replanning” closed-loop mechanism, which facilitates sophisticated iterative reasoning for anomalous meteorological signals during extreme weather events. To bridge gaps within existing evaluation frameworks, we further introduce a novel benchmark focused on atomic-level sub-tasks. Experimental evidence demonstrates that the system excels in complex diagnostic scenarios.

The paper argues that progress in weather forecasting does not by itself resolve these diagnostic demands. Expert meteorological knowledge is integrated into this process. Their experiments report strong performance in complex diagnostic scenarios. The combined contribution is a specialist reasoning architecture and an evaluation approach that examines the smaller tasks involved in carrying out an extended meteorological diagnosis.
summary.tldr: HVR-Met combines meteorological expertise with repeated hypothesis testing and replanning for complex extreme-weather diagnosis.

abstract: The visual world offers a critical axis for advancing foundation models beyond language. Despite growing interest in this direction, the design space for native multimodal models remains opaque. We provide empirical clarity through controlled, from-scratch pretraining experiments, isolating the factors that govern multimodal pretraining without interference from language pretraining. We adopt the Transfusion framework, using next-token prediction for language and diffusion for vision, to train on diverse data including text, video, image-text pairs, and even action-conditioned video. Our experiments yield four key insights: (i) Representation Autoencoder (RAE) provides an optimal unified visual representation by excelling at both visual understanding and generation; (ii) visual and language data are complementary and yield synergy for downstream capabilities; (iii) unified multimodal pretraining leads naturally to world modeling, with capabilities emerging from general training; and (iv) Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables efficient and effective multimodal scaling while naturally inducing modality specialization. Through IsoFLOP analysis, we compute scaling laws for both modalities and uncover a scaling asymmetry: vision is significantly more data-hungry than language. We demonstrate that the MoE architecture harmonizes this scaling asymmetry by providing the high model capacity required by language while accommodating the data-intensive nature of vision, paving the way for truly unified multimodal models.

Together, the findings offer empirical guidance on representation, data mixture, and architecture choices for unified multimodal pretraining.
summary.tldr: Controlled multimodal pretraining experiments reveal complementary benefits of language and vision, alongside different scaling needs that Mixture-of-Experts can accommodate.

title: Beyond Language Modeling: An Exploration of Multimodal Pretraining

abstract: Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) relies on retrieval from large-scale knowledge bases, yet this stage is often treated simplistically. Existing methods typically adopt single-view indexing or naive multi-view fusion, leading to systematic coverage gaps. In this work, we demonstrate that different views exhibit strong complementarity in retrieval. Motivated by this observation, we propose SCAR, a Structure-aware Cross-View Retrieval framework that exploits cross-view structural complementarity at inference time without additional training. SCAR enhances retrieval via structure-aware similarity propagation within each view and explicit cross-view redundancy regulation. Experiments on multiple KB-VQA benchmarks demonstrate that SCAR substantially improves retrieval recall, approaches retrieval coverage upper bounds, and consistently boosts end-to-end KB-VQA performance with negligible inference overhead.

paragraphs: Answering a question about an image sometimes requires facts from an external knowledge base. Retrieval determines which facts the answering system can use, so systematic omissions at this stage can limit the final answer. This paper finds that different retrieval views strongly complement one another: relevant information missed by one view can be covered by another.

SCAR uses this complementarity during inference without additional training. Within each view, it propagates similarity in a way that accounts for that view’s structure. Across views, it explicitly regulates redundancy. These two operations aim to make combined retrieval cover useful information more effectively than single-view indexing or a simple fusion of several views.

Across multiple knowledge-based visual question answering benchmarks, SCAR substantially improves retrieval recall and approaches the retrieval coverage upper bounds considered in the study. It also consistently improves the complete question-answering system with negligible inference overhead. These results connect a change in how evidence is retrieved to better final answers, showing that retrieval organization itself can be a productive improvement point.
summary.tldr: SCAR combines complementary retrieval views using structural similarity and redundancy control, improving knowledge-based visual question answering without additional training.

title: Beyond Single-View Indexing: Structure-Aware Multi-View Retrieval for Knowledge-Based VQA

abstract: It is increasingly common in machine learning to use learned models to label data and then employ such data to train more capable models. The phenomenon of weak-to-strong generalization exemplifies the advantage of this two-stage procedure: a strong student is trained on imperfect labels obtained from a weak teacher, and yet the strong student outperforms the weak teacher. In this paper, we show that the potential improvement is substantial, in the sense that it affects the scaling law followed by the test error. Specifically, we consider students and teachers trained via random features ridge regression (RFRR). Our main technical contribution is to derive a deterministic equivalent for the excess test error of the student trained on labels obtained via the teacher. Via this deterministic equivalent, we then identify regimes in which the scaling law of the student improves upon that of the teacher, unveiling that the improvement can be achieved both in bias-dominated and variance-dominated settings. Strikingly, the student may attain the minimax optimal rate regardless of the scaling law of the teacher—in fact, when the test error of the teacher does not even decay with the sample size.

paragraphs: A stronger model can sometimes learn from a weaker model’s imperfect labels and still outperform its teacher. This paper examines how large that advantage can become as sample size grows. It studies teachers and students trained with random-feature ridge regression, providing a mathematical setting for analyzing weak-to-strong generalization.

The main technical contribution is a deterministic equivalent for the student’s excess test error when its training labels come from the teacher. This expression allows the authors to identify regimes in which the student’s error follows a better scaling law. The improvement can occur when error is dominated by bias and when it is dominated by variance, broadening the settings in which the benefit appears.

In some regimes, the student may achieve the minimax-optimal rate even when the teacher’s test error does not decrease with sample size. This is a conditional result within the regression framework. It shows that imperfect supervision can support improvements in the rate of learning itself, beyond a fixed reduction in error.
summary.tldr: In identified random-feature ridge-regression regimes, a student trained on weak labels can achieve a better error scaling law than its teacher.

title: Improved Scaling Laws via Weak-to-Strong Generalization in Random Feature Ridge Regression

abstract: We introduce Equilibrium State Estimation (ESE), a novel paradigm for simultaneous prediction, where multiple interacting systems require separate yet coordinated forecasts. Such scenarios often arise in real-world such as economics and healthcare modeling. Unlike existing approaches that predict one system at a time, ESE forecasts all systems in a single pass. It first estimates the equilibrium state across systems, then generates holistic forecasts based on the difference between the current state and the estimated equilibrium. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including currency exchange and COVID-19 spread modeling, demonstrate that ESE is at least as accurate as state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while being significantly faster. In addition, ESE integrates seamlessly with conventional predictors, combining their accuracy with its exceptional efficiency and delivering a 10–70$\times$ speedup. With linear-time complexity, ESE scales far better than SOTA methods as the number of systems increases. Moreover, it remains accurate under diverse perturbations, establishing ESE as a fast, generalizable, robust, and scalable multi-prediction method.

paragraphs: Forecasting several interacting systems requires predictions that are individually useful and mutually coordinated. Equilibrium State Estimation, or ESE, addresses this by forecasting all systems in one pass. The setting includes problems such as currency exchange and disease spread, where predicting each system separately can create substantial computational work.

ESE first estimates an equilibrium across the systems. It then uses the difference between their current state and that estimated equilibrium to generate coordinated forecasts. This shared estimation step provides a common basis for prediction. The framework can also integrate with conventional predictors, combining their predictive capability with its simultaneous forecasting procedure.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report accuracy at least matching state-of-the-art methods alongside substantially faster execution. Integration with conventional predictors delivers reported speedups of 10–70 times. The method has linear-time complexity as the number of systems grows and remains accurate under the tested perturbations. These findings support equilibrium-based coordination as a scalable approach to forecasting multiple interacting processes.
summary.tldr: ESE uses an estimated shared equilibrium to forecast interacting systems together, achieving comparable accuracy with substantial reported speedups.

title: Once-for-All: Scalable Simultaneous Forecasting via Equilibrium State Estimation

abstract: Building Virtual Cells that can accurately simulate cellular responses to perturbations is a long-standing goal in systems biology. A fundamental challenge is that high-throughput single-cell sequencing is destructive: the same cell cannot be observed both before and after a perturbation. Thus, perturbation prediction requires mapping unpaired control and perturbed populations. Existing models address this by learning maps between distributions, but typically assume a single fixed response distribution when conditioned on observed cellular context (e.g., cell type) and the perturbation type. In reality, responses vary systematically due to unobservable latent factors such as microenvironmental fluctuations and complex batch effects, forming a manifold of possible distributions for the same observed conditions. To capture this variability, we introduce PerturbDiff, which shifts modeling from individual cells to entire distributions. By embedding distributions as points in a Hilbert space, we define a diffusion-based generative process operating directly over probability distributions. This allows PerturbDiff to capture population-level response shifts across hidden factors, improving generalization. Benchmarks on established datasets show that PerturbDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance in single-cell response prediction and generalizes substantially better to unseen perturbations. See our project page (https://katarinayuan.github.io/PerturbDiff-ProjectPage/), where code and data (https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/PerturbDiff) are publicly available.

paragraphs: Predicting cellular responses is difficult because single-cell sequencing destroys the measured cell. Researchers therefore observe separate control and perturbed populations rather than matched before-and-after measurements. Many models learn a mapping between these populations while assuming one response distribution for a given observed cell context and perturbation. The paper argues that hidden factors create systematic variation beyond that assumption.

PerturbDiff models entire response distributions as the objects that vary. It embeds probability distributions as points in a Hilbert space and defines a diffusion-based generative process over those points. This allows the same observed conditions to correspond to multiple possible population-level responses, accounting for variability associated with unobserved influences such as microenvironmental changes and complex batch effects.

The approach aims to capture shifts in the response population itself, rather than only variation among cells within one fixed response distribution. Benchmarks on established datasets show state-of-the-art single-cell response prediction and substantially better generalization to unseen perturbations. The results support representing uncertainty and variability at the distribution level when learning how cell populations respond.
summary.tldr: PerturbDiff generates distributions of cellular responses to capture hidden population-level variability and improve prediction of unseen perturbations.

title: PerturbDiff: Functional Diffusion for Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling

abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful paradigm for training autonomous agents and has achieved impressive performance in complex environments. However, this success often comes at the cost of interpretability, diminishing trust and complicating efforts to debug and improve agent behavior. To address these challenges, we introduce CausalXRL, a novel framework for explainable reinforcement learning (XRL). A key feature of CausalXRL is its use of causal graph reasoning, which provides transparent, structured, multi-level explanations of agent decision-making. We validate CausalXRL through comprehensive case studies and a two-part evaluation: (1) a quantitative analysis of explanation fidelity and causal-structure learning efficiency in benchmark RL environments, and (2) a qualitative expert study assessing explainability in the real-time strategy (RTS) benchmark MicroRTS. The quantitative results show that CausalXRL can provide faithful explanations while efficiently learning causal structures, and the qualitative expert study suggests that participants found CausalXRL useful for inspecting high-level RTS strategies.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can perform well while leaving its decisions difficult to understand. That makes inspecting behavior and identifying problems harder. CausalXRL addresses this interpretability problem through causal graph reasoning, producing structured explanations at multiple levels of an agent’s decision-making. The framework aims to make the relationships behind behavior available for inspection.

The evaluation separates two questions: whether explanations faithfully represent agent behavior, and whether people find them useful. Quantitative experiments in benchmark reinforcement learning environments assess explanation fidelity and the efficiency of learning causal structures. Case studies provide additional examination of the framework, while an expert study evaluates explanations in the real-time strategy environment MicroRTS.

The quantitative results indicate that CausalXRL can generate faithful explanations while learning causal structures efficiently. The qualitative study suggests that participants found it useful for inspecting high-level strategies. Together, these findings support both technical fidelity and practical interpretability in the evaluated settings. The human study specifically concerns understanding strategy, giving the explanation framework a concrete use beyond simply displaying a graph.
summary.tldr: CausalXRL uses causal graphs to explain agent decisions, with evidence of faithful explanations and expert usefulness for inspecting strategies.

title: CausalXRL: Explainable Reinforcement Learning through Causal Graph Reasoning

abstract: We propose DualOptim+, a novel optimization framework for improving machine unlearning in large language models. It introduces a base state to capture common representations shared by forgetting and retaining objectives and delta states to preserve objective-specific residuals. This architecture allows the optimizer to adaptively bridge shared and decoupled states based on the directional conflict between forgetting and retaining gradients. We further introduce DualOptim+ 8bit, a quantized variant that reduces memory overhead without compromising performance. Extensive experiments across fictitious and real-world unlearning, safety alignment, and multi-task learning tasks demonstrate that DualOptim+ consistently achieves a superior trade-off between different objectives. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU-MLO/DualOptimPlus.

It introduces a base state to capture common representations shared by forgetting and retaining objectives and delta states to preserve objective-specific residuals. We further introduce DualOptim+ 8bit, a quantized variant that reduces memory overhead without compromising performance. Extensive experiments across fictitious and real-world unlearning, safety alignment, and multi-task learning tasks demonstrate that DualOptim+ consistently achieves a superior trade-off between different objectives. paragraphs: Machine unlearning asks a language model to forget selected information while retaining other capabilities. Those objectives can push parameter updates in conflicting directions. DualOptim+ addresses this tension through the optimizer's internal state, providing a way to share information between objectives while preserving what is specific to each one.

The framework separates optimizer state into a common base and objective-specific delta states. The base captures representations shared by forgetting and retaining, while the deltas preserve their distinct residual components. The optimizer adapts the relationship between shared and separate states according to the directional conflict between the two gradients. This makes the degree of sharing responsive to the objectives' current interaction.

The authors also introduce an 8-bit variant that reduces memory overhead without compromising performance in their reported results. Experiments cover fictitious and real-world unlearning, safety alignment, and multi-task learning, with consistently better trade-offs between objectives. These findings suggest that managing common and objective-specific optimizer information can improve competing-objective training across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: DualOptim+ adapts shared and objective-specific optimizer states to improve the balance between forgetting and retaining information.

title: DualOptim+: Bridging Shared and Decoupled Optimizer States for Better Machine Unlearning in Large Language Models

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, standard actor-critic methods, such as PPO, rely on scalar value functions that estimate only the expectation of cumulative returns. This reduction inherently discards higher-order statistical information (e.g., variance and multimodality), leading to inaccurate value estimation and suboptimal credit assignment in complex tasks. While Distributional RL offers a solution by modeling the full return distribution, its application to LLMs remains challenging due to the computational intractability of value-based operations over large vocabularies and the instability and memory burden of off-policy replay mechanisms. In this paper, we propose DisPPO, a novel on-policy framework that seamlessly integrates non-parametric quantile regression into PPO. Theoretically, we prove that our distributional update operator—composed of the $\lambda$-return Bellman operator and quantile projection—is a contraction mapping in the Wasserstein metric, guaranteeing convergence to a unique fixed point. Empirically, we evaluate DisPPO using Llama and Qwen models across diverse benchmarks, including mathematical reasoning and Text-to-SQL generation. DisPPO consistently outperforms standard PPO and recent group-based baselines in both Pass@1 and Pass@$k$ metrics, demonstrating that distributional critics provide a richer, more robust learning signal for large-scale reasoning models.

paragraphs: Standard PPO training uses a critic that summarizes future cumulative reward with a single expected value. That summary discards information about how outcomes vary or cluster into different possibilities. DisPPO gives the critic a richer description of possible returns, aiming to improve the learning signal used to assign credit during language-model reasoning.

The method integrates nonparametric quantile regression into an on-policy PPO framework. Quantiles describe different positions within a return distribution instead of reducing it to one mean. This design addresses the vocabulary-scale computation and replay-related burdens that complicate applying distributional reinforcement learning to language models. The authors prove that their distributional update operator contracts under a Wasserstein distance and converges to a unique fixed point.

Experiments with Llama and Qwen cover mathematical reasoning and text-to-SQL generation. DisPPO outperforms standard PPO and recent group-based methods on both single-attempt and multiple-attempt success metrics. These results support distributional critics as useful learning signals; the operator convergence theorem concerns the specified distributional update, rather than establishing convergence of the entire language-model training process.
summary.tldr: DisPPO improves language-model reinforcement learning by estimating return distributions through quantiles instead of using only expected returns.

paragraphs: Tangent Distance is a method for invariant pattern classification, but conventional use requires tangent vectors to be available beforehand. The paper identifies obtaining those vectors as difficult for objects beyond images. It aims to extend the approach to more general classification tasks by changing how the required variation information is represented.

The basic assumption is that pattern variations can approximately represent tangent vectors. The authors introduce three probabilistic models for encoding those variations: a linear subspace model, a nonlinear subspace model, and a manifold subspace model. They bring these alternatives together in a common framework called Probabilistic Tangent Subspace.

Experiments on non-image datasets show promising classification performance. These results support the proposed extension in settings where conventional tangent vectors are difficult to obtain. The framework's significance lies in connecting the needed tangent information to modeled pattern variations, with three related modeling choices organized under one view and the approximation assumption remaining central to the approach.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic Tangent Subspace extends tangent-based classification by assuming pattern variations can approximate tangent vectors.

title: Probabilistic tangent subspace: a unified view

abstract: We study an approach for performing concurrent activities in Markov decision processes (MDPs) based on the coarticulation framework. We assume that the agent has multiple degrees of freedom (DOF) in the action space which enables it to perform activities simultaneously. We demonstrate that one natural way for generating concurrency in the system is by coarticulating among the set of learned activities available to the agent. In general due to the multiple DOF in the system, often there exists a redundant set of admissible sub-optimal policies associated with each learned activity. Such flexibility enables the agent to concurrently commit to several subgoals according to their priority levels, given a new task defined in terms of a set of prioritized subgoals . We present efficient approximate algorithms for computing such policies and for generating concurrent plans. We also evaluate our approach in a simulated domain.

It assumes an action space with multiple degrees of freedom, giving the agent the capacity for concurrent behavior. New tasks are expressed as collections of subgoals with different priorities, so planning must account for their relative importance.

The central idea is to combine previously learned activities through coarticulation. Multiple degrees of freedom often allow several admissible, though suboptimal, policies for the same activity. This flexibility gives the agent alternative ways to pursue an activity while also committing to other subgoals. Concurrency can emerge by selecting compatible behavior from these alternatives.

The authors provide efficient approximate algorithms for computing such policies and assembling concurrent plans, and evaluate the approach in a simulated domain. The contribution shows how flexibility within learned activities can support their combination. Its scope depends on the stated action-space assumption and on the available policy alternatives, rather than implying that arbitrary activities can always run together.
summary.tldr: Coarticulation combines flexible policies for learned activities to pursue prioritized subgoals concurrently in suitable Markov decision processes.

title: Coarticulation: an approach for generating concurrent plans in Markov decision processes

abstract: This paper presents several novel generalization bounds for the problem of learning kernels based on a combinatorial analysis of the Rademacher complexity of the corresponding hypothesis sets. Our bound for learning kernels with a convex combination of p base kernels using L_1 regularization admits only a \sqrt{\log p} dependency on the number of kernels, which is *tight* and considerably more favorable than the previous best bound given for the same problem. We also give a novel bound for learning with a non-negative combination of p base kernels with an L_2 regularization whose dependency on p is also*tight* and only in p^{1/4}. We present similar results for L_q regularization with other values of q, and outline the relevance of our proof techniques to the analysis of the complexity of the class of linear functions. Experiments with a large number of kernels further validate the behavior of the generalization error as a function of p predicted by our bounds.

paragraphs: Learning a kernel from multiple base kernels adds flexibility, but it also raises questions about performance on unseen data. This paper develops generalization bounds for that problem by analyzing the Rademacher complexity of the resulting predictor classes. Its central concern is how the number of available kernels affects the bounds.

For a convex combination of p base kernels with L1 regularization, the bound depends on p through only √log p. The authors show this dependence is tight and substantially better than the previous best bound for the same problem. For nonnegative combinations with L2 regularization, they establish a tight dependence of p to the one-quarter power.

The paper gives related results for other Lq regularizers and discusses how its proof techniques apply to classes of linear functions. Experiments with many kernels support the predicted behavior of generalization error as p changes. The results clarify that expanding the kernel collection can have a much milder complexity cost than earlier bounds suggested, particularly under L1 regularization.
summary.tldr: Tight generalization bounds show mild dependence on the number of learned base kernels under L1 and L2 regularization.

title: Generalization Bounds for Learning Kernels

abstract: We consider the fully automated recognition of actions in uncontrolled environment. Most existing work relies on domain knowledge to construct complex handcrafted features from inputs. In addition, the environments are usually assumed to be controlled. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a type of deep models that can act directly on the raw inputs, thus automating the process of feature construction. However, such models are currently limited to handle 2D inputs. In this paper, we develop a novel 3D CNN model for action recognition. This model extracts features from both spatial and temporal dimensions by performing 3D convolutions, thereby capturing the motion information encoded in multiple adjacent frames. The developed model generates multiple channels of information from the input frames, and the final feature representation is obtained by combining information from all channels. We apply the developed model to recognize human actions in real-world environment, and it achieves superior performance without relying on handcrafted features.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in video requires understanding both what appears in a scene and how it changes over time. This paper addresses automated recognition in uncontrolled environments, where carefully designed visual features and assumptions about the setting can be restrictive. Its approach uses a convolutional neural network to construct features directly from the input.

The central change is to perform convolutions across three dimensions, incorporating time alongside the spatial dimensions of an image. Processing multiple neighboring frames together allows the model to capture motion information within its learned features. The model also produces multiple channels of information from the frames and combines them into a final representation for recognizing actions.

The authors apply this model to human actions in real-world environments and report superior performance without handcrafted features. The stated result supports learning spatial and temporal representations together for this task. The contribution is an architecture that makes motion part of feature construction, while retaining the automation that motivates convolutional networks.
summary.tldr: A 3D convolutional network learns spatial and temporal video features for human action recognition without handcrafted features.

title: 3D Convolutional Neural Networks for Human Action Recognition
